mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on the subject of global warming, on which ignorance goes hand in hand with very strong judgments, i shall confine myself to a few questions. first question: is there really significant and sustainable warming? this now seems to be firmly established, particularly by measurements made on ocean masses or on large glaciers. secondly, does this warming have only negative effects? this is not necessarily the case in siberia, for example, where the taiga and tundra could give way to other landscapes, but it is certainly different in the case of the terrible progress of desertification in africa or weather disasters such as el niño. thirdly, if we decide to combat this phenomenon, is it certain that it is mainly due to human activity? there have been at least four warming and freezing periods in the quaternary that could not be attributed to man. fourthly, if the warming is due to the release of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere from the human combustion of fossil organic energy sources, then action is certainly needed, but is it worthwhile for western europe to make an effort at the expense of its own competitiveness, while other powers, such as the united states and china, the world's first and second largest polluters, wash their hands of it, thus jeopardizing the success of the operation, despite the encouraging information from some americans that the previous speaker has just given us? finally, fifth and last, systematic reforestation and the use of renewable or new energy sources must be encouraged. but be realistic, it will take a long time before they are sufficient for the needs. in the meantime, should we not, even from an ecological point of view, consider diversifying energy sources, particularly nuclear energy? the french national front, 25 years ago, was the first political force to legitimately draw attention to the risks of nuclear energy, a prediction which was unfortunately confirmed by the chernobyl disaster. but as science advances and technology can evolve, fusion would use the material without leaving the sustainably hazardous waste of current processes. and until we get there, even in the fission process, there may be elements, like thorium, that are less dangerous than the ones we know today. this is certainly the way science can go. it requires considerable effort and it must be free from dogmatism.

on behalf of the group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there is one word missing from this constitution: the word 'sovereignty'. it is replaced by the word 'identity'. it is not the same thing at all, because, in all corners of the world, as we know, there are peoples who are strong in their identity and who demand, precisely, sovereignty: the palestinians, the iraqis, so many others. but now, in europe, there will be peoples who, at a time when they are threatened with losing their identity with the entry of turkey into the european union, will lose their sovereignty with the constitution. one word has disappeared, the word 'sovereignty', another has appeared, the word 'law', european law, a word which is the very symbol of national democracies. there will therefore be a european law, which will now be legally superior to national laws, even constitutional ones. so our constitution will become for each of our peoples the equivalent of the internal rules of a region of europe. this supranational european law will now be adopted by majority vote and not by unanimity. so there is no longer any possibility of opposition from a particular people, even to defend its vital interests. thirdly, this supranational european law will be produced by a brussels bureaucracy which sees itself as having the attributes of a state. this bureaucracy becomes a full-fledged international actor, which will have the right to conclude international agreements, it will have a minister of foreign affairs - the word does not mislead - it will benefit from the transfer, in its heritage of attributions, of the powers of a superstate: definition of rights, definition of public services, immigration and border issues. at the same time, and this is my last word, national democracies will be trampled underfoot. the national parliaments are being deprived of the power to legislate. in compensation, they are given the right to give opinions.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, mr council representative, ladies and gentlemen, i have the honour to inform parliament that the green paper on economic migration which i presented by common accord with my colleague, commissioner spidla, has been adopted today by the college. with this green paper, the commission wishes to contribute to the ongoing debate, which began with the tampere mandate, on the most appropriate approach to the admission of economic migrants and the added value of adopting such a common framework. in the context of the hague programme, the european council invited the commission to present, before the end of 2005, a proposal for a common european approach to legal immigration for economic reasons. the commission sent a proposal to the council on this subject three years ago, but no action was taken because of the reluctance of several member states to approach the problem from a community perspective. however, the changes which have taken place on the international scene, the need for europe to manage the migration phenomenon in a balanced way and its many political, social and security implications, and the signing of the constitutional treaty which clearly distinguishes between matters which fall within national competence and those which also or exclusively have a community dimension, are all factors which have prompted the council to reflect on this matter in a timely manner and have put it back on the agenda. the hague strategy sets objectives and a timetable which the commission intends to respect. it goes without saying that the preparation of a proposal in this area requires a broad, comprehensive and transparent debate, and above all the participation of the institutional and social actors in the search for evaluations, proposals and contributions. the authorities responsible for the investigations and the police forces cannot have all the information they need to draw up a picture of the local situation, of the migration flows from different parts of the world to each european country, and of the integration conditions already achieved or to be promoted for communities of non-community citizens who already reside in the union or who are moving there. the aim of the green paper is therefore to gather new and updated information by launching a public debate involving as many stakeholders as possible, including civil society, who are interested in a new european strategy on economic migration. the commission is invited to propose a strategy before the end of 2005 which we must regard as the cornerstone of a wider political project capable of preventing, combating and eradicating intolerance, violence and all forms of extremism. these are the causes of the feeling of insecurity felt by our fellow citizens and they must be combated, not just by military or police action. on the contrary, we must also take political action and start planning initiatives to manage the flow of increasing economic emigration that inevitably flows into our countries and which sometimes constitutes an undeniable benefit for the european economy. finally, the public debate which the commission is launching with its green paper will enable it to collect a mass of data and information on which it can base itself in order to draw up the proposals which the council asks it to make and which we will present within the deadlines which have been set.

textile and clothing, which established a ten-year period for the elimination of the quotas, expired on 31 december 2004, and trade in textile and clothing products is henceforth subject to the general wto rules. quota removal is likely to reshape the export of textile and clothing and global outsourcing trends. there may be a substitution effect among suppliers to the advantage of the countries that are able to offer a full range of products, economies of scale, competitive prices and efficient services. the impact of abolishing quotas will indeed be considerable, though it is difficult to assess at this stage. moreover, it is likely to vary greatly depending on country conditions, the ability to achieve competitive advantages in the higher value added production segment challenges in the sector. as far as europe is concerned, this sector definitely has assets for the future. investment, a move upmarket and world leadership in the fashion industry have made europe the sector strengthen its competitiveness and remain a key industry in the eu, and keep a special focus on the poorest and more vulnerable developing countries. the commission communication of 13 october mr president, i would like to thank you. when i voted for the corbett report, i thought that this constitution was not the end of history, but that it was not the result of chance either. i first thought of the long struggles which accompanied the european convention on human rights in 1949 and the turin social charter in 1961, supported by all the trade union forces. these are now contained in part 2 of the constitutional treaty through the charter of fundamental rights. but i thought especially of the father, the real father of the constitution, the one who is not mentioned enough, altiero spinelli, a member of the communist youth, who was put under house arrest for ten years by mussolini, and who foreshadowed today's text from the very beginning of the first term of this european parliament elected by universal suffrage. i also thought of olivier duhamel, who inspired us during the previous mandate to hold an open convention to implement this constitutional treaty, and i thought that a man of the left could today, without any feeling, lend his support to this draft constitutional treaty, which opens a promising page in the history of the union.
in writing. - i welcome the progress made by the constitutional treaty in the field of development and international solidarity, the principle of which is enshrined among the fundamental values of the union. for the first time, the treaty includes a separate chapter on cooperation with third countries and humanitarian aid. it emphasises the specific objectives of this policy, namely the eradication of poverty, the promotion of health and the fight against infectious diseases. it gives priority to the rights of the child. it has made many advances in the field of women's rights and their decisive role in development. the european union is therefore taking an important step forward by recognising in its constitutional treaty that solidarity cannot be limited to its own territory and its own citizens, but must extend beyond its borders. of course, i have some regrets, not least the lack of reference to the 'global public goods' on which i had made proposals. but i intend to continue the fight with my socialist comrades to put into practice what we have not been able to put into the treaty.
in writing. i abstained from voting on this report for several reasons. firstly, i cannot vote in favour of this resolution, since my criticisms of the constitution are far greater than the very few and weak advances it contains. beyond my serious doubts about the achievement of social and political europe, my first complaint is that a constitution organizes the powers and lists the rights and duties of citizens. the constitutional treaty defines policies and ideological choices which do not belong to a constitution; they forbid any possibility of different policies. moreover, the report was prepared with the sole aim of mentioning only the positive and "advanced" aspects of the constitution. the ban on criticism, however slight, is in contrast to the reservations which parliament expressed when it adopted its previous resolution on the intergovernmental conference. i am not sure that this resolution or this treaty will bring our fellow citizens closer to the construction of europe and to their demands for justice, equality and democracy.
in writing. the corbett report, on which the european parliament was voting today, recognises the undeniable progress of the treaty establishing a constitution for europe. the treaty provides the essential tools for making europe more efficient, more readable and more democratic, by clarifying the role of the institutions, reducing the possibilities of blocking and increasing the powers of the european parliament and its representatives elected by the people. at the same time, it strengthens community solidarity and contributes to ensuring genuine cohesion in the union. social cohesion first of all, thanks to the charter of fundamental rights, which lays down rules on civil, political and social rights. the treaty also affirms europe's objectives in the direction of a social market economy, sustainable development and the fight against discrimination. secondly, territorial cohesion through a set of provisions which will help the regions of the union to pursue their own development. from the point of view of the octs, and more particularly of the french overseas departments, the treaty reaffirms the recognition of their specific features. by consolidating the mechanisms for derogating from community rules, it guarantees genuine protection for the french overseas departments against the destructive logic which would tend to regard europe as a uniform and homogeneous territory. in writing. it is not a report that we are voting on today, it is an act of faith and even an act of bad faith. contrary to what you say, mr president, this text creates a super-state, centralized, omnipotent, totalitarian, but without identity or soul. the european union is a centralised state, because everything is decided in brussels, in all areas, and all decisions, whether legislative or not, national or local, must be in accordance with european laws and the exclusive interests of the union. the principle of subsidiarity will continue to be flouted, as it has been for the past 12 years. the european union is becoming an omnipotent state, because it is becoming competent in absolutely all areas and all policies are or will be communitarianised. the european parliament has been a totalitarian state, because the real power is in the hands of a handful of officials: the technocrats in the commission who have a monopoly on legislative initiative and the judges in luxembourg, the controllers of the europeanist orthodoxy. the common feature is that they are appointed and are not subject to any democratic control. finally, a state without a soul or identity, which denies its christian-hellenic roots, accepts to integrate turkey despite the opposition of the people, believes only in globalisation, competition and the market. so today, as in the referendum held in my country, i am voting no.

for the gue/ngl group mr president, mr president of the council, mr president of the commission, the european union has been slow to recognise the failure of the lisbon strategy in the light of the objectives set for the year 2000. i have had the opportunity to quote here from a report by the commission last january. he pointed out that in the course of the march towards full employment, more jobs had been destroyed than created in the past year for the first time in ten years. as for the construction of a knowledge-based economy, the same report noted that it was in fact reflected in an "overall decline" in public and private investment in the key areas for the future of training, education and research. the report also revealed that more than one in six young europeans, at the age of 15, did not have, i quote, 'the minimum skills required: reading, writing, arithmetic'. it was a harsh but clear-sighted observation. the remedies that have been announced since then, namely to go faster and further along the liberal path, appear to us to be profoundly wrong and extremely dangerous. the key word here is competitiveness. but what conception of competitiveness is this? the one at work in the union is based on falling wage costs, flexible labour markets, longer working hours. it creates wage, social and fiscal competition between the 25 countries themselves. it considers the democratic achievements of the labour code as obstacles. it encourages the reduction of public expenditure and the strict and restrictive regulation of services of general economic interest. the health and environmental requirements themselves are at risk - this has just been said - of being revised downwards in the name of competitiveness, as is the case in the reach programme. the cultural exception to the competition rules is on the table for the same reason. this is probably what mr barroso had in mind when he referred to the friendly business environment in the report which was given to us. i am convinced that this liberal orientation, this race to say the least, runs counter to the official objectives of the lisbon agenda. it counters them, firstly, because fiscal and wage austerity contribute to the stagnation of consumption - the essential engine of growth - and play against employment. secondly, because this restrictive policy is weighing in favour of the necessary increases in expenditure for men and women, starting with training, this increasingly crucial need. finally, because this obsession with the market, with the financialization of the economy, with competition for everything, breaks an essential, if not decisive, principle of the proper functioning of the economy and of society, namely the motivation of people, their creativity, their confidence in the future. mr barroso, you yourself have said in your communication that a significant part of european public opinion is not convinced that europe is on the right track. i think it is a litte. so what do you do? among the immediate measures, we believe that public deficits should be excluded from the evaluation of expenditure on research, education, health, even expenditure on certain infrastructures, as well as expenditure on employment. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european union. in addition, as parliament has expressly requested, we believe it necessary to have a serious assessment of the effects of liberalizations, such as rail, before any new steps are taken, and we of course reiterate our request for the bolkestein directive to be withdrawn. i would point out, mr president, that for the first time this draft directive is no longer mentioned in a commission text, except in my own case. i would like to believe that this is equivalent to your accepting the request for withdrawal, but given what is at stake, a confirmation of this change from the president of the commission himself would be welcome. finally, we believe that structural changes are needed to move towards a common control of the markets and, therefore, towards a return to the primacy of political choice. i am thinking, for example, of choices that emphasize job security or training, which is available to all and which prepares for employment. the means must also be provided, and this raises the question of the tasks and the status of the european central bank. mr president, mr barroso has just stressed the need to be aware of the concerns of the citizens, and i think that many of the concerns i have mentioned are shared far beyond the circles closest to my group. the commission would therefore be well advised not to ignore them.

mr president, the most infamous of hitler's concentration camps, auschwitz, was officially opened on 14 june 1940. it was then intended for polish political prisoners whom the nazis wished to treat with particular harshness. the camp is headed by a former common law criminal who, in 1946, boasted of having exterminated three million people. he will be gassing up to 6,000 victims a day from 1942, mostly jews from all over europe. as soon as we arrive, we sort and weed out those too weak to work. the others are used up to the point of exhaustion. during the summer of 1944, the nazis resorted to mass shooting to kill more jews. russian prisoners of war were also exterminated at auschwitz, roma, homosexuals, the disabled, anti-fascist resistance fighters. auschwitz will again provide subjects for experiments on living beings. an extension of the camp at birkenau was specially allocated for the extermination of the jews. the crematoria burned more than 20,000 corpses a day. here the majority of the jews brought from western europe and the balkans were killed. this would wipe out most of the jews of eastern europe, including nearly three million polish jews. with them was destroyed a world of traditions and culture that had now vanished. in any case, this genocide is fundamentally linked to anti-semitism and, more broadly, to nazi racism. hitler's worldview in particular was of paramount importance based as it was on the obsession with racial purity. hitler's racism was genocidal from the start. besides the jews, other peoples, such as the gypsies and the slavs, were exposed to the deadly effects of this racism. hitler said they all deserved to die. it was in february 1940 that the deadly gas zyclon b was tested on 250 roma children, and then began the massive agony, hunger, cold, exhausting work, diseases, brutality, pseudo-medical experiments; the last 4,000 gypsies were gassed and burned on august 1, 1944 to make way for new deportees. will there ever be an end to anti-semitism, racism and xenophobia? they will probably disappear only when all the human families, faithful to their cultures and traditions, come together in a universal community. the jews have suffered and are still suffering, the minorities are often oppressed and suffer far too much. so fighting anti-semitism, fighting racism, is not fighting for the jews, it's not fighting for minorities, it's fighting for humanity.

president of the commission. mr president, distinguished members of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, before i address you all on the european commission's legislative and work programme for 2005, i would like to convey briefly my satisfaction with the results of the referendum on the european constitution held in spain yesterday, and i will try to do so in spanish. the spanish people have said a clear and resounding yes to the european constitution. (applause) i would like to thank i would like to express to you the european commission's satisfaction with this result. spain has said yes to a europe united in its diversity. i would like to thank all those who have participated in the referendum process with their commitment, in particular all the members of this parliament who have contributed their voice and opinion to this important result. in this connection, i called yesterday the president of the spanish government, josé luis rodríguez zapatero, to congratulate him and to express my gratitude for the great commitment shown by his government in the conduct of the electoral campaign. this clear and unambiguous 'yes' opens the way for the rest of the european citizens who will also be called upon to express their views on the european constitution in the coming months. this was a very important step in the process of ratifying the european constitution, which the commission considers to be a unique instrument which will enable all europeans to consolidate our ideas of peace, prosperity, solidarity and security in europe. mr president, one month ago i presented the commission's proposed strategic objectives, designed to guide european action until the end of the decade. this is a political roadmap based on three pillars: prosperity, solidarity and security. being mutually reinforcing, they address the concrete and challenging concerns of european citizens. i also presented the first delivery of the strategic objectives: the legislative work programme for this year. let me remind you of some of its most important elements. first of all, the programme is more focused in political terms. the proposed initiatives are structured around the three strategic objectives and their external dimension, and represent the first concrete translation of the balanced approach pursued by the commission. this applies to new initiatives as well as areas where we propose to reinforce an existing action. second, the commission is fully committed to delivering its work programme. to this end, the commission intends to adopt a list of just over 100 priority initiatives by the end of the year. finally, we do not only want to deliver on time we also want to deliver in a better way. we want to be serious about the principles of better regulation. this means ensuring quality of legislation; respect for the principles of proportionality, subsidiarity and added value; and widespread use of impact assessments. in addition to this work programme, i announced that the commission will regularly inform parliament about its planning agenda for legislative proposals in preparation. i am happy to be able to say that this information channel is now operational. in the meantime, the commission has gone further in implementing its proposals. on 2 february, i presented to you our proposals for a mid-term review of the lisbon strategy. by focusing on growth and jobs, it aims to create the conditions for proper living standards, social justice for all and environmental sustainability. on 6 january and 2 february we had an initial exchange of views. i was pleased to hear that, broadly speaking, the commission's proposals met many of the expectations and concerns of members of this house. i welcome the detailed motions for resolutions tabled today by the political groups on the work programme. when we talk about partnership, dialogue and consultation, we know that we will not always agree on everything. as in any partnership, the important thing is to have positions on the table clearly spelt out, and to work together to achieve common objectives. i would like to comment briefly on some of the important issues raised in the comments and motions for resolutions. first, actions count more than words. the european union has a responsibility to turn its aspirations into reality. it must promote prosperity, cohesion and social justice, both at home and beyond our borders. the commission is fully committed to this task. we have already started to work towards this goal by implementing our work programme for 2005: we are on track. second, competitiveness and social cohesion need to go hand in hand. we all know that striking a balance is difficult. i want the commission to be helpful in this regard. this requires listening carefully to your opinions and contributions. take the reach initiative, for example. let me assure you that we have taken due note of the concerns expressed. we all agree on the need to protect the safety of individuals and the environment properly. on the other hand, we should also address the fear that certain elements of the proposal would put a key european industry in serious difficulty without adding real value in the fields of health and the environment. throughout the legislative process, we will continue to look at further possibilities to refine and improve the balance between regulation and competitiveness. with regard to the draft services directive, here too we are pursuing an aim which commands general support the completion of the single market for services by 2010. again i can assure you that we have taken due note of the concerns expressed. i am fully convinced that, via the legislative process, we will be able to settle upon an instrument which will tap the single market's hidden potential without jeopardising legitimate public interest objectives. let us do this on an informed basis and dispel the myths. our proposals do not call into question the responsibility of member states when it comes to organising and financing key public services as required by their societal needs, nor do they undermine the rules on the posting of workers as laid down in the directive. finally, i shall mention the stability and growth pact. the commission is committed to helping improve the pact and ensuring it fully complies with the treaty. the improvements proposed by the commission aim to increase its economic rationale and refine its implementation. we want better incentives to foster 'good policies' in 'good times'. we want a better definition of the medium-term objectives of fiscal policy by taking into account elements such as the debt level and the up-front costs of structural reforms. we want to avoid undesirable fiscal restraint in a downturn, because, ultimately, we want our budgets to be in a position to enhance prosperity by focusing expenditure on growth-oriented sectors and by investing for the future. these are not academic issues this is about quality of life, people's opportunities to earn a living and reap the benefits of their savings and pensions. this is about the chances of current and future generations to lead as full a life as they can legitimately expect to. as part of this balanced approach, the commission has made progress through its recently adopted proposal on the revised social agenda for the period up to 2010. this shows the commission's full commitment to modernising and developing european social systems, tackling social exclusion and poverty, and achieving the target of more and better jobs. when liberalizing markets, individuals must not be forgotten. that is why last week we adopted two new proposals to strengthen passengers' rights. this brings me to a key issue: the european union needs to be given sufficient financial means to act. cohesion policy is and must remain central to the purpose of the union. without solidarity, we can never be united. it is an essential complement to competitiveness and the lisbon strategy raising prosperity levels in the less-developed regions of the union benefits the union as a whole. we should also bear in mind that there are now 25 member states. the new member states are waiting for tangible proof of our solidarity. this is why our proposals for a new generation of cohesion policies for the next financial perspective are of critical importance for the union, both economically and politically. we cannot afford to see our obligations in this area watered down. in addition, the commission is currently preparing its third package of proposals for the next financial perspective, which are based on a careful examination of their european added value with regard to providing citizens with opportunities that complement national approaches or fill existing gaps. this set of instruments will include proposals on the seventh framework programme for research and development; consumer protection and public health; energy including renewable energy sources; the next item is the recommendation for second reading by mrs corien wortmann-kool (a6-0013/2005) on the common position of the council with a view to the adoption of a directive of the european parliament and of the council on pollution caused by ships and the introduction of penalties for infringements.
the commission's vice-president mr president, i will try to be brief, but i still want to answer a couple of questions. firstly, i cannot allow that there is a contradiction between this draft directive and the marpol convention: that is totally wrong. marpol only provides for sanctions for those who have acted deliberately and those who have committed an unforgivable offence. but this same convention must be read in conjunction with the convention on the law of the sea: it gives the coastal states the opportunity to strengthen their measures to prevent and combat pollution in their territorial sea, and it is this provision which is contained in the convention on the law of the sea which we have invoked. since each member state can invoke it, the union can also do so. i have explained this to the secretary-general of the imo. so i do not understand this criticism: we are in compliance with the marpol convention and the law of the sea convention. i would add, as the rapporteur has very well said, that the sanctions are proportionate: it is a question of punishing serious negligence and it is of course a question of proportioning our sanctions. it is not a question of criminalising, mr president, but of making people accountable. i put a little passion into my words because i believe in this cause, which is that of our common heritage. so i am very kindly answering the question, of course, but is the honourable member not here? sanctions may be imposed on ships registered under the flags of third states when they enter a community port. on this side of the spectrum, there is no discrimination against european flags. that's what i'm talking about! i would add that not only do we not see any objection to this approach from the international maritime organisation, but we also want to cooperate, as i said to the secretary-general. we are building on the work of this maritime organisation which will also promote black boxes and has even set out a specific timetable for this. mr president, the conclusion of all this is that we have, after all, obtained a unanimous political agreement in the council. that is why i am warning parliament against this agreement which is being drawn up in europe with a large majority, achieved in the trilogue with the council. i would like to conclude by saying that we should not wait for the next disaster to suddenly become aware of what is happening and be accountable. so far, the law of the sea has progressed as disasters have arisen. well, this time, we have a tremendous chance of being able to prevent that. that is why i personally believe that this text is balanced, that it is not intended to criminalize anyone, but to make everyone responsible. i therefore thank parliament in advance, madam rapporteur, for its willingness to accept this text as far as possible. commission position on the amendments: see annex

the debate which has just ended, commissioner, has shown you how much my colleagues and i attach importance to the notion of the credibility of the common fisheries policy, either to strengthen it or - for some of my colleagues - to challenge it. in this challenge to the justification of a common fisheries policy, one of the arguments most frequently raised against us concerns the mass of discards that the current regulations lead our fishermen to make, discards of fish which, most of the time, will not survive their capture anyway. this problem has been a concern of our committee for years, as you know, and it has led your committee, in agreement with ours, to initiate the implementation of a few hundred study projects aimed at finding a solution if possible. that is why i have put this oral question to you on behalf of the committee which i have the honour of chairing. it is indeed - and i quote the text of this question - a global issue and one of the main problems of fisheries, for which there is at present no international action plan, either from fao or from anyone else. the adoption of an international plan for the reduction of by-catches is urgently needed and could play a key role in reducing by-catches at international level. many leading scientists and non-governmental organisations, specialists in the marine environment, advocate the adoption of such a reduction plan. in fact, several fao member states have already committed themselves to supporting such a proposal at the next meeting of the fao fisheries committee in march. no nation has yet committed itself to take the initiative of such a proposal. given that the european union is a leading fishing power, is the european commission prepared to take the initiative in proposing an international action plan on the reduction of by-catches? is the commission aware that if an international action plan is not on the agenda of fao in 2005, it will have to wait until the next session in 2007? i thank you, commissioner, for agreeing to come and answer this question and the supplementary questions which my colleagues will put to you.
member of the commission. mr president, firstly i would like to thank the members for all their comments and remarks. i will group the interventions into four points. first, the by-catch problem being a worldwide problem and the question of the commission taking leadership. as i said in my original response, we are willing to do so but we have to have the necessary resources made available to us because this will be a mammoth task. we will be taking the matter up with the council in the very short term. with regard to the forthcoming fao meeting, the commission, as i said before, is ready to support the development of an international plan of action on by-catch and again we will seek member states' agreement to convey this position to fao and its members during the forthcoming committee on fisheries meeting, in particular when the work programme for the short and medium-term will be discussed. with regard to discards, we are actively considering this problem and hopefully we will be coming up with specific proposals soon. another point concerned declining fish stocks and by-catch being all the more regrettable as a result. here i would like to say that one way in which the commission tries to reduce discards is by improving selectivity by technical measures such as enforcing minimum mesh sizes or closed areas which can limit the catches of juveniles. other measures such as the use of separator trawls or separator grids can reduce the by-catch of non-target species. well-applied technical measures can be effective but they are not without problems. for example, it is difficult to find the appropriate mesh size in mixed fisheries. the minimum mesh size needed to protect juvenile cod, for example, would be too big to catch adult haddock and whiting. nevertheless technical measures have a part to play. the commission intends to revise completely the technical measures regulation in 2005 to follow up its communication on environmentally-friendly fishing. to deal with mixed fisheries the commission tries to propose tacs to take into account associations between species. this is difficult to do but steps in this direction have already been taken. the commission has asked isis to give its advice on a fisheries basis rather than on a single stock basis. these are the first steps in adopting an ecosystem approach to fisheries management. another approach advocated by the commission is to manage the fisheries through effort control rather than rely on individual tacs. in principle it could be used instead of tacs, with fishermen allowed to land all catches, but in practice effort control will usually complement rather than replace tacs. at the end of 2002 the commission presented a discard action plan which discussed the problems of discards more fully and the ways in which the problem could be tackled. following up this plan, the commission will consult with member states and the industry during 2005 with a view to initiating a number of pilot projects to eliminate or at least reduce discards in selected fisheries. my final point concerning racs is that they can be involved and certainly we find no problem in involving racs in giving advice on the formulation of such plans.
thank you very much, commissioner. we have now exhausted our agenda. i wish everyone a very happy end to the evening.

mr president, mr president-in-office, commissioner, what prospects has the barcelona process opened up ten years later? during this period, europe invested heavily in its organisation and enlargement. she hasn't always paid her southern flank the attention it deserves. at the same time, the israeli-palestinian conflict has blocked the momentum of global development by capturing all the attention in this region. today, there is an urgent need to revitalise this process. tools have been put in place: association agreements, a neighbourhood policy and, above all, the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly, which is a major democratic step forward in this process. there is also the establishment of the anna lindh foundation to promote dialogue between cultures and civilizations. there is also the idea of creating a euro-mediterranean development bank to promote employment, health and education in the countries of the south. other civil society organisations are being set up. all these projects are progressing, but their effectiveness will depend on two imperatives. the first is to create a climate of political reform, and the people of the south are ready to support it. the second is to establish a just and lasting peace between israelis and palestinians. the current circumstances are favourable but very fragile. europe must be more involved. all these projects are converging towards more peace, more security and more shared prosperity, but far too slowly. europe has understood that there is no war of civilizations, but that an alliance of civilizations is necessary, because after having destroyed a wall in the east, europe must now build a bridge in the south.
mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, madam commissioner, the barcelona process is about to celebrate its tenth anniversary and peace in the middle east has never seemed so close. it is time to recall the objectives which are still relevant: the establishment of a common area of peace, stability and security; an area of shared prosperity; the rapprochement of peoples and cultures. as javier solanna pointed out in june 2004, this partnership is a strategic challenge for europe, provided that it is able to achieve its ambitions. firstly, the barcelona process must be the first pillar of the european neighbourhood policy, since this policy proposes to go much further than mere cooperation, to a certain degree of political and economic integration. the euro-mediterranean parliamentary assembly must be the democratic framework for this; it needs to be strengthened. the european presidency of apem must make it possible to consolidate a balanced partnership. let us talk about co-development based on a foundation of common values: democracy, good governance, the status of women, sustainable development, intercultural dialogue. finally, these objectives require europe to make its mediterranean policy a budgetary priority.

in writing. brussels likes agencies. there are those from everywhere, from the european environment agency in copenhagen to the european food safety agency in parma to the european agency for safety and health at work in bilbao. now there will also be a community fisheries control agency, a real european fisheries ministry. the task of this fbi at sea will be to coordinate the control and inspection activities of the states in the fisheries sector. it will be the arm of a control which has so far been very modest. this is the control that parliament wants in both community and international waters. multinational inspection teams at sea and on land will therefore be set up. the agency may charter and operate surveillance vessels which it shall make available to observers. but who are these agents ? inspectors from other countries, foreign to national regulations, which negates the specific competence of each member state. they will therefore be able to inspect without necessarily finding infringements, without necessarily improving control. the question of the territorial waters of sovereign countries is no longer merely to consolidate community sovereignty but also foreign sovereignty.
on behalf of the group. mr president, when we talk about hunger, we also talk, it seems obvious, about agricultural policy. we cannot, on the one hand, discuss the possibility of increasing development aid and, on the other, pursue agricultural policies which are contributing to worsening the situation in many countries. i will take one example: at the moment we are negotiating economic partnership agreements with the acp countries (africa, the caribbean and the pacific), which are causing a great deal of concern and even controversy as to the guidelines envisaged today. the discussions are almost exclusively focused on greater trade liberalization, indiscriminately, without taking account of local situations, whereas even today many of our countries' exports, at low prices and often subsidized, are contributing to the considerable destabilization of the peasantry in these countries. so i think that at the acp-eu joint assembly meeting in bamako in april all these issues will have to be discussed. i hope, on behalf of my group, that the european union's approach in this area will evolve in such a way as to bring much more coherence between what we are saying today on hunger and poverty and what we are saying elsewhere, in other fora, on agricultural policies and the liberalisation of trade in agricultural products. this is a very important question. let us begin by matching what we say on the one hand and what we do on the other, and i think we have already made some progress.

since the 1960s, the french textile and clothing sector has lost two thirds of its workforce, or about 20 000 jobs a year, and today we are suffering from 2 000 job cuts a month. in my own region of nord-pas-de-calais, which has historically been a textile region, towns such as elesmes, roubaix and tourcoing have seen their businesses close. the social situation is already dramatic and yet tomorrow it will be worse. until now, quotas have been used to limit imports of textiles from third countries, but since 1 january 2005 the door has been opened to massive imports from china. france and europe must now choose a strategy to defend their textile industry. it is urgent to demand safeguard clauses from the wto. this possibility is open to member states when there is a sudden increase in imports causing serious damage to a local industry. this is the case today in europe and in france. since the end of quotas on 1 january, imports have soared and the chinese rush is destroying whole sections of what remains of our textile industry. the increase in imports of trousers produced in china between 1 january 2005 and 2 february 2005 was 792% compared to the same period in 2004. companies, we must not wait until we see that our internal market is overwhelmed to demand a return to customs barriers and safeguard clauses. the extreme liberals who drew up article 314 of the mr president, mr president-in-office, madam commissioner, my colleagues have repeatedly reminded me that the textile industry represents more than two and a half million jobs, and i myself come from a region, nord-pas-de-calais, in france, which knows what it is talking about, because it is suffering greatly today from this loss of jobs. these figures show how useful and necessary it is to have a strategy in place to help the textile and clothing industry to overcome the changes associated with the end of quotas. we have only partial data at present, but it is already alarming. in europe, according to the statements of chinese importers, since the end of quotas on 1 january 2005, imports of several categories of textile products have doubled or even tripled. the union must have trade policy instruments to respond to sudden changes in imports. in this respect, commissioner, it is becoming very urgent that the commission publish the guidelines on the specific safeguard clause for textile products for china announced since october 2004, without which the industries throughout their countries will not be able to react. the eu is fulfilling its wto commitments. it is now necessary for all its members to respect these commitments. the textile and clothing market must remain an open competitive market. the european union must also be aware that many of the so-called vulnerable textile producing countries are also likely to be severely affected by this lifting of quotas. i am thinking of bangladesh, cambodia and our mediterranean neighbours. for almost a decade now, the european union has chosen a partnership that promotes the development of the euro-mediterranean area. the textile question therefore brings us closer than ever to the need to rapidly establish a genuine free trade area.
mr president, my colleagues have pointed out that the consequences of the abolition of quotas have been immediate and that the threat to the european textile and clothing industry is very real. i would also like to give you an example of my region, which is very much affected by the decline of the textile industry. the castres-mazamet basin acquired its industrial culture through the de-inking and leather industry. for several years now, smes in this sector have been closing one after another. some have been able to reconvert themselves through skills acquired in international trade, industrial techniques and the development of new products. but do we have the right to condemn those who wish to pursue their trade in textiles and clothing? mr president-in-office of the council, madam commissioner, do we not have a duty to protect the european textile and clothing industry? pending the implementation of the high level group proposals on which parliament will vote, the european union has defined a strategy to overcome the changes resulting from the disappearance of quotas, which seems to be expressed in concrete commitments: the elaboration of the draft protocol on textile rules of origin, the adoption of the guidelines on the china-specific safeguard clause for textiles, the establishment of the community preferences system, the likely setting of a 10% threshold to preserve the market share of traditional eu suppliers, negotiations at the wto to obtain substantial concessions from emerging countries that maintain high duties, as well as the maintenance of non-tariff barriers in textile matters, and finally the adoption of the strategic framework for the allocation of public funds, in order to improve the competitiveness and the timeliness of these public funds, and finally the implementation of the regional and local cohesion policy, in particular by improving the flexibility and the timeframe of the allocation of public funds.
mr president, the upheaval in the world textile and clothing industry is being felt most strongly in the european regions where textile production is highly concentrated. this is the case in my french region of nord-pas-de-calais, which has already been hit in recent years by restructuring and relocations and where this sector, the second largest industrial employer, still employs nearly 30 000 workers. in 2004, parliament, in a resolution, and the high level group on textiles and clothing called for a specific programme for this sector, particularly in the regions in difficulty, which have many smes and a high female employment rate. in these regions, european aid has in recent years helped to mitigate the socioeconomic consequences of sectoral crises, to preserve jobs and to cushion the effects of economic restructuring, in particular through innovation, integration, training and the development of modern industry. as the european union is drawing up its new financial perspective, these regions are worried about the future of the structural funds which have helped to bring about economic recovery. i am sure that the commission and the council will be anxious to reassure them and to prove to them that the economic and social cohesion to which these funds contribute is a priority for the european union.

the rapporteur. mr president, it is exactly five years since the european parliament, in an owninitiative report, embarked on a dialogue with the european investment bank. i was already your rapporteur five years ago and can therefore testify to the extraordinary progress made in these five years in the quality of the dialogue between the european investment bank and parliament, in the quality of this dialogue with civil society, in the adequacy of the policy of the european investment bank with the tasks entrusted to it at the outset of the european union. i would therefore like to begin by expressing my sincere thanks on behalf of all those of us who were already here during the previous parliamentary term and, i hope, on behalf of all those who will be interested today in the work and contribution of the european investment bank to the implementation of european policy. i would like to thank the eib's management for the dialogue we have had with them. it was a demanding dialogue, it was a rich dialogue, with real interaction on both sides. we have evolved in our perception of the eib, the eib has evolved in its own perception of its responsibilities. i should therefore like to take the few moments i have been given to summarize the unanimous report of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and to highlight the five most important points of our report, in questioning terms of course. firstly, we can no longer be satisfied with the talk about lisbon and gothenburg, we must now try to make progress in the definition of objectives. the eib recognises that it is there to support the policy of the european union; it needs to develop criteria and quantitative indicators in dialogue with parliament. secondly, we in parliament have been among the first to ask the european investment bank to lend to small and mediumsized enterprises. this can only be done through global loans, collectivized funds, lent to banks which themselves distribute these credits. in that case we risk losing control of the appropriateness of these appropriations for the objectives of the european union and it would be necessary to find a way of controlling the use of these global appropriations, ex post of course. thirdly, this policy of micro-credit must be able to extend to a very important area in a society which is both a knowledge-based economy and an ageing economy. i am talking about the third sector companies, which deal with aid to individuals, aid to families. fourth problem: a potential conflict emerged during the hearing we had organized. the european investment bank is making a great effort to provide local and regional authorities with cheap, long-term loans. these appropriations, however attractive, obviously run up against the limits of the stability pact. the tendency to circumvent this difficulty by means of loans to private enterprises but guaranteed by the state therefore obviously introduces a risk of going "off balance sheet". we suggest that the european investment bank should work with the ecb to establish ethical rules. finally, a final point: in the first version of my report, we included criticism in the press, from a certain press, mainly outside the european union, against possible conflicts of interest among the members of the eib's management, because of their past activities at the head of large private companies that could benefit from eib loans. since then, the eib has provided us with a whole series of new internal codes to avoid these conflicts of interest or at least to take them into account ex ante by eliminating them in advance. i therefore tabled an amendment which, i believe, was adopted by all the group coordinators or fictitious rapporteurs, to thank and record this clarification by the european investment bank after our vote in the committee on economic and monetary affairs.

the rapporteur's proposal for a transitional period until january 2006 seems to me the most reasonable one in this respect, especially when we know that these long and complex procedures have always limited the use of the scheme by poor countries. the european union must give priority to harmonizing the rules of origin at international level, particularly within the wto, even though i welcome the greater flexibility provided for in the text. developing countries have to adapt to the specific rules of origin of each country which gives them a preferential system, which makes the procedures very complicated and expensive, to the point of sometimes losing all commercial value. i would also like to stress that parliament asks the commission to monitor very closely the application of the new system in order to determine whether it is achieving the objectives set for it, and this country by country. the commission must regularly assess the system, monitor its implementation and keep parliament informed, which has not been done in the past. i would like to end by saying that the gsp is not one of the instruments designed to promote the development of the poorest countries and their full integration into international trade. if we really want to help poor countries to benefit from globalisation, we need to rethink the rules of global trade as a whole in a more equitable way, linking trade and sustainable development in our thinking.

in writing. the system of generalized tariff preferences for developing countries is a system of generalized preference for foreign trade, a customs disarmament of the european union. you claim that this system is good for the beneficiary countries. but you admit that the reform proposed today is not based on any assessment of the functioning and effectiveness of the previous system. the negative consequences for industry and agriculture in the european union are, however, foreseeable: - non-existent or preferential customs duties are granted to more products, exacerbating global competition for many sectors, including agriculture and fisheries. - the market share, beyond which a country is no longer entitled to benefit from customs preferences, is so high that it heralds the ruin of entire sectors of our industry. the textile sector, in particular, will be particularly affected, as it is being hit hard by the end of quotas. - the safeguards are still inadequate, bureaucratic and never applied... but as usual, the commission is concerned with the ultra-tradesman's ideology. it is not by impoverishing europe, by creating unemployment in europe, that the third world countries will be allowed to develop. that is why we shall vote against this report.
in writing. the commission has accelerated the reform of the generalised system of preferences, citing the urgency of supporting the economies of the countries affected by the tsunami of 26 december. the new system is due to come into force on 1 april. but in the face of this disaster, the people and the states of europe have shown that their generosity can be counted on. the commission, on the other hand, intends to make the european industry, especially the textile industry, pay the full price for its extravagance. the textile industry, although suffering from the increasingly unfair competition from china, still employs 2.5 million people in europe and generates a turnover of 230 billion. by requiring a threshold of 12.5% of community imports on these products to deprive a country of the benefit of gsp duties, the commission is imposing competition at reduced duties on indian textiles, which are considered competitive under the current gsp, whereas a 10% threshold would allow customs duties to be maintained, thus allowing for balanced competition despite wage and social disparities. it is anti-liberal to make a part of the economy pay for public aid, and it is anti-social to destroy hundreds of thousands of jobs in europe in this way.
in writing. the system of generalised tariff preferences is over 30 years old. its philosophical inspiration is older, since it actually dates back to the unctad of 1963, which created the concept of compensatory inequalities". what we would now call "positive customs discrimination". apparently, poor countries like peru and colombia have benefited from this by being able to send us their asparagus or shrimp duty-free. even if there were some traffic diversions through obscurity on the original rules. the gsp, like the whole gatt and wto system, is based on an inadequate paradigm: the reduction of customs duties to achieve their abolition. it would be more innovative to go to the deduction of customs duties. the exporter would benefit in the importing country from a customs credit equal to the customs duties borne and deductible on purchases to be made in the importing country. these customs credits could be mobilised on a stock market futures market. thus the problem of economic and social asymmetries would be solved and neutrality would exist in global trade.
in writing. the lisbon strategy had the stated objective of making europe the 'most competitive knowledge-based economy in the world' by 2010. it was a total failure. by contrast, brussels europe has succeeded in making the european union the least dynamic economy in the world, with a special mention for the even less successful eurozone. of course, this is not the fault of brussels. this europe never questions itself. so what do we do to get out of it? more europe, of course. more liberalization of markets, more regulatory constraints on businesses, fewer public services, more european and global competition, less public funding, less social protection... the social and environmental objectives of lisbon, first version, are over: there is room for 'all competition', 'all productivity'. man is a commodity. the market will reallocate it and take care of the unemployment ! what the barroso commission is proposing is a nightmare. oh, of course, the text is very "soft". it is just a programme and objectives, sometimes common sense. but we are accustomed to seeing in this chamber the actual text of the directives which implement these programmes and try to achieve these objectives. the bolkestein directive is a prime example of this!
in writing. we have to decide today on the mid-term evaluation of the lisbon strategy. at a time when 68 million of our citizens in the european union are still living in poverty, we can only confirm the lisbon strategy of 2000 and reaffirm the objective of eradicating poverty. progress has been made, such as the national plans for inclusion, the inclusion of the poverty reduction objective in the european charter of fundamental rights. but that is not enough, we must keep going, we owe it to our fellow citizens who are waiting for our promises to be fulfilled, and i insist that everything be done at the spring summit to that end.

on behalf of the alde group. mr president, the lisbon strategy, the stability and growth pact, the whole question of economic policy is at the heart of the next spring council. with unemployment reaching 9% in europe and growth forecast at only 1.6% in the euro zone, we can see that we cannot be satisfied with mere talk and that we must take decisive action to restore growth and employment. we need common budgetary discipline. we must make this clear again so that there is no doubt. it is the responsibility of each member state to control public spending, to combat the deficit and to stabilise or even reduce the debt burden. if not, future generations will have to pay the price and the more member states try to circumvent the rules they have set themselves, the more they will destabilize the whole system. if we have rules, well, obviously we should enforce them. without that, it's no use. only after agreement has been reached on these basic principles and common sense will it be appropriate to start thinking about a possible development of the pact. and this development should take account of the nature of business cycles and the necessary distinction between operating deficits and investment deficits. we have another question before us, an even more important one: can we live sustainably with common budgetary discipline, while pursuing different economic policies? mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on 21 february the committee on agriculture and rural development adopted by 31 votes to 35 a common position on the reform of the sugar com. this large majority is a sign of the balance we have managed to achieve, which takes account of the views of most of the political groups and nationalities represented in this parliament. the case is complex. on the one hand, in view of the international economic context, the reform of the sugar cmo is now necessary and indispensable. but at the same time, it must not neglect the place and future of the women and men who depend on the sector in europe and in our trading partners. with this in mind, the draft resolution sets out clear guiding principles: adaptation of the sugar moc to the rules of world trade, increasing the competitiveness of the sugar sector, a social objective of guaranteeing a decent standard of living for the operators in the sector while maintaining their activity or, if necessary, in their conversion, and respect for the principle of community solidarity which takes account of the most fragile regions and states of the union and our historical partners, the acp countries and the least developed countries. to meet these requirements, four main lines must be identified which will guide the future reform of the sector. firstly, in terms of timing: the forthcoming reform must remain in force until the end of 2012 in order to give the industry the visibility it needs to carry out its investments. secondly, the reduction in prices and quotas must be limited to what is strictly necessary to take account of the interests of european farmers. it must also be accompanied by a level of compensation which is really responsive to needs. the resolution also proposes that the quota transfer mechanism, which is unfair and destructive for the most vulnerable countries, be replaced by a specific budget-neutral fund managed by europe, which will make it possible to organise the restructuring of the sector. fourthly, the members of the committee on agriculture finally voted overwhelmingly in favour of market regulation, in particular by adapting the 'everything but arms' initiative in the sugar sector. this major axis aims to maintain the coherence and sustainability of the cmo by requiring that the european union be able to maintain control of the supply of sugar on its market. but it also responds to the repeated requests of the least developed countries themselves, who have clearly understood that illegal triangular trade, which can be promoted by unlimited access to the european market, will not offer any benefit to the development of the economic and social structures of the least developed countries. finally, in parallel with these four main lines, the draft resolution stresses the need to take account of the particular situation of the outermost regions of the union, taking into account their geographical and structural constraints and their specific needs for economic and productive development. the text stresses the major and irreplaceable role played by sugarcane in some of these regions and strongly advocates full compensation for any loss of income suffered by overseas farmers and equally strongly calls for the essential mechanism of aid for the disposal of sugar beet to be maintained. ladies and gentlemen, in view of the current deadlock caused by the commission's radical measures in the council of ministers, only the european parliament is now in a position to play a leading role in defining the terms of the reform of the sugar com. that is the ambition of our text, which takes a position which i consider to be balanced, coherent and voluntary in the sense of effective but supportive reform.
mr president, for reasons of vague compromise with the wto, tens of thousands of workers are about to be thrown out of work, dozens of companies are about to be closed, european agriculture is about to be dealt a terrible blow, and the development of many countries is about to be called into question. but who will benefit from this reform? the farmers? who would believe such stupidity when the gross revenue loss is reported to be 50%. to the consumers? this is doubtful, because a fall in agricultural prices has never had an impact on households' purchasing power. small producers in the south? the experience of the coffee market and of sugar production in brazil can only make us doubtful. on the other hand, multinational food companies have reason to rejoice. they will, thanks to the commission and the wto, be able to put more young children to work in sugar cane fields. they will be able to exploit a little bit more of the suffering men and women, often on less than $100 a month. they will be able to watch their profits swell immeasurably against the backdrop of social disaster. this reform also raises grave concerns in all the outermost regions. our group recently went to réunion, at the invitation of our colleague verges. we have seen that for this island this reform was a disaster. beyond the need to compensate fully, there is a problem of consistency which arises. even though the bulk of the european union's agricultural investment has been devoted for more than 40 years to the development of the sugar cane sector, which accounts for one third of final agricultural production, 25% of electricity production and three quarters of exports, it is proposed today to fundamentally challenge this strategic act of development without an alternative commensurate with the consequences of the situation being possible. the consequences of this reform in all its dimensions must be understood. at the request of mr verges, our group would like the commission to undertake to submit to parliament a study of the social impact of the situation in the peripheral regions. we also want the same type of study to be carried out on a european scale. mr president, let me conclude by saying that we are convinced that the solutions lie in a genuine policy for the regulation of the sugar market, which europe would be the promoter of.
the canary industry is a major issue for the french overseas departments (dom) in terms of social, economic and environmental balance. the sector no longer has room for industrial restructuring and it is not realistic to envisage a global conversion, given the context of international competition for tropical agricultural products. the commission must indicate what measures it envisages to avoid the outermost regions (ors) being doubly penalised by the reform in question. these regions risk being treated proportionately more favourably by the acp countries with which they are in direct competition and their development capacity being limited, even though they do not participate in the community's sugar surplus. the commission must, in its forthcoming proposals for reform of the sugar cmo, transpose the 'specific treatment' promised for the outermost regions into concrete technical measures with financial resources corresponding to the real needs of the sector and the development objectives of these regions. i hope that you will support me, commissioner, in the legislative proposals for reform which the commission will present shortly, so that we can better understand our situation in the outermost regions.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, when we talk about organic farming, there is a real paradox. everyone - including you, madam commissioner, and the european commission as a whole - recognises the undeniable benefits of organic farming, not only for the environment, biodiversity and health, but also for employment and rural development. however, despite increasing consumer demand for organically produced products, organically grown areas and production are stagnating and still represent a very marginal share of overall agricultural production. we were very surprised to learn of the commission's action plan for organic farming, which we hoped would be particularly ambitious and well-funded. this is not the case, although we are of course pleased to note some good proposals, such as awareness and information campaigns or the emphasis on collective catering and school catering in particular. we could start by restoring the european parliament itself to organic products. so you are not providing special, additional resources, nor are there any voluntary measures - much less binding - for the member states, whereas the need to harmonize the different policies of the member states in the field of organic farming is obvious to everyone if we really want to contribute to the development of organic farming and reduce disparities. we also see no progress on the crucial question of genetically modified organisms, the coexistence of conventional and organic farming, or responsibility in the event of contamination. we are waiting for your proposals in this area, without the member states being left entirely to themselves in these matters which are essential for organic farming. that is why the members of the european parliament wanted a much stronger commitment to organic farming, much stronger than information campaigns, which are useful but which we believe are insufficient to meet the challenges. we therefore believe that a lot of investment is needed, in particular to make the specifications for the different products in the different member states more consistent and precise, to make better use of the rural development funds, by defining much more clearly the share of organic farming. we hope that the eafrd programme for rural development will help to answer these questions. these rural development funds must also be strengthened. but they are facing serious threats and we cannot accept plans to reduce the overall budget of the european union which would risk undermining them. we also want to make organic farming a priority research objective in the framework of european research programmes. we want more support for the economic structuring of the organic sector, from production and processing to redistribution and marketing. without the support of this channel, we will not be able to make real progress. it is also important to resolve the question of genetically modified organisms and to significantly improve controls and the fight against fraud in this area. all this must be done in consultation with the professionals concerned, with the associations, consumers, cooperatives and all those who have been committed for many years to organic farming, and unfortunately without much support. the european parliament must also be fully involved in these policies, and i would draw your attention to the fact that any amendment to the organic farming regulation should also be the subject of consultations with the european parliamentarians. in conclusion, we really need to move beyond the concept of 'niche' when it comes to organic farming. this is not a small, isolated sector that would be for a friendly, environmentally-minded, high-income clientele that could afford to have access to this type of food. we believe that organic farming can be the spearhead of a truly sustainable agriculture. in the context of the forthcoming reforms of the common agricultural policy, which we all know are inevitable, we believe that organic farming can be a model, obviously not reproducible, not 100% everywhere, but we believe that this agriculture, whose merits and benefits are recognized by everyone, must be strongly supported, encouraged, so as to achieve much higher percentages of overall agricultural production. we therefore count on the action of the european parliamentarians and hope that the commission will hear this desire to affirm much more strongly the support for organic farming.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, once men used nitrates, pesticides, herbicides and they were driven out of the agricultural paradise. since then, we can't even eat golden apples. before, with good organic pork you could get tapeworm and parasites, with good jams from grandmothers you would die of botulism. now, because of industrial agriculture, well, we live 25 years longer! we must therefore change this situation, go back to the time of the cro-magnon man, where in the landscapes of biodiversity, the 130 000 organic farmers roam, the 230 000 organic cows live, the 400 000 organic sheep, the 230 000 organic pigs. it's only one percent of agriculture, but it's one percent that changes everything. it's like the red sea parting, muhammad riding his mule, jesus returning at easter, that's what organic is, it's useless, but it makes life bearable.
member of the commission. mr president, i should like to make a few comments on the report. first, with regard to public support for sustainable agriculture, the action plan acknowledges the role of organic farming in society. in delivering public goods, organic farmers incur high production costs. they should be entitled to be compensated for income foregone and costs incurred when delivering those public goods. that is exactly what we recommend that member states do within their own development programmes. on the other hand, as stated in the report, the successful development of organic farming depends crucially on customers’ willingness to pay a higher price to have organic food. that brings me to the next point: promotion and marketing. consumers must be given the correct information in order to stimulate demand. the commission has already contributed to organic food information and promotion campaigns. i am fully aware that we need to make use of the best expertise available when taking the further steps set out in the plan. i have a great deal of sympathy for your call to promote organic food for children and school canteens, but want to have advice on this from specialists. we need to be sure that we reach our target groups, and must therefore use the right channels in our marketing campaigns. regarding the internal market, i share your concerns about the obstacles that might hamper trade. organic food that has been produced in accordance with all the requirements of eu legislation should have access to all eu organic markets. the european logo can play an important role in making this happen. at the same time, i see no contradiction in organic producers underlining the region of origin of their own products if they wish to. innovation in organic farming and food processing relies, to a great extent, on research. we have already seen an increase in organic research and there is more to come. however, it is not up to the commission to prescribe in detail the different research subjects. with regard to coexistence, the action plan is not the right place to address this issue, since organic farming is not the only area concerned. at the end of the year the commission will issue a report on the national coexistence measures which will show what further steps need to be taken. the action plan recommends that member states make full use of the rural development policy possibilities available; not only agri-environmental measures, but also investment, extension services, quality schemes and all the other rural development elements that can be used to help organic farmers extend their production. i appreciate the comments you have made and look forward to working with you on this important issue in the future.
