president. - mr president of the council, mr vice-president of the commission, the oral questions put to you by the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs deal with three preconditions which parliament has repeatedly referred to since the treaty of amsterdam set us the objective of transforming the union into an area of freedom, security and justice. we have been convinced since 1999 that this objective can only be achieved if three conditions are met: greater legitimacy, more efficiency and more credibility for our political action. firstly, greater legitimacy means for parliament greater respect for the democratic principle that the european parliament must be more seriously involved in the drafting of european legislation and in the negotiation of international agreements. the european council in the hague decided to move to codecision on illegal immigration, but it excluded - which is rather bizarre - legal immigration, which is the one most interested in among european citizens. parliament is still merely consulted on criminal matters, which is the most sensitive area of the relationship between citizens and the european institutions. the council has not yet grasped that unless this relationship is based on very high standards and a courageous policy to promote fundamental rights, any initiative launched by the union is likely to be opposed by those same member states which are holding back the development of the union. this discrepancy between public statements and concrete decisions is already facing us in the court of justice on the regulations on family reunification, data protection and perhaps, tomorrow, on the asylum procedure. secondly, more efficiency, since most of the answers given by the institutions to requests concerning the free movement of persons, the fight against organised crime and the fight against terrorism are very vague, if not virtual declarations. we have seen this again in the fact that we are still trying to find solutions to border controls, to develop schengen cooperation, but also to prevent conflicts and to promote integration. the absence of clear objectives and priorities leads us to disperse our energies as much as the obvious lack of links with other community policies which are complementary to the policies of the area of freedom, security and justice. another essential element to be defined is the relationship between the european institutions and the national institutions. we will hardly be able to achieve greater mutual trust if we are not able to define the tasks of each decision-making level, the expected responses and the measures to be taken in the event of failure. we must not forget that when it comes to the freedoms or security of citizens, the strength of the chain is that of its weakest link. finally, mr president, we need more credibility. last year the european council faced an impressive rate of non-implementation of the action plan against terrorism and was only able to appoint a representative of the secretary-general, adding, if necessary, a new piece to a kind of institutional meccano that is already lacking in transparency and certainly not in efficiency. to date, agencies such as europol or cepol still have to prove themselves and have difficulty integrating into national security systems. the european parliament has repeatedly called on the council to create credible bodies that are better integrated into the union's institutional framework, but it has never received any truly credible answers. in some cases, as in the development of intelligence agencies, the answers have even been so vague that one begins to wonder whether their design really lives up to the questions raised. i shall listen very carefully, or rather - since i have to leave the chamber in a few minutes because of the french election campaign - i shall read carefully the replies to this debate as early as tomorrow morning. i can already commit myself to presenting to the competent parliamentary committee proposals to relaunch a dialogue between our institutions that meets our expectations, those of our citizens and also those generated by the tasks entrusted to us by the treaties, and which calls for a clear political perspective, not delayed technocratic responses.
author. mr president, the year 2004 saw significant progress for the european area of freedom, security and justice. firstly, with the adoption of the hague programme which sets out the new priorities for the coming years. then, with a council decision of 22 december, which allows the transition to codecision for border control, asylum, immigration, judicial cooperation in criminal matters and police cooperation. we can only welcome the fact that the council has listened to our requests and we wish to continue in this spirit of dialogue between equal partners to ensure continuity of the progress to be made. unfortunately, the european immigration policy has mainly developed repressive measures and the fight against illegal immigration. i therefore welcome the fact that the commission has presented a green paper on economic immigration. but i hope that this green paper will open up a wider debate on the opening up of legal immigration and not be limited to the needs of the european labour market. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we must work to find sustainable solutions for migrants that respect their fundamental rights. i therefore call on the member states to allow the transition to codecision on legal immigration. the year 2004 also saw the presentation of the proposal for a directive on procedures for granting and withdrawing refugee status. i would like to draw the attention of the council and the commission to our serious concern about this proposal. the proposal is simply a bottom-up approach to asylum policy, allowing too many derogations. in the worst case, it may jeopardise the more protective asylum policies of some member states. i regret that the council has not allowed codecision on this matter and i call on it to take account of the concerns of the european parliament. we want to ask the council where its proposal on data retention is, since commissioner frattini has told us that the commission wants to put forward its own proposal. will you allow a personal data protection instrument in the third pillar? the question is asked. we're hoping for an answer. finally, i would ask the council to decide at this week's jha council to consult the european parliament again on the framework directive on racism and xenophobia, and i thank you for your replies.
mr president, i would like to express my surprise at the fact that your remarks - whether those of the commissioner or those of the president-in-office of the council - have given little attention to the external dimension of asylum and immigration policy. you are aware that the european parliament decided to discuss the situation in lampedusa and the camps in libya in its emergency resolutions on thursday, that the delegation for relations with the maghreb countries and the arab maghreb union (including libya), which will be visiting libya next week, has decided to visit a reception centre for foreigners and that the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs is considering a mission on the ground. in these circumstances, i think that the interest of the european parliament, which has repeatedly rejected the outsourcing of asylum and the setting up of camps on europe's borders, would have deserved a more detailed statement from you. in lampedusa and libya, several of the fundamental rights enshrined in both the charter of fundamental rights, the european convention on human rights and the geneva convention relating to the status of refugees are clearly being violated. in these circumstances, does the council intend to demonstrate to the offending state the situation of repeated and systematic violation of rights, since we are today in lampedusa iii, i believe?
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i should like to begin by thanking our rapporteur for this excellent report, which i wish to support wholeheartedly. we should have introduced a minimum harmonisation of procedural rights in parallel with the introduction of the european arrest warrant. by adopting this report, we are affirming that the area of freedom, security and justice is not only a crime-fighting area but also a rights area. despite a significant convergence of procedures in europe, differences persist. it is therefore essential to establish common rules guaranteeing everyone the assistance of a lawyer, the right to interpretation, protection and in particular the protection of the most vulnerable. the establishment of a genuine european area of security and justice requires first and foremost the protection and promotion of the fundamental rights of european citizens. we are showing our intention to defend this political vision of an area of freedom, security and justice by strengthening the commission's proposal, which establishes these minimum guarantees for individual rights in criminal proceedings. we also want to ensure the right to legal counsel within 24 hours, the proper information of the suspect, the charges against him and these rights through a letter of rights provided in a language he understands. finally, we must certify the competence of interpreting services and that is why we propose their registration in a national register of interpreters. while terrorist crimes - barbaric crimes - must be dealt with with particular care, the fight against terrorism remains inseparable from the protection of fundamental rights in our democracies. while it may be necessary to make special provisions for suspects in connection with terrorist investigations, the right of everyone must be respected. the establishment of a genuine european area of justice is a priority. improvements in judicial cooperation and mutual recognition require the harmonisation of rights and procedures.
mr president, i would first like to congratulate mrs buitenweg on her excellent report. i think it has shown perfectly well why the questions of freedom and justice cannot be separated from those of security. today, thanks to this report, we have an opportunity to rebalance things, because for several years the repressive aspect of justice and home affairs was the most developed, or sometimes the only one. it is absolutely essential today to go further and ensure that the system of extradition applies, with the same respect for the person, to all suspects, including in cases of terrorism-related crimes. we also need a corrective mechanism for cases where a national judicial system does not meet minimum standards. such measures will thus give more substance to the principle of the right to a fair trial, as guaranteed by the european convention on human rights. these measures are - as has been said before - a late addition, absolutely essential to the european arrest warrant. let us remember - and let us remember this all the more as we have heard a number of rather shocking remarks - that this is not about sparing criminals but about increasing confidence in each other's legal systems to encourage member states to work together. it is an absolutely essential step towards strengthening mutual trust between the member states and the principle of mutual recognition of judicial decisions. this is an essential condition for the construction of the european judicial area, and i am sure we all want this.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteur on his excellent work and also on the fruitful cooperation which has enabled us to reach a number of compromises together in order to arrive at the text which i hope we will vote on wednesday. i would remind you that our aim here is to make up for the shortcomings resulting from the inadequacy of the current structure of cepol to the tasks assigned to it, namely: first, the improvement of mutual knowledge of the european police services; secondly, the approximation of their operating methods and finally the development of better practices in police action. i am unfortunately aware of the many differences on this issue within the council, together with the extreme sensitivity of the member states, since even a tiny part of the royal power is the subject of european projects, and this despite the objective sought by all of us of greater efficiency in the fight against crossborder crime. so i know it's going to be very difficult to achieve. i have therefore no illusions as to what the council will do with this opinion of the european parliament, which unfortunately remains purely advisory at the moment. it will take some time before we can make any progress in this area. that is why the european constitution, which i very much hope will be ratified, should help us to do so. in the meantime, however, i call on the council to make every effort to achieve a genuine community approach to police training, because only in this way can we best ensure the safety of european citizens, who are confronted every day with violence and other crimes that are becoming less and less national in scope.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am a newly elected member of this parliament and this own-initiative report is therefore my first report as a member of the european parliament. before i give you the main points, i would like to thank the committee on transport and tourism and my political group, the pse, for entrusting me with the task of working on this very important subject of short sea shipping and motorways of the sea. i would like to thank in particular the administrators of the european parliament, mr ioannis darmis and mr jean préat, and my parliamentary assistants, mr guy caballé and mr alexandre polack. they have accompanied me throughout the consultation, synthesis and drafting of this report. finally, i would like to thank the commission departments, the energy and transport dg and the main professional players in the sectors, in particular shipowners, ports and logistics, who have actively participated in our consultation work. i should like to take this opportunity to express my surprise at the lack of human and financial resources for the investigation of the members of the european parliament. the european parliament, with its continually increasing budgetary and legislative powers, has become the voice of the citizens within the european union. i was surprised to find that a member of the european parliament, as rapporteur, cannot organise observation missions funded by the european parliament other than the official missions of parliamentary committees, which take place only once or twice a year. as you know, ladies and gentlemen, the devil is in the details and if the european parliament is to carry out its monitoring work effectively, it should be able to benefit in future from increased capacities of its own expertise, in particular to ensure the independence and impartiality of its members. let me first of all remind you of the context in which the question of the development of maritime transport in europe is placed. in its 2001 white paper on european transport policy for 2010, the european commission recalled the important role of short sea shipping in reducing greenhouse gases and stressed the need to simplify its regulatory framework. it introduced the concept of motorways of the sea, recalling the need to promote massive and rapid shipping lines, particularly to bypass bottlenecks such as the alps and the pyrenees. the european parliament supported these proposals on the tmcd in its white paper report adopted on 2 january 2003. the rapporteur was mr izquierdo collado. the last commission communication published in 2004 that we looked at is above all a progress document; the aim of the report is to take stock of the situation of short sea shipping, the obstacles it faces and the measures taken to overcome them. my report first of all wants to give you an overview of the state of short sea shipping in europe. i would like to draw your attention to two main facts. first, the share of short sea shipping in total intra-european transport grew by 25% between 1995 and 2002, representing 40% of total goods transported within europe compared to 45% for road. secondly, recent data on the environmental impact of short sea shipping show that it has a significantly lower negative impact than road transport. the conclusion of this situation is obvious. our duty is to advance short sea shipping to reconcile environmental protection, quality of life and economic growth. however, there are many obstacles to the development of short sea shipping. i do not wish to give you an exhaustive list of all the obstacles which i have highlighted in my report. i would like to draw your attention to two main issues. firstly, the report stresses the absence of a genuine voluntary policy to attract and orientate the major road transport organisers and operators towards short sea shipping. secondly, our meetings with the sector's leaders have convinced us of the urgent need to adopt effective, clear and sufficient financing arrangements for the actions to be carried out. the various existing aids must allow for optimum complementarity, making it possible to start new permanent lines. in the face of these obstacles, my report stresses the need to address the issue of standardisation of intermodal loading units and to facilitate the integration of short sea shipping into the chain. we also propose to reactivate community thinking on the unification of the legal regime for the multimodal chain. this report was unanimously approved by the members of the committee on transport and tourism. our concerted work has enabled us to reach compromises on crucial points. the report stresses the potential for developing short sea shipping for passenger transport, the possibilities of creating thousands of jobs, the importance of links between short sea shipping and inland waterways, the role of short sea shipping for islands, compliance with community competition rules and, finally, the improvement of the environmental performance of short sea shipping. to correct our missions and for the sake of consistency, i would like to table an oral amendment, mr president, which is purely technical. this amendment is intended to bring the definition of short sea shipping in recital a, where we have integrated passenger transport and inland waterways, into line with that in recital c, where we have failed to do so. my amendment therefore adds the words 'and passenger' and 'or inland waterway' in recital c, so that the definition of tmcd is identical throughout the report. in conclusion, i would like to remind you, ladies and gentlemen, of the three main reasons why i am asking you to support my report on short sea shipping and motorways of the sea. firstly, the widespread use of short sea shipping, which would irrigate all sectors of the european economy, would have an extremely positive impact on the development of all regions of the european union and would be a fantastic way of creating hundreds of thousands of jobs on our continent. secondly, short sea shipping is one of the relevant solutions for reconciling the safeguarding of our natural heritage with the economic and social development of our regions. finally, short sea shipping has a key role to play in spatial planning and in strengthening territorial cohesion within the european union. as such, i believe that the concept of motorways of the sea should be firmly integrated into the problem of strengthening solidarity within the union. this is why this report, on behalf of the committee on transport, proposes that consideration be given to the possibility of recognising the status of services of general economic interest for priority projects in the field of short sea shipping, which plays an important role in improving territorial cohesion within the union. i hope that i can have the widest possible support from this parliament on a subject as crucial as the development of short sea shipping and intermodal transport. the european union's policy of environmental protection, regional development and territorial cohesion will thus be strengthened for the well-being of our citizens and future generations. i hope, therefore, that i can count on your broad support.
for the gue/ngl group mr president, yes, short sea shipping must be developed in the european union in the same way as rail transport. it is a question of making it possible to transport throughout europe the goods needed to keep our economies running, while seeking maximum safety for our citizens and constantly ensuring the preservation of our environment. why would you do that? because it is clear that the trucks continue to pile up in the bottlenecks, causing many inconveniences that allow us to observe human exploitation in all its glory. many of the cabotage vessels are often garbage boats that ply our coasts, often in such a state that they do not cause real ecological disasters. this is why only a public service action at european level, including direct industrial and economic intervention, can unlock the situation. the development of short sea shipping cannot be seen as a strategic choice for spatial planning. the growth of short sea shipping must be seen not as a competitive force with the necessary investments in rail freight and railway transport, but as a synergy. i would like to stress that in maritime matters safety and respect for the environment must be paramount, competition secondary. the administrative procedures for cabotage can and must be improved, but there can be no question of skipping everything just to save time. all means of surveillance must be maintained to oppose trafficking of all kinds. in conclusion, mr president, i would say that short sea shipping has a great future in europe if it is the work of seafarers and states and not of large groups whose only motivation is absolute profitability, whatever the economic, social and human cost.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think it is necessary to recall what a discharge is. discharge should be given to ensure that the european budget is properly implemented and to give guarantees as to the reliability of the accounts and the legality and regularity of operations. the discharge should also allow the assessment of progress in implementing the recommendations contained in the previous discharge. i would therefore like to express my surprise at the substance and the form of this report, particularly the one concerning the european parliament's section. i do not understand the very unpleasant tone used by the rapporteur and the authors of certain amendments in relation to all members of this institution. the catalogue of reproaches does indeed imply a form of dishonesty, which i will not condone at all. i do not think that the european parliamentarians can be so shamed. i would add that until we have a single statute for members of the european parliament, it is not possible to change the current rules on allowances. is this dump also intended to deal with the issue of tobacco and cigarettes on our premises, which is totally out of the question even though, i would like to think, it is a real problem? and what about the fact that the european parliament's seat in strasbourg is once again being called into question? i would first like to point out that parliament has no competence in this area, contrary to what is stated in the report presented today. in addition to the decision of the 1992 edinburgh european council, at which the heads of state or government unanimously decided to fix the seat of the european parliament in strasbourg for political reasons, this decision was set out, so that it could be guaranteed by the treaties, in protocol no 12 annexed to the treaty of amsterdam. a year ago a similar proposal was made to remove the seat of parliament from strasbourg and transfer it to brussels, and the members of the european parliament, in their great wisdom, rejected this proposal in plenary, as the convention members also recalled during their discussion of the constitutional treaty. the discharge for 2003 must not be an opportunity for the opponents of strasbourg to try to change the seat of parliament once again. this is a matter which is outside the scope of the law and outside its jurisdiction.
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission naturally welcomes very much the report by mrs kinnock on the role of the european union in achieving the millennium development goals (mdgs). i would like to congratulate mrs kinnock and the committee on development on this report, which should stimulate discussions and negotiations on the measures required to achieve the mdgs. your report, madam president, rightly stresses the importance of governments adopting strategies to achieve the millennium development goals. it also stressed that the eu's development policies, whose main objective should be poverty reduction, should be anchored in the millennium declaration and the mdgs. the european union's consolidated report on the mdgs shows the progress made in this regard. the european union has stressed on several occasions that the evaluation of the millennium development goals at the un high level meeting in september 2005 was a crucial opportunity to accelerate progress towards the mdgs. in november 2004, the council invited the commission, with a view to the european union's contribution to the high-level event, to prepare specific and ambitious proposals on action to be taken in particular with a view to financing the development of policy coherence for development and the priority to be given to africa. the commission is today adopting a set of communications which constitute its response to the council's invitation. this comprehensive policy package takes stock of the union's development contribution and identifies measures to be taken to accelerate the achievement of the mdgs. your report and our communications share many of the same concerns and recommendations. i would like to mention some of the conclusions of your report which we think are of great importance and which are key points in the package of communications we are presenting. first of all, it is essential, as you have said, to continue to increase development aid. the commission proposes new intermediate objectives for 2010 in this respect; in addition to the public aid budgets, new sources of funding must also be considered as a complement. i also welcome your attention to the coherence of development policies; it is essential to examine how policies other than aid can help achieve the millennium development goals. the communication on policy coherence for development identifies no less than eleven priority areas where the challenge of achieving synergies with development policy objectives is considered particularly relevant, for example in the area of trade - of course - research, the environment, agriculture, fisheries, and so on. important synergies are possible with these different skills. many of the recommendations in your report are included in the consolidated report of the european union on the millennium development goals, for example - and you were right to mention this - the special attention to be paid to girls' education, the need to meet the needs of the most vulnerable groups, especially children, orphans, young women and the elderly. in response to the challenges facing africa, it is essential that development partners give priority to the continent. the european union must and will do more to enable africa to achieve the millennium development goals. africa must be at the heart of our attention and increasing aid resources for sub-saharan africa is vital. the european union must ensure that a significant proportion of additional official development assistance is directed to africa. our proposals on coherence must also apply with priority to the african continent. finally, in addition to all our existing programmes, particularly in the framework of the cotonou agreement, the commission is proposing new commitments in areas with a clear multiplier effect. i think about governance, about connectivity and about equity. preparations for the new york event are accelerating. i thank you for your contribution and i look forward to continuing to work with you to ensure that the european position meets the challenge of achieving the millennium development goals. now, madam president, a few words on the communications which i shall be submitting to the college of commissioners in a few hours. the preparatory process for the september summit showed the progress made in many poor countries and the importance of the efforts made by the international community, and by the european union in particular, to achieve the millennium development goals. all the reports, the secretary-general's report and the report of the millennium project, which was carried out under the leadership of professor sax, also show that the objectives set for 2015 can still be achieved if we want to. but this -- and you said this -- requires a major investment from developing countries, as well as, of course, from donor countries. the european union, the leading international donor and trading partner of poor countries, therefore has a special responsibility towards our own citizens, who expect us to set an example at international level, because this is an imperative of human solidarity, but it is also in our own interest. if we want a more stable and secure world, we must invest more heavily in development. the union also has a responsibility towards partners for whom europe often appears as a model: look for example at the african union, which has taken the european union as a reference. i believe that the proposals i am going to defend this afternoon meet that challenge. these proposals are based on three fundamental pillars: first, financing for development and aid effectiveness; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. on the question of financing, the european union - and this is my answer to your question - has fulfilled its commitments and in 2006 its aid effort is likely to exceed the collective target of 0.39% of the gross national income of the member states. it is clear that this effort must continue and i propose that the member states set themselves a new individual intermediate target of a minimum of 0.51% in 2010, corresponding to a collective effort of 0.56%. this would make it possible to reach the 0.7% target set by the united nations and considered necessary by the millennium project experts to achieve the mdgs by 2015. in terms of annual aid, this would represent an increase of as much as €20 billion per year in 2010, with eu aid rising from €46 billion in 2006 to €66 billion in 2010. in addition, new sources of finance should also be encouraged. i forget to say that i will propose to the new member states that they should reach 0.17% by 2010 - we are introducing a differentiation because they come from much further away - which should enable us to reach 0.7% in 2015. in addition, new sources of funding must be encouraged, but this should not be a pretext for postponing or reducing the european union's commitments for 2010. the second element is the improvement of aid efficiency, which is another important area of work. substantial progress has been made in recent years in the management of community aid. at eu level, the main challenge today is to implement the commitments made by the european union to better policy coordination, complementarity on the ground and harmonisation of procedures. europe must be much more than the simple sum of the budgets of our individual states. the second element is the use of budgetary aid - which i would like to give priority to - although the efficiency of aid would be greatly improved. but it's not just about money. the real challenge is to manage globalisation through the exercise of solidarity that lays the foundations for a global social contract, which implies not only increased official development assistance but also comprehensive public policies that allow the gains of globalisation to be distributed in a more equitable way. in the same way, this is the first time that the commission - and i am quite happy about that - has agreed to talk about coherence and to identify, in the other areas of competence than development aid, no less than eleven areas which are related to development and which can bring added value to it. i think it's important. i'm going to go with you. this is the first time the college has taken up this challenge and i think it is quite useful to be reminded of it. the third component of our proposals concerns the priority to be given to africa. the reason is threefold. sub-saharan africa is the region most lagging behind. europe is a key partner, and africa is a geopolitical partner that will become increasingly important. the united states and china have already understood this, which explains their increased interest in this part of the world. i propose that we step up our action in areas where there is a clear multiplier effect. three things in this regard: first, in the area of governance, we must support the implementation of reforms resulting from the african peer review mechanism. we must also ensure the refinancing of the peace facility to support the work of the african union and subregional organisations in conflict prevention. secondly, the first, i would call it the political axis in the general sense of the term, the second is the economic axis. infrastructure and network interconnection should be supported on the basis of african union and nepad strategies to facilitate south-south trade. in fact, i am thinking here of really getting the trans-african networks off the ground, as we had to do in europe with the trans-european networks. we must make the construction and implementation of these large trans-african networks a priority and a concrete objective. this is the economic axis. i think about all the infrastructure, all the things that are related to communication, technology transfer, and i go beyond that. the third axis is the social axis. it is obviously the policy of equity. the european union must develop incentive measures and support african countries in their efforts to promote social cohesion, employment and environmental protection. i am thinking more specifically of education, health and culture. i said during my hearing that culture is a much more important vehicle for development than we think and i would like to use it to the full. the ambition of this set of communications is to be able to unite the member states around a european vision which would give the union the capacity of influence, credibility and visibility necessary to contribute effectively to the high-level event of september 2005. i am currently touring the capitals to mobilise national parliaments and member states on this issue. these three communications must lead in september to the complete redefinition of development policy, as i announced, in the form of a new declaration of development policy which i intend to translate into a common european development strategy. what we have been able to do for the common security strategy, i see absolutely no reason why we should not be able to do for development. i would also come up with a real battle plan for africa, articulated on the three axes i have just mentioned. that is the answer i wanted to give, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, mr president. i hope i was complete. if there are any other questions, if i have inadvertently omitted to address any of the questions, please do not hesitate to ask me. i am, of course, at your disposal to answer.

deputy author. mr president, the alstom power boiler case puts us all on the back foot of our commitment to building a europe of full employment, with strong industry and advanced technology, a europe which cares about the environment, a europe which is free from american technological and financial domination. what's this about? a member of the alstom group, with creative, research and production capacities in europe 250 employees in france, in vélizy, 300 employees in germany, in stuttgart, a number of establishments in the czech republic, portugal and poland and with its headquarters in connecticut, usa. the know-how of this company lies in the manufacture of boilers for the production of steam and electricity. it is the world leader in clean coal production and is developing new co2 capture technologies. with the implementation of the kyoto protocol and the need to diversify energy sources, it is clear that such technologies have enormous potential. for reasons that are not entirely clear, alstom's management decided to transfer european know-how to the united states and to divide the workforce at vélizy by five and that of stuttgart by two, with the probable objective of eventually closing the main european sites. the pretext for this vampirisation of european know-how is a pseudo-study conducted by the americans, which predicts a foreseeable reduction of the market by one third over four years. like the employees of power boiler, one can only doubt the seriousness of this study, especially when one considers the gigantic needs in this field that are emerging all over the world. but don't we say in my country that when you want to kill your dog, you accuse him of rabies? the alstom group has been characterized by a complete lack of longterm industrial strategy and a frantic search for immediate profits since its privatization. the commission, like the french government, also has a share of responsibility. fortunately, the employees of the european sites concerned, supported by their unions, did not give up. vélizy's employees devised a counter-project, which involved the exit of the company from the alstom group for a sales price of around the symbolic euro, the creation of a european public limited company combining the vélizy and stuttgart sites and preserving the establishments located in the czech republic, poland and portugal. this project is based on the voluntary participation of employees. it has the advantage of being part of the requests made by the european commission to alstom on 7 july 2004 concerning the sale of assets, the aim being to preserve and develop european employment and technological potential vis-à-vis the united states. it is a cooperation between european employees which is at the forefront of the application of european law, leading to the creation of a european public limited company. but we must act quickly, the company's intellectual property is about to be transferred to the united states and switzerland and alstom's management is working to put the company in financial difficulty. if, ladies and gentlemen, we are committed to the development of industry and employment, we must do everything we can to support this initiative. the european company law directive and the regulation on employee involvement in company management have not yet been transposed into french law, but it is still possible to anticipate. it is a question of political will and i expect the commission to show that will. so let us not disappoint those workers who are threatened in their jobs but who are so proud of their unparalleled technical achievements and always ready to innovate.

deputy author. mr president, i am here to replace my colleague, hélène flautre, with whom i have been working on this dossier for five years. i think mr. harlem desire's intervention is the real problem. i have been telling former commissioner monti for years that there would come a day when the main job of the directorate-general for competition would not be so much to refuse aid but to see whether it was used well. what is the basis for a country granting state aid in apparent contradiction with article 87 of the treaty? for the greens/efa group mr president, this resolution is certainly moving in the right direction. we have all seen at the last olympic games a number of athletes - in fact very few compared to the thousands of athletes present - being caught for having ingested a few doses of prohibited substances. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the matter. clearly, the first thing we need to do is to take a stand to defend the public health of our athletes, top athletes, professional athletes. but there is a contradiction here, as we have seen recently. the world anti-doping agency, which is doing extremely important work, has just decided, particularly with regard to corticosteroids, that tests will be carried out and that a certain dose will be accepted - i believe it is 30% - of corticosteroids in the samples that will be operated. this is a position taken with regard to the medical profession, a position which amounts to accepting a certain dose. it reminds us and it reminds me that, in the world of professional cycling and hematocrit, we accept a rate of less or equal to 50% but not more. there is one request missing from our resolution. this is an expensive but essential requirement to ensure independent and continuous medical monitoring of athletes. in this way, we can see, regardless of the age of the athlete and the sport they play, how athletes treat themselves throughout their career, starting from a zero level because athletes also have the right to treat themselves and what legal or unfortunately illegal doping they may have taken. if we do not have this kind of instrument in the field of doping, in europe, in the european union and in the world, well, everything we have said before is of little use, unless there is this independent and longitudinal medical monitoring.
the negotiations under way at unesco are of great importance to us europeans. we have so far succeeded in making our principles prevail in international forums. these principles have been reiterated in this house by my predecessors. cultural goods and services are not commodities like other commodities. cultural diversity is a wealth for all mankind. every government must have the right to support the creation and dissemination of its own culture without being subject to the sacrosanct requirements of free trade or the authority of the wto. we have succeeded in enforcing these principles so far and the cultural sector has been excluded from the international negotiations on the liberalization of services at the world trade organization. but those who consider cultural goods and services to be part of the entertainment industry are again on the offensive. at their initiative, bilateral free trade agreements involving the cultural sector are increasing. at unesco, representatives of the united states and its allies sought, and to a large extent succeeded, in weakening the original text proposed for the convention. the only effective way to guarantee our right to cultural identity and diversity is to make it a universal right recognized by all peoples and defended in international institutions by their representatives. the unesco convention must become the international legal instrument of reference on cultural policy issues. it must not be subordinated to other trade agreements. it shall have an effective dispute settlement mechanism. finally, it must be ready for the next unesco general conference in october 2005, at which time it can be adopted.

the next item is the report (a6-0051/2005) by mrs rosa miguélez ramos on the proposal for a council regulation establishing measures to restore the southern hake and norway lobster stocks in the cantabrian sea and the west of the iberian peninsula and amending regulation (ec) no 850/98 and the report (a6-0050/2005) by mr philippe morillon on the proposal for a council regulation establishing measures to restore the western channel and the bay of biscay sole stocks.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, the proposal from the committee on fisheries for measures to restore the stocks of sole in the western channel and the bay of biscay has been submitted to parliament in the consultation procedure. it is the result of the proposals submitted to the council in december 2002 for the conservation and sustainable exploitation of fisheries resources, as you said, in the context of the reform of the common fisheries policy. the aim of this proposal is to ensure that stocks are maintained or restored within safe biological limits in the two regions concerned within a period of five to ten years. it has five chapters. the first, setting out the criteria to be met in order to achieve the objectives of the plan, provided that, where stocks could be considered to be within the limits, the council could decide to cancel the plan on a proposal from the commission. the other chapters specified technical and control measures to enable the plan to be implemented. in the course of the debate on this subject it became clear, as you said, that for at least one of the two regions concerned, that of the bay of biscay, the latest scientific reports indicated that the stock situation was not below biological limits. consequently, instead of adopting a recovery plan as referred to in article 5 of the 2002 regulation, it appeared preferable to adopt a management plan as provided for in article 6 of the same regulation. the proposal does not, of course, leave fishermen free to resume intensive fishing without any control, which would inevitably have catastrophic consequences for the future of the species. it has led to the amendment of the technical provisions proposed by the commission, but in such a way as to ensure that these stocks remain within biological limits, while recalling that the new common fisheries policy aims to enable the sustainable exploitation of living aquatic resources, taking into account in a balanced way the environmental, social and economic implications. i would point out that parliament's proposals make it clear in this connection that if the commission should find, in the light of the annual assessments, that any of the stocks of sole concerned are at risk of collapse, it should propose to the council additional measures to be implemented to ensure the recovery of the stock concerned. in summary, mr commissioner, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this is the essence of the proposals in the report which will shortly be put to the vote in parliament without amendment and which received very broad approval in committee, demonstrating the desire to involve fishermen themselves in the thinking of scientists and politicians and to reconcile the expertise of the latter with the experience of the former. i would add that the discussions which led to the drafting of this report were conducted in an excellent atmosphere and i would like to conclude, commissioner, by expressing my sincere gratitude to you.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, congratulations to the rapporteur on a report which does not present any major problems. i take this opportunity to thank the fishermen for catching one of the best fish, the sole, which nature, for some, or god, for others, has put at our disposal. let them keep on fishing for it! there are a number of lessons to be learned from this report and this proposal. firstly, we must know how to adapt when necessary and the decisions taken are not taken against the fishing vessel owners. if there are more suns than expected, you have to be able to adapt to the situation and not be confined or stuck. secondly, the calm of the ports and the confidence in the future depend to a large extent on the good work done by the fishermen and the scientists. some people don't necessarily believe each other, and i think we need to persevere in deepening our relationships. i think that one place that has been set up within the framework of the common fisheries policy is very useful: the regional advisory councils. these bodies must be used to ensure that these two broad categories of professionals and scientists understand each other as well as possible. in this case, commissioner, your work is all the easier and we share the same aim: to conserve as many fish stocks as possible on the seabed because without fish, there are no fishermen at work and without fishermen, there is no fish for the consumer.
for the greens/efa group mr president, i am sorry to make a slightly discordant note in this fine consensus. we would have liked to have supported the commission's proposal in a much more voluntary way and we regret that systematically, in the face of the serious situation of the constant decline in fisheries resources - albeit with nuances depending on the species - the member states, aided by many members of parliament, continue to want to mitigate the objectives to be achieved at all costs. although everyone says they want to conserve resources, in reality this is not the case and we cannot accept this situation. that is why we shall not vote on both reports. there is no doubt that there is a need to discuss with local actors and fishermen the adaptation and simplification of measures which are sometimes too complex. it is also important, of course, to take account of the socioeconomic impacts, to provide for compensation, which must be made fair so that they do not always go the same way, and to preserve small-scale fishing and small-scale fishing, which must also survive. we agree with all this, but we cannot accept that the commission's objectives, which are based on scientific data, are systematically reduced. we can't keep arguing about the situation. that is why we shall vote against both reports, but we shall support the commission's intention in this area.
member of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by thanking the rapporteurs for their hard and constructive work. i also wish to thank mr varela suanzes-carpegna for his good work on the hake plan. concerning the proposal for a council regulation establishing measures for the recovery of the southern hake and norway lobster stocks in the cantabrian sea and western iberian peninsula and amending regulation (ec) no 850/98, i can fully agree with 14 of the 26 amendments considered by the committee on fisheries. these are amendments 2, 4, 10 in part, 11, 12, 13, 14, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 and 26. it is appropriate to remove the out-of-date proposals concerning management by kilowatt days, to adapt the minimum quantities concerning control arrangements according to the measures set up for 2005, to establish tolerance margins and conversion factors consistent with those in the northern hake recovery plan, and i can agree with the deletion of obsolete provisions concerning effort messages. the fishing mortality rate of 0.27 is acceptable because it is consistent with the implementation plan of the world summit on sustainable development adopted in johannesburg in 2002. i also agree that it is appropriate that a recovery plan should anticipate a recovery taking place within less than five years. although estimates of biomass of fish stocks are uncertain, observations of stock size above a precautionary level for two years in a row could be a way to signal the need to move from a recovery phase into a long-term management plan. concerning amendment 10, we can, therefore, accept the 35 000 tonnes exit criterion, but not the requirement of a ten-year delay in recovery or the reference to ‘in a sufficient period of time’. such an approach would be contrary to the fao code of conduct. we do not fix the duration of the plans: we set an objective and estimate the approximate time we will need to achieve it. i cannot accept amendments 15 or 16 because the 10% constraint on tac changes is too tight to allow an adaptation to real circumstances. in line with the opinion of the advisory committee on fisheries and aquaculture, the figure should be retained at 15% rather than 10%, but the 15% could apply in the first year of the plan. i support the principles behind amendment 17 and can accept paragraphs 1 and 2 of that amendment, with modifications committing the council, as well as the commission, and making reference to maintaining the arrangements embodied in annex ivb of regulation (ec) no 27/2005 on a comparable basis to the cod recovery plan. for these reasons, i cannot support amendment 27. in relation to paragraphs 3 and 4 of amendment 17, and amendments 3, 28 and 30, state aids should be decided in the context of the financial instrument for fisheries guidance and the european fisheries fund, so that comparable financial resources are made available to all fishermen who find themselves in similar situations. as is the case with sole stocks, which i will come to later, it is appropriate to have an interim review procedure, but this should be done at reasonable intervals. i could support amendment 25, subject to the extension of the review period to four years rather than two years. i cannot support attempts to rebuild stock size year-by-year, because of the disruptions that this is likely to cause industry, and i cannot support amendment 5.after extensive consultation with my officials and with officials and fishing representatives in member states, i can agree to some modification in the size and number of closed areas for fishing for nephrops. however, complete deletion of any reference to closed areas, as in amendments 6, 7, and 24, goes too far to be compatible with precautionary management at this stage. management of hake and nephrops in the gulf of cadiz is an important issue given the abundance of juvenile hake in that area. on the basis of the precautionary principle, greater uncertainty in this area is not a reason to be less cautious, so i cannot support amendments 1, 8 or 9, which would exclude this area. however, i accept that measures for the gulf of cadiz may need to be different. i cannot accept amendment 30. capacity needs to be managed so as to be in balance with the productivity of the fish stocks. if either or both fishing effort and capacity were allowed to increase again once the stocks are recovered, the result would be a decline in the stocks and a reduction in the amount of fish available to the industry. this would not achieve the aim of sustainable exploitation. turning now to the morillon report, i am pleased to say i can fully agree with amendments 7, 16, 17, 18 19, 20, 21 and 22. it is entirely appropriate to remove the chapter concerning management of effort by kilowatt days, to apply control measures only to landings above 100 kg instead of 50 kg. i accept that the provision for the margin of tolerance in logbooks should be the same as that already adopted for northern hake. i also accept that, as a general rule, variations in tac should be limited to no more than 15% for these stocks. notwithstanding the deletion of the kilowatt days scheme from the proposal, it will be necessary to substitute alternative effort management measures. for the western channel sole, these should be based on the measures already introduced under annex ivc of the current tac and quota regulation. the biological state of sole in the bay of biscay is apparently better than previously thought and it is appropriate to apply a management plan to this stock, rather than a recovery plan. i can therefore accept the substance of amendments 1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12 and 13, but only insofar as it relates to bay of biscay sole. the biological conditions prevailing for western channel sole are sufficiently serious for recovery plan provisions to apply to that stock. i also support the idea of an interim report mechanism as mooted in amendment 11, as i mentioned when discussing southern hake and nephrops. however, the plan needs to be given time to take effect before a review is useful, so a four-year interval would be appropriate here, which is a similar timescale to the one used for the interim evaluations of long-term measures agreed for the northern stocks shared with norway. i can also agree with the idea of setting a target fishing mortality rate for bay of biscay sole, as in amendment 15. however, we should take account of the scientific advice that will be provided by stecf in june on this topic, and i will reserve my position on the right figure to use until i have seen that report. however, i cannot agree with the idea of setting a tac according to an annual increase in the quantity of adult fish in the sea. the scientific advice is simply not precise enough to allow such an approach and i fear the result would be an unwarranted, overly erratic adaptation of tacs. the fishing industry needs more stability than this method can provide. i am not therefore in a position to support amendments 8 or 14. i see legal problems with certain amendments. amendment 5 would be in contradiction to the requirements of the last sentence of article 5(2) of regulation (ec) no 2371/2002 and the last sentence of article 6(2) of the same regulation. and while regional advisory councils, where they exist, should be consulted when developing new legislation, the implementation of regulations is the responsibility of member states. for this technical reason, i cannot support amendments 5 or 6. however, we would certainly have no problem with member state authorities consulting the regional advisory council, on a voluntary basis, concerning such plans. (applause)

mr president, many migrants arrive regularly on the island of lampedusa in italy. these people have made the painful decision to leave their country because they are mostly fleeing political situations in which their lives are threatened. on 18 march, the italian authorities deported 180 people from the centre of lampedusa to libya. the lack of transparency and access around the centre and the conditions of these expulsions raise questions about the respect of the right of asylum and the geneva convention. the speed of the expulsions and the fact that the deported persons were sorted by nationality shows that the applications could not be examined individually and with the necessary care. it cannot therefore be certain that well-meaning asylum seekers have not been returned to dangerous situations. we are also particularly concerned that the high commissioner for refugees is being prevented from fulfilling its mandate. the latter must have access to asylum seekers in order to ensure that any person who wishes to make an application for asylum can do so and that his application is carefully examined. these expulsions are all the more alarming as we are sending vulnerable people back to a country that does not allow them to be protected. libya is not a signatory to the geneva convention and has no asylum system. it cannot therefore provide international protection for those who need it. finally, it is itself deporting refugees outside its borders to dangerous areas. we therefore call on the italian authorities to grant the high commissioner for refugees unlimited access to the lampedusa centre immediately. the expulsions must also be stopped until the lampedusa centre is in conformity with community and international law.

member of the commission. mr president, on 16 march 2004 the commission adopted a proposal for a council and parliament recommendation on the protection of film heritage and the competitiveness of related industrial activities. cinematography is an art form contained on a fragile medium, which therefore requires positive, quick and effective action from the public authorities to ensure its preservation. films bear comprehensive witness to our times. the protection of the european film heritage, including co-productions with third countries, is therefore in the interest of future generations. in order to ensure that the european film heritage is passed down to future generations, it has to be systematically collected, catalogued, preserved and restored. it should also be made accessible for educational, cultural, research or other non-commercial use; in all cases, in compliance with copyright and related rights. it is therefore the commission’s intention to promote european standards on the cataloguing of films and we have therefore given a mandate to the european committee for standardisation to go ahead with preparatory work. that will facilitate the exchange of information and the interoperability of the databases that are kept by the film archives in all member states. the commission will also promote cooperation between film archives. one advantage of this cooperation will be the possibility of recuperating and restoring so-called ‘lost films’. the report and the amendments discussed today reflect the thorough work by the rapporteur and shadow rapporteurs on the one hand, and the presidency on the other. i would like to thank mr hegyi for his very constructive work in that respect. the commission is grateful to all the key players who made it possible to reach a good compromise today. the commission proposal, as amended by parliament, recommends that member states introduce an obligation to deposit cinematographic works that form part of a member state’s audiovisual heritage and that have received public funding. also, and in compliance with the principle of subsidiarity, the text gives member states the option as to how to implement this obligation, by law or by means of contract: we leave that up to member states. a recommendation is the best-adapted instrument available for achieving the objectives of the proposed measures. they are: first, strengthening of the film industry by laying the foundations for the explanation of sleeping catalogues by rights holders; and secondly, the systematic deposit, collection and conservation of member states’ visual heritages. the commission is very satisfied –– and i think the citizens are, too – with the prospect of a first reading agreement. the commission accepts parliament’s amendments insofar as they correspond to the political agreement reached between parliament and the presidency and confirmed by coreper on 2 may 2005.
the european parliament has a duty to protect the environment. mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, cinema as a whole - past, present and future - is and will remain one of the most vivid artistic testimonies of our member states. europe has an identity which has been shaped by an exceptional accumulation of cultural heritage, including cinema, which has helped both to forge this identity and to safeguard and develop cultural diversity. the aim of the gyula hegyi report is therefore, on the one hand, to ensure the preservation and conservation of our national and european film heritage and, on the other hand, to improve the conditions necessary for the competitiveness of industrial activities linked to this heritage. to achieve these results, it is recommended that the cinematographic works forming part of this heritage be systematically collected, catalogued, preserved, restored while ensuring respect for copyright. another key point in this report is the nature of the deposit of cinematographic works with the bodies authorized by the member states, which should be compulsory by law or by contract. in addition, the material deposited would be a copy of high technical quality, so that future use of the work would be guaranteed. it is also specified that this film heritage would include productions, but also co-productions of films between member states or between a member state and a third state. the idea is also proposed, which i think is interesting, namely the establishment of a network of databases for the european audiovisual heritage, in cooperation with the council of europe and more particularly with eurimage and the european audiovisual observatory. finally, there is one point in this report which i consider essential: it aims to ensure that cinema can be taught at all levels of education and that younger generations also learn a little history, a little daily life, a little sociology thanks to the richness of the european film heritage.

in practice the mercosur market is already fully open - but about reaching agreement on rules that give legal certainty to our operators in the region. the mercosur has specifically refused to make a bid for such rules on public procurement, intellectual property and geographical indications in the european union - a sensitive subject for countries such as spain, italy and france when it comes to wines and spirits. in short, the commission is at the disposal of the members of parliament to provide them, before they begin their work, with all the information they need to help establish, as quickly as possible and under the best possible conditions, a balanced relationship between the two parts of the world concerned.

on behalf of the alde group. madam president, commissioner, this text is not, of course, aimed at uniformising working conditions in the union, which would be neither desirable nor possible today, but rather seeks to establish common bases for the protection of employees. the more favourable social systems, such as french labour law, are therefore not called into question and will remain applicable. this is essential, as you will appreciate, in the context of the debate on the constitution in france and in the face of the concerns raised by the development of european rules in the social field. but the stakes are high. it is up to us as members of parliament to send a clear signal as to the social system we wish to promote at european level. the ambitious objectives of the lisbon strategy make it necessary for the european economy to adapt to new challenges. it is clear that companies need to have a certain amount of flexibility in the management of working time, but we sincerely believe that greater flexibility is not incompatible with a high level of protection of the health and safety of employees. the balance between flexibility in time management and safety of employees requires the definition of minimum standards, safeguarding rules and adequate controls. the debate on the opt-out clause therefore takes on particular prominence in this context. the possibility for an employer to derogate from the legal limit of 48 hours of work per week with the individual agreement of the employees clearly contradicts the spirit of the directive. i would remind you that the plenary, when considering the 2004 report, opposed the continuation of this individual opt-out clause. however, if in a text which does not seek to achieve standardization we wanted the individual opt-out clause to be phased out, we supported the maintenance of an opt-out option which, in accordance with national traditions, would be governed by negotiation and collective agreements. as regards the reference periods, we agree with the rapporteur and the commission to allow an extension of up to 12 months, which corresponds to the flexibility needs of firms, which naturally have to be able to cope with fluctuations in demand. finally, we are convinced that all watch periods should be regarded as working hours. however, the committee on employment and social affairs proposes that member states may allow the calculation of the inactive parts of the childcare period to be carried out according to a specific system in order to comply with the maximum weekly working time. we support this provision, which again takes account of national specificities in this area.
madam president, i expected from this directive what the charter of fundamental rights of the draft european constitution did not contain: harmonization of social rights from the top down. it's not. it's the opposite. the flexibility of the workforce is thus strengthened. while the chicago hangmen died in 1886 for the 8-hour day and the 40-hour week, now at the beginning of the 21st century the great social innovation of the european union should be to raise the ceiling on the maximum weekly working time from 48 hours to 65 hours or even beyond in the case of individual or collective agreement, the reference period for the calculation of the maximum weekly working time being increased from four to twelve months. generally, a compensatory rest period is guaranteed after 72 hours of work. we can only appreciate the social audacity of this text which will probably make the european employers tremble! to top it all off, the concept of a period of inactivity in the care of a child is introduced, a period which would be excluded from working time in complete contradiction to the case law of the court of justice of the european communities. no need for further explanation. the zealous servants of the european employers' organizations have done a good job and although they know, as do those who will choose to vote on this text, that the president has withdrawn the speaker, they are not prepared to accept the amendments which have been tabled.
madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, not the 60-hour week, the opt-out clause must be abolished. i have no hesitation in supporting the text presented by mr cercas. i would first like to support this by referring to the common sense that we should work for a living and not the other way around. it is common sense to understand that, except for tasks clearly demanded by the person who is carrying them out, working, as is the case in some countries of the european union, 60 hours a week - or even worse, 63 hours with the authorization granted in 1993 - eventually poses problems of adaptation to one's personal, family and social environment. in the social field, as in the political field, progress is achieved through compromise. the desire to make the practice of 60 or 65 hours general is contrary to social progress. in this sense, the opt-out clause must be abolished.

in writing. in order to better protect europe's cultural heritage, europe intends to establish exceptional conservation and protection measures that will preserve the cinematographic heritage and promote the defence of the linguistic, cultural and artistic identities of our old continent. one of the recommendations is to extend the benefit of state aid to cinema. it is a question of extending the cultural exception and of extending the status of exception, which is the exact transposition of what we are defending for france, namely national preference! the commission has decided to extend the current system of state aid for film and television works for three years, even though these arrangements, which are far from satisfactory, would need to be assessed and reformed. in these circumstances, why limit this protection to crops and not extend it to textiles, agriculture, steel, shipbuilding, etc.? does not the commission's globalist logic condemn this moratorium, which distorts free competition, in the long run? only a clear defence of national and european preference will preserve europe from global ultra-liberalism.
in writing. the terrorist attacks of 11 september 2001 have put transport safety at the top of the political agenda. the commission has already proposed that ports, as the essential links in the transport chain linking the flows of goods and passengers by sea and by land, should be subject to security measures. i can only support such an initiative because, as an elected member of the european parliament for the greater north-west region, more than 15 major seaports, vital to local and national economic life, are involved. france is sensitive to this issue because it has three particularly well-exposed maritime facades. the north channel-sea facade (ports of le havre, dunkerque, calais, boulogne or rouen), the atlantic facade (ports of bordeaux, nantes, saint-nazaire or la rochelle which are gateways for trade to the east, north and south of europe), and finally, the mediterranean facade (port of marseille-fos). these security measures should not, of course, be confined to port terminals alone, but should also extend to the whole port and its activities.

in writing. the recognition of professional qualifications within the union would be a real step forward if it were not part of a wider strategy to eliminate national borders, which are seen as obstacles to the free movement of goods and people. the nomadism is now promoted as a community value by making geographical and occupational mobility the alpha and omega of the new european man. the system of recognition of qualifications will have to adapt to changes in the world of work or in education systems, in line with the ultra-liberal philosophy which guides the european institutions. in this spirit, the commission has defined a very specific social policy which encourages the qualification and mobility of workers on the basis of minimum training conditions which are supposed to allow better adaptability to labour markets. on the other hand, regulatory and professional bodies have expressed many concerns about the future of certain professions and the quality of training provided in different countries, particularly in the field of public health. finally, the directive on the recognition of professional qualifications is a consequence of the directive on the liberalization of services. the bolkestein directive is more relevant than ever!

member of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by congratulating mr moreno sánchez on his excellent report, which reflects very well not only on its author but also on this house as a whole. i welcome this debate, because i regard parliament as the commission's essential partner in the conduct of our trade policies, that is, in particular, the case in advance of the doha round, which remains our number one priority. mr moreno sánchez has underlined the need to make progress on all the issues in this wide-ranging agenda, with a clear emphasis - which i strongly support - on the objectives of poverty reduction and sustainable development. those were at the heart of the founding charter of this round, and they remain as important today as they were when they were first articulated. since i took office, i have made every effort to advance the dda and to keep it on track. i want doha to put trade at the service of development. that is what i believe in and stand for, and it is at the heart of the policies i am pursuing. however, europe cannot do this on its own. as i said in geneva on my very first day as trade commissioner, the eu cannot be the wto's sole banker. last summer, europe had the courage to put its agricultural export subsidies on the negotiating table. it is now up to others to show their hand. in concrete terms, this round has to yield improved market access and increased business opportunities all round, not only for developing countries - i expect and want them to be the biggest winners of this round - but also for our own industry and service providers in europe. that will enable us to build on europe's strengths in the knowledge economy, for the prosperity and benefit of all. market access in industrial products - nama - and services too are key issues in the round. without progress on these issues, there can be no conclusion to the round. to achieve this, i want to ensure that the more advanced developing countries engage more intensively on non-agricultural issues. thus far, they have pushed hard their case on agriculture, as they are perfectly entitled to do, and as i would expect them to do. however, they have shown little willingness to embrace the necessity of real movement on their part on nama and on services, even where objective analysis suggests this would be in their own economic interest. this has to change. we all have to show a willingness to adapt, to change and to accommodate others' interests. that is why we have made our move on agriculture. the other main industrialised countries now need to follow our example to be more proactive on services and to work on their own agricultural reforms in order to match what we in europe have put forward. last week, several informal meetings of wto trade ministers took place in paris. i expressed my very real concern about the slow pace of the present negotiations. i called on all members to stop playing their cards so close to their chests and start putting them on the table. that goes for all of us, i am not just pointing the finger at others. we all need to do that, not europe alone. i also explained our idea of what an ambitious round should amount to. it requires parallel progress on all three pillars of the agricultural negotiations - not just export subsidies - including the tariffs and quotas that restrict market access. there must be visible efforts by all industrialised countries - not only the eu - to reform their farm policies; and a substantial and real - not just paper - reduction of industrial tariffs by all countries in a position to do this, including the advanced developing countries, always respecting the special circumstances of the weak. offers on services that provide genuine new business opportunities must be tabled and the wto's rulebook substantially strengthened, be this in regard to trade facilitation, anti-dumping or geographical indications. i also renewed my plea for additional efforts to address the specific concerns of the developing countries, and especially - though not exclusively - the poor and vulnerable ones, through special and differential treatment in the round and by the richer parts of the world substantially stepping up aid for trade. you are quite right to identify capacity-building - the essential support we need to give - to enable trade to take place to facilitate that adjustment, so that developing countries, in particular the weaker ones, can genuinely participate in the opportunities for trade that we are advancing through this round. we made progress in paris. we reached agreement on the vital but highly technical issue of the conversion of specific duties - so many euros per bushel of this, so many euros per kilo of that - into their percentage ad valorem equivalents. while the core issue of how much and on what basis these tariff equivalents will be reduced remains to be discussed - that will come later - we now have a basis on which we can move forward on agriculture and, as a result, on all other aspects of the dda. on this i should like to acknowledge and pay tribute to the work of mrs fischer boel. agriculture is a tough subject and i respect how she handles it. we can also expect progress in relation to industrial tariffs in the months to come. many members also reaffirm their intention to submit improved offers on services by the end of this month. we expect intensified discussions among key players between now and the mini-ministerial in china, which will take place on 12 and 13 july. before the summer break, we should see a first approximation of what a possible hong kong package could look like. if there is any chance of an ambitious outcome in hong kong at the end of this year, and thus an ambitious round, this first approximation, which i hope that we can see in july, should, at the very least, firstly, establish areas of growing convergence amongst wto members issue by issue. it should also provide clarity about our shared level of ambition on the core market access issues -
