mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the wto has been the subject of criticism since its inception. today, on the tenth anniversary of the wto, we can take stock and ask ourselves: do we need the wto? in the context of ever-increasing globalisation, we are undeniably forced to recognise that we need a multilateral organisation. but to the other question, do we need this organization in its present form? i will answer in a much more reserved way. the world today still fails to distribute its resources in an equitable way. trade has a great role to play in bringing this balance about, but its current rules have so far remained largely deaf to the demands and needs of much of the world. in view of this, i sometimes naively hope that the hong kong conference, which will take mr president, the chinese textile case is just one example, mr mandelson, of a much larger problem. in international trade, two contradictory elements must be reconciled: first, of course, the need to trade and therefore to remove barriers; second, the need to maintain the balance of trade and the need to eliminate barriers to trade. the second is the need to ensure job security, social acquis, etc. in golf, we solve this problem by creating a handicap between the pro and the amateur. in international trade, the handicap of tariffs had been created. but since 1947, under gatt and the wto, it has been decided to reduce customs duties first and then to abolish them. article 341 of the constitution confirms this. the consequence is obviously the chinese affair. the solution, mr mandelson, is to invent a new customs technology. instead of reducing and abolishing customs duties, you, commissioner mandelson, should propose to the wto the deduction of customs duties by which the importer would open up to the exporter a customs credit, a kind of economic drawback on the importer's economy. under this system, chinese textiles arriving in europe would be subject to a customs duty; it would open up a customs credit to china, which could only be used for the purchase of products from the european economy. it would create a virtuous circle. it's the system of offset contracts, offshore contracts. it is the marshall plan system, but the credit is opened, in this case, by the customs duty itself. this would solve the insoluble problem of relocations by means of a new customs technology.
mr president, commissioner, china's accession to the wto in 2001 was in principle a guarantee of balance in trade relations between china and the european union. however, this balance is distorted when the rules of the game in international trade are not respected. i would like to speak first of all about the measures needed to protect intellectual property, and let us not forget that this is in accordance with the wto agreements. these measures contribute to an effective fight against counterfeiting and piracy. it is now up to the european union to enforce these agreements protecting textile designs and designs, in order to ensure the sustainability of our textile industry. finally, when we are faced with what is recognised as a disruption of the market, and i am of course referring here to the spectacular growth of chinese textile products, as you yourself have confirmed, then we must apply the legal instruments available to us in the wto. so do you not think, commissioner, that it is imperative today, when all the indicators are in the red, to initiate an emergency procedure to allow the implementation of safeguard measures? why are you taking so long at the expense of our industries, at the expense of industries in countries close to us? commissioner, time is running out. it is not a question of implementing protectionist measures, but of making china understand that its membership of the wto entails both rights and duties.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs laperrouze, for having taken over this proposal on the guidelines for trans-european energy networks and for having carried out a focused analysis in her report which was adopted by a large majority in the committee on industry, research and energy. i would like in particular to express my gratitude for her commitment, together with that of the shadow rapporteurs, in aiming for an agreement at first reading which, i very much regret, has not been achieved. let me recall on this occasion the objectives of the proposal. the challenge of the proposal is to build a legal instrument that will be efficient in delivering the necessary energy transmission infrastructure, while developing the appropriate cooperation with the private sector and the member states. the security of energy supply and the functioning of the internal energy market are key policy issues. these objectives are taken up in the trans-european energy – ten-e – guidelines aiming at the installation of an electricity and gas network of truly european character by better linking the fragmented national networks. concerning natural gas, there is a strong growth perspective. the trans-european energy networks policy aims at securing and diversifying additional gas import capacity from sources in russia, norway, the caspian basin region, northern africa and the middle east, and providing the necessary interconnection capacity between member states. concerning the electricity networks, the main function is to create and foster a real european electricity market. for this objective, sufficient interconnection capacity between member states is essential. since the adoption of the existing guidelines for trans-european energy networks in june 2003, the need has arisen fully to integrate the new member states and candidate countries in these guidelines and further to adapt those guidelines to the new european neighbourhood policy. the revision of the ten-e guidelines proposed by the commission in december 2003 should be seen as a complement to and an improvement on the existing guidelines. it aims at explicitly incorporating the ten new member states into the priority projects, as well as the incorporation of essential energy connections with third countries. as to the choice of the projects, we have proposed to introduce a top-down approach, identifying the projects of highest priority on the priority axes from the larger family of projects of common interest. the projects of european interest are those of highest priority. they have the objective of supporting the rapid implementation of the most important cross-border interconnection capacity. to achieve this aim, the projects of european interest need to comply with special criteria. they must be situated on a priority axis. they are of a cross-border nature or have significant impact on cross-border transmission capacity. they must be mature: that means that a firm commitment must exist to start before the end of 2006 and that the projects need to be completed by 2010 at the latest. another essential element of our proposal is the european coordinator. the european coordinator will encourage cooperation with users and operators, and promote the projects amongst private investors and financial institutions. a coordinator may be designated by the commission and will act in the name of, and on behalf of, the commission. i now look forward with great interest to your debate on the proposal.
the rapporteur. madam president, i would like to thank the commissioner for his kind words. ladies and gentlemen, i should also like to thank my fellow rapporteurs for their opinions, who have accompanied me throughout my reflections and have made a major contribution to the report i am presenting to you today. i would also like to thank the representatives of the european commission and the representatives of the council for their attention and for the answers to the many questions raised. i would also like to thank the secretariat of the committee on industry, research and energy and my assistant for their help. commissioner, you have mentioned the objectives of this proposal for a decision. the aim is to adapt the guidelines to the configuration of the european union of 25 member states, to allow the financing of projects of common interest, to enable the completion of the internal market in gas and electricity and, above all, to ensure security of supply through interconnections between the member states and with neighbouring countries: south-east europe, mediterranean countries, ukraine, belarus. this approach for the transeuropean energy networks corresponds in fact to the approach adopted for the transeuropean land transport networks. the committee on industry, research and energy supports the new concepts introduced by the european commission to define priorities for action, in particular the qualification of projects of european interest on priority axes and the appointment of a european coordinator, provided, however, that this is limited to complex projects with particularly difficult implementation conditions and that it is done in consultation with the member states. parliament must also be consulted on the appointment of the coordinator, that is the meaning of the amendment proposed by my group. the report voted by the committee on industry encourages the member states to cooperate with each other where necessary by implementing transnational investigation procedures taking into account determining criteria such as security of supply, the impact of the project on the environment, the opinion of the population of the territory concerned, etc. on the basis of the information provided by the council, the industry committee considered that the approach advocated by the council was consistent and simplified the original proposal of the european commission. the report voted by the committee on industry thus establishes a hierarchy of projects: projects of common interest which form the basis of transeuropean projects are listed in annex iii and priority projects qualified as projects of european interest are listed in annex i. the industry committee did not wish to challenge the projects drawn up by the member states because it did not consider itself to have a sufficient level of competence or information to criticise the choice of projects. however, following the comments made by the rapporteur. mr president, i would first like to thank the fictitious rapporteurs, with whom i have worked a lot in recent months to produce a comprehensive and coherent report on highly sensitive issues. my report deals with legal and illegal immigration and integration policies. from time immemorial, human beings have migrated to escape poverty, persecution, in search of happiness, in search of a better future. today, with globalisation and the proliferation of transport, migration flows have become more complex and dense. they are the result of a new aspiration of men and women around the world to go to work in other countries, to gain other experiences. they are also the result of inequalities that are sweeping the planet, the result of poverty, the curse of too many regions in the world. in the context of national elections in some member states, immigration is a recurring theme in electoral campaigns. some countries decide to close their borders and take strong measures, while others regulate thousands of undocumented immigrants. the european union appears to be divided on the issue of immigration. it is true that each member state has the right to decide how many immigrants it intends to take in. but europe no longer has internal borders. consequently, each national measure has direct and significant repercussions on the other states. it is therefore essential that the member states organise themselves together at european level. the solution to many of the problems they face must be both european and national. some political parties systematically take advantage of election periods to make harmful amalgams between insecurity, terrorism, immigration, feeding fear of immigrants and foreigners in our fellow citizens. this is unacceptable. it is essential, on the one hand, to provide objective, transparent and regular information on immigration policies and, on the other hand, to launch information campaigns among the general public in order to decriminalise the perception of immigrants. i have tried to take a responsible, balanced and comprehensive approach to this problem in my report. responsible, because we must approach these matters with a great sense of responsibility: let us not forget that these are men and women, not commodities! i also wanted to have a balanced approach: member states should not write their policies in the sense of 'all safe' or 'all liberal'. the european union must therefore overcome national divisions and dispassionate debate in order to establish a humane and effective european immigration policy. finally, i wanted to have a global approach for greater coherence and efficiency. i would like to address several aspects which i have developed in my report. first, the need for an active policy of co-development to tackle the root causes of immigration. secondly, the fight against illegal immigration through increased checks at our external borders, the dismantling of human trafficking networks, and more stringent, very stringent sanctions against companies that employ illegal workers. thirdly, legal immigration: if the union is to open its borders to legal immigrants in order to respond to the foreseeable decline in the labour force, it will have to do so in an orderly, concerted way. finally, the integration policy for migrants: admission and integration policies are inseparable. member states must put in place more voluntary policies. for their part, migrants must understand and respect the fundamental values of the host country: language learning, civic education courses and better integration into the labour market are among the important elements. ladies and gentlemen, i believe that immigration is good for the countries of origin, for the countries of destination and for the migrants themselves when it is controlled and managed. it's the principle of win-win, win-win, jointly controlled and managed immigration. welcoming everyone or making the myth of zero immigration a goal are not realistic or truly responsible positions. each state must take in immigrants according to its capacity for integration, its own interests and those of the countries of origin. immigration is too sensitive, often too dramatic, to continue to be the subject of political debate. a vision must prevail when approached: and man in all this? it is true that we must be realistic, but we must also take into account the inevitable human brotherhood and the solidarity that this implies. ladies and gentlemen, parliament must send a strong and united signal to the council and to the citizens of europe that progress on immigration and integration policies must be made quickly. i hope therefore that this report will be adopted by a large majority tomorrow.

what has just happened is not a french or dutch thunderclap in a serene european sky. yes, mr schulz, the crisis of confidence between the citizens and the european institutions has been widening and deepening ever since the great liberalization of the single market and the maastricht treaty. over the years, it is not only the lower classes, but the middle classes themselves who experience this shift as a shift towards a model of society that they reject. the competition for everything, the rampant precariousness, the cynical and ruthless balance of power, the consensus reached at the top, behind closed doors, this is no longer acceptable! there's a surge of dignity in this non-massive. many of these people would still like to dream of europe, but we do not dream of the stability pact or the bolkestein directive. the crisis in europe today is indeed an existential crisis. we have had other difficulties before, mr barroso said. no, this time it's about something else. until now, the political storms triggered by the reforms, which have proved costly to the liberals in the council and the commission, have stopped at the borders of the member states. on the left, what a massacre since the not so distant past when it headed more than two thirds of the governments of the union. where the right wing held the reins a short while ago, the sanction has been equally devastating, has it not, mr barroso? what did the european leaders, the council and the commission, do after each of these popular disapproval? they congratulated the winners and continued the same policy: business as usual! this time - and this is the radical novelty of the situation - it is the heart of the system that the citizens have started to target. now, sooner or later, you're gonna have to answer for it and accept real change. so how do we get out of this impasse? first, by showing that the depth of european unease has been measured by clearly declaring the constitutional treaty to be obsolete. secondly, by announcing in the same spirit the withdrawal of the most controversial texts, because they are the most emblematic of a drift that must be stopped: the bolkestein directive, the working time directive, as well as the series of directives under discussion liberalizing all aspects, without the slightest assessment of the effects of previous measures of the same nature. finally, by opening a large free citizens' debate, not a convention but a free citizens' debate free of any pressure at the level of the whole union to establish a state of affairs of the present europe and determine what needs to change to design a europe in which the majority of europeans can again recognize themselves and invest themselves. i would like to conclude, mr president, by addressing myself to the forces of the left, who, whatever their position on the constitution, share the conviction that we must now embark on this path to rebuild europe. let us meet and do what we can to restore confidence and hope. regions. the structural funds must thus support industrial development and serve as an instrument to assist the conversion of areas facing industrial relocations. we must respond specifically to this the agenda calls for the report by mrs carmen fraga estévez, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation on management measures for the sustainable exploitation of fisheries resources in the mediterranean and amending regulations (ec) no 2847/93 and (ec) no 973/2001 (com (2003) 0589 - c5-0480/2003 - 2003/0229 (cns)) (a6-0112/2005).
for the greens/efa group mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am also glad that we can adopt this compromise. i would like to congratulate mrs fraga, who has done a difficult and delicate but urgent job of regulating and enabling sustainable fishing in the mediterranean, a sea which is itself threatened by extremely problematic developments: various forms of pollution, diminishing resources, threats to biodiversity. i welcome this compromise in several respects. firstly, it defines in a particularly clear way the fishing gear which is permitted or prohibited; it specifies, for example, driftnets, mesh sizes, minimum fish sizes, deep trawling, etc. it also ensures the consistency of european policy with regard to other seas which concern us, whether in the atlantic or the north sea. it was essential to have management tools and policies for managing fisheries resources in the mediterranean. it is also a fair compromise, which allows the majority of the countries concerned to strike a good balance between what each side has had to accept or refuse in order to reach this compromise. however, a number of questions remain to be resolved, which were raised by previous speakers. the first is the management of the whole mediterranean basin, since we are only talking about the member states of the european union in this compromise. we must strengthen the work of regional organisations and, within the framework of the european union's neighbourhood policy, determine how we can reach agreements with the other countries bordering the mediterranean basin. another problem is the endangered bluefin tuna, and fishing practices such as the use of gillnets for aquaculture, which are increasingly problematic. this compromise, this regulation, does not directly concern this type of fishing, but it is understandable that the small-scale fishermen who are concerned by this regulation feel that it is unfair not to regulate further a type of fishing that is developing and poses enormous problems for the preservation of ecosystems, given the way it is practiced. finally, i would like to take up what has been said by my colleagues about the urgency and the need for the european union to pursue a much more active research policy in the mediterranean. however, we lack a lot of elements, a lot of data that would allow us to refine these policies and tools. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules are applied. that's the whole point of this debate.
on behalf of the ind/dem group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the concern to preserve fisheries resources in the mediterranean is entirely legitimate. it is necessary to preserve for future generations a rich and diverse environment and vital food resources. sustainable management of the marine ecosystem is an imperative. but among all the living creatures that inhabit this planet, there is one that has duties, i mean human beings, but also has rights. the regulation before us is a compromise, and i certainly understand the intention of this compromise: it is a compromise between the various sovereign nations which make up europe, but also between the use and preservation of the environment. however, amendment no 10 by our rapporteur directly concerns a traditional mediterranean fishing activity in france, the tuna fishery. the latter is an ancient technique of fishing for bluefin tuna, using a surface anchored net, which is specific to the french mediterranean. i would like to point out, ladies and gentlemen, that by approving this amendment you will be putting an end to the death sentence of 1200 direct and indirect jobs linked to this activity. on the field, it's misunderstanding, and legitimate anger is roaring. for years, fishermen in this sector have made considerable efforts to limit the impact of their activity on the ecosystem, in particular with regard to the protection of cetaceans. their accidental catches are now only residual. scientific studies have shown that this fishery is environmentally friendly. i know that this compromise was difficult to reach, but i appeal to the commission, the council and above all the french government. what are a few more days of negotiation compared to the plight of 300 families and an entire region? what will be the weight of the argument of the package and that of pandora's box, which should not be opened in a french public opinion which understands more and more that brussels is far from the reality in which it lives? let us not forget that 80% of the fisheries in the mediterranean are artisanal, so why should we always favour the remaining 20%? madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, please reopen the negotiations to save these jobs! commissioner borg has just told us that he refuses to accept our amendment no 34, on the grounds that the second paragraph of article 7 on which our amendment is based is based on a classification which does not correspond to the text. i think this is a legal argument which concerns the details of what the commissioner and his services have to deal with, but it does not take into account the substance of the amendment, namely the protection of the rights of fishermen which he has to ensure that they are respected. to do this, i ask you to vote against amendment no 10 by our rapporteur, whom i congratulate nonetheless on her hard work, and i ask you to vote for our amendment no 34. on behalf of the fishermen you're going to save, i thank you.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place at noon.

in writing. european industry is currently facing major difficulties. it is subject to a formidable scissor effect between, on the one hand, the unilateral opening up of european markets to fierce global competition and, on the other, the eu's dogmatic policies: competition policy which prevents the emergence of european champions or the support of new activities which the market alone could not bring about, regulations in all areas which multiply constraints and costs... what happens to industrial competitiveness when we look at the 1200 pages of the reach directive on the chemical industry, a veritable regulatory monster that nobody understands anything about, except that it is likely, as it stands, to increase the number of company closures and relocations, and to end european research in this sector. not all of mr vlasto's proposals are bad. but the major flaw in his report is that it treats ultra-liberal globalization as an inevitable and fundamentally beneficial fact. and to see solutions, as usual, only in more europe. by continuing to go astray in this direction, the european union has so far only succeeded in creating unemployment, poverty, disappointment and rejection.
in writing. this report was the occasion for good collaboration between the three european institutions and industry with convergence on environmental requirements. the agreement was reached on a fundamental point, the abandonment of harmful pahs and the implementation of safer substitute products. the european parliament has agreed to give industry an extra year to achieve this objective and allows the disposal of existing stocks, which are ultimately low. we have here a case where environmental ambition, backed up by research, makes it possible to consolidate this industrial sector and hence employment and improve the quality of products. a conclusion can therefore be drawn from the first reading.
in writing. the reform of the stability pact proposed today is only marginal, but it is nonetheless important. the unfortunate thing is that it took eight years to realise that the deficits were not only estimated on the basis of the fateful and completely arbitrary figure of 3% of gdp, but also on the basis of 'relevant factors': persistently low growth, ageing populations, the consequences of sloppy eu enlargement or rampant globalisation... it's about time. but that's not enough. the europe of brussels has just spent the last ten years sacrificing millions of jobs in order to meet dogmatically stated targets (3% of gdp for the public deficit, 60% for the public debt, or a maximum inflation rate set by the european central bank at 2%...). it is now necessary for the community to make employment and the prosperity of the people its primary objective, to which all, absolutely all others, must submit, no matter how much the bank of frankfurt, the advocates of pure and perfect competition or those of free world trade without any obstacles, dislike it.
in writing. this report is a monument of banalities, untruths, nonsense and immigration propaganda. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to take the necessary measures to ensure that the migration flows of thirdcountry nationals are not affected by the change in the immigration policy of one member state. these are the obvious consequences of schengen and a borderless area! this does not prevent mr gaubert from proposing in paragraph 32 incentives for mass immigration operations. the illogic and irresponsibility of this report does not stop there. after calling for the optimisation of the potential of immigration, reaffirming the right not to be turned back at the borders, to access the labour market and to participate in public and political life for non-nationals, the report recalls that all these policies must be part of the principles of solidarity and responsibility sharing laid down in the constitutional treaty! is it necessary to recall that this text was buried by the double french and dutch no and the british freeze ? the immigration lobby should come down from its ivory tower and start listening to the voice from below, the voice of the people.
in writing. this report, which is intended to "organize" immigration and promote "integration", is a classic of its kind, discreet about the causes, blind to the consequences and totally demagogic about the solutions to be found. the rapporteur, a right-wing mep and leader of an 'anti-racist' association, is planning to import additional immigration, which will hurt our economy and weaken our national cohesion, in the face of an ageing europe, a still-failing birth rate and an expected decline in the working population of some 20 million between 2005 and 2030. european policy, which is designed to 'establish an intercultural society', i.e. organised around ethnic or religious considerations, is disconnected from social, economic or community realities and potentially conflictual. to integrate immigrant populations, however, they must also show the desire and make the necessary efforts to assimilate. the european demagogues ignore the need to revive the european birth rate, to have a family policy worthy of the name and to adapt our labour market to demand in order to curb unemployment. finally, the report fails to address the question of the establishment of radical islam on our soil with all the consequences this implies for women's rights, security and democracy.

before i turn to the next speaker, i will answer our colleague, mr fernández martín, who asked me to clarify a point of our rules. mr fernández, when it comes to speakers speaking on behalf of their group, the order of their passage is determined by the size of the groups: so, the ppe, followed by the pse and so on. in the case of speakers or the debate on resolutions, the order of passage is determined by the chronological order in which the requests to intervene were tabled. so it's not about being the biggest group, it's about being the fastest. to return to your question on monday night, the third in order was the liberals, the socialists and the greens. the epp was not on the podium. however, you will be able to speak in your turn without any problem. i would remind you that this is a practice as old as our house.
member of the commission. mr president, the european commission is extremely concerned about the critical political situation in bolivia. we are following the situation very closely. many countries in the andean region have faced serious political and institutional crises in recent years, but events in bolivia have shown it to be a particularly fragile and vulnerable state, not least because it is one of the poorest, least-developed and most unequal south american countries. the current increasingly anarchic climate, which culminated in monday evening’s resignation of president carlos mesa, is deeply worrying. at this delicate moment the commission urges all bolivian citizens, rich and poor, of all ethnic origins and from all regions of the country, to pursue their respective demands and aspirations peacefully, by means of dialogue, within the framework of democracy and the rule of law and in accordance with the constitution. whilst we are relieved to note that up to now, as far as we are informed, there have been few injuries during the recent unrest, it is now absolutely vital that bolivia’s political leaders and civil society work together to extricate their country from its current difficulties in a spirit of peace, dialogue, tolerance and national reconciliation. the histories of both europe and latin america show that violence or non-democratic solutions do nothing to bring lasting peace or prosperity to their citizens. their heartfelt but often conflicting demands and aspirations can only be tackled successfully by working together to generate consensus and unity. in that regard, the commission hopes that the efforts of the catholic church to organise a national dialogue and ensure a smooth constitutional succession will continue and will be successful. the commission has been making a real and practical contribution to supporting dialogue in bolivia by using our rapid reaction mechanism to provide up to eur 185 000 to the club of madrid to implement a six-month programme of high-level consultancy and support for consensus building and strengthening of leadership skills, which started in mid-april and will continue in the run-up to the long-awaited constituent assembly. the commission and the council have also worked in close collaboration to prepare an eu action plan for bolivia, which was adopted in mid-may. it provides a framework for coherent and structured common action by eu institutions and by the member states jointly and individually. the action includes engaging in constructive political dialogue, providing support for the constituent assembly, respect for the rights of indigenous peoples, exchanges of experience with different models of regional autonomy and providing constructive input and the benefit of eu experience in securing the benefits of foreign investment for all bolivians. bolivia has also been included in the list of eligible countries for the european initiative on democracy and human rights for 2005-2006. in the bolivian context, projects related to training, monitoring and consciousness-raising in the fields of democracy and human rights, projects that promote the rights of minorities and indigenous peoples and projects that support the role of civil society in conflict prevention are all eligible for support. there is, unfortunately, only limited scope for such support to be implemented while bolivia is gripped by its present crisis. the commission welcomes the motion for a resolution by the european parliament, which would underline the need for full respect for democracy and the rule of law and would add a further very important eu voice to the calls for dialogue.

member of the commission. mr president, the european commission shares the concerns of the european parliament and the international community on democracy in algeria. with the assistance of our delegation in algiers, we are following events in the country very closely, particularly as regards fundamental freedoms, media and freedom of the press. all these issues must be seen against the background of a political dialogue with algeria that has been relatively neglected in the past. so far, in the absence of a legal framework, the commission has had somewhat limited scope for raising these issues with the algerian authorities. even under those circumstances, however, in bilateral encounters with algerian official counterparts or at euromed ministerial meetings, the commission has always urged respect for fundamental values such as democracy, observance of human rights and the rule of law. as you know, the eu-algeria association agreement has recently been ratified by all eu and algerian partners. it is expected to enter into force on 1 september 2005. the ratification of the association agreement has created political momentum for a renewed political dialogue on all sensitive matters, including those related to the enforcement of article 2 of the agreement regarding the promotion of democracy and the rule of law and respect for fundamental freedoms. the first association council should meet by the end of the year, under the uk presidency. on that occasion, the commission will wish to establish links and contacts with its algerian counterparts with a view to working on key issues relating to the implementation of the association agreement, including human rights and democratisation. once the key issues and links have been established, we intend to set up technical subcommittees as quickly as possible to implement the most important aspects of the association agreement, including human rights and democratisation. once algeria is ready to enter a new phase in the reinforcement of its bilateral dialogue with its european partners, this preparatory work will be the basis for finalisation of a joint european neighbourhood policy action plan, in which issues such as human rights, democratisation, political and institutional reform will feature prominently. in the meantime, the commission will use all the means at its disposal to pursue a constructive dialogue with algeria on those issues and will continue to encourage the algerian authorities to abandon their attempt to criminalise defamation.

author. mr president, no political transition is easy. it is probably even more difficult for some of the former autonomous republics of the soviet empire: if the three countries of the south caucasus are now experiencing conflicts over their territories, this is largely due to the odious legacy of stalin, who, in his strategy of "divide and rule", had attached nagorno-karabakh to azerbaijan. today, the frozen conflict in nagorno-karabakh is one of the main reasons for the stagnation of this region. until it is resolved, there is no hope of development in this region, which is a natural bridge between the european union and asia. the difficult economic, social and political situation in azerbaijan is a direct result of this tense status quo, if only because of the large number of refugees and internally displaced persons who are a heavy burden on the country. if, thanks to the opening of the baku-tbilisi-ceyhan oil pipeline and the dividends from the extraction of caspian sea oil, hope is being revived for an improvement in the overall situation of the country, this in no way excuses the repressive attitude of the authorities towards the opposition. azerbaijan has made a voluntary choice to turn to europe by applying for membership of the council of europe. it has set itself the rules of democracy as a guideline. by signing a first partnership and cooperation agreement in 1999 and by incorporating it into its new neighbourhood policy, the european union has shown its willingness to support azerbaijan in its democratic process. today the union is entitled to expect progress in this direction. while the release of political prisoners and the presidential decree requiring the application of international standards for respecting the democratic rights of citizens are welcome, the events in baku in may - banning the opposition from holding meetings, arrest and detention of opposition activists - are not acceptable. because we want above all to support our friends in the south caucasus in general and in azerbaijan in particular, we ask president aliyev and his government to do everything possible to ensure that the next parliamentary elections in november 2005 take place in a fair and transparent manner and that opposition candidates can campaign freely, safely and with fair access to the media. this will be a strong sign of the government's willingness to commit itself more fully to the path of democracy, as it officially promised to do at the meeting with our parliamentary delegation.

the rapporteur. mr president, my report concerns the world summit on the information society, a process initiated by the united nations. the first stage was held in geneva in 2003 and concluded with a declaration of principles and an action plan. the second stage, to be held in tunis in november, will focus on the implementation of the plan and two outstanding issues: financing and internet governance. the european union is involved in this process with a coordinated position and a strong voice, because it is unique. if my colleagues adopt this resolution, our parliament will support the union's position and will show its commitment to the success of the process. ict is part of the millennium development goals, which aim to eradicate poverty. this is linked to the material means of subsistence; it also concerns access to online services, whether for training, health, administration or commerce. the rise of the internet and mobile telephony has opened up new opportunities for development, competitiveness and growth. europe is suffering from the four-fold dimension of the digital divide: territorial, social, economic and cultural. this gap is exacerbated in the ldcs, the least developed countries, which have neither adequate infrastructure nor facilities for mass access to these technologies. the first issue to be highlighted is the contribution of icts to democracy. they are necessary to reduce inequalities and promote the dignity of persons, while also providing a means of ensuring freedom of expression, information, pluralism of opinion and citizen participation. these human rights must be respected in the context of the information society. the concern of the smsi, which is to ensure a better regulatory framework, adequate governance, to prevent risks and deviations that would undermine the security and integrity of individuals, communities, or even states, cannot justify any encroachment on respect for these rights. cultural and linguistic diversity must be one of the driving forces behind the progress made by the world summit. this will be more easily achieved in a democratic context, and our parliament should remind tunisia, which will be hosting the summit, of this. the second challenge is a new form of partnership with the countries of the south. these countries need trust and duration to act. the cancellation of the debt of the very poor countries is a positive if it does not reduce their access to finance. replacing access to borrowing with donations alone would be ineffective. the european union did not want to create a new fund at the united nations, which means that we must use the resources available in our development programmes, the cprd and the competitiveness and innovation programme, to encourage cooperation. i also proposed that the unspent development funds should be directed to the action plan. the creation of the digital solidarity fund on a voluntary basis is welcome, but remains complementary. the union must promote multi-stakeholder actions involving states, the private sector, local and regional authorities and ngos. everyone must be able to be both a consumer and a participant in ict enabling services linked to quality of life, entrepreneurial development and the production of content that respects local cultures and know-how. multi-partnership is a sign of trust and mobilisation. parliament will meet the civil society concerned before travelling to tunis to establish a lasting working relationship. in conclusion, the key issue is the promotion of equitable and sustainable development. this is the whole point of our inclusive vision of the information society. that is why i would like the lisbon and i2010 timetables to be linked to the action plan and the involvement of the european union to be thought of in terms of co-development and co-responsibility. our partners must be assured, as we are, of their representativeness in governance and their sovereignty in decision-making. whether it's health, prevention, environmental risks, waste management, or conservation of resources, we are interdependent. european growth cannot be conceived without solidarity.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have just come to the end of a long and beautiful parliamentary battle. i need to be reminded of the stakes, even if five minutes is a little bit ridiculous for such a complicated problem. there are three issues. the principle of free movement of ideas, respect for competition and rejection of the monopoly effect of patents and, finally, protection of individual creators and small and mediumsized enterprises against the overwhelming power of a few very large companies. everyone here wants to clarify the law and thinks that a directive is necessary. no one here wants all software to be patentable. so there should be no difficulty, but a recent development, which is barely twenty years old, has complicated matters. when the computer industry was born and the first software was created, no one thought of patenting. silicon valley, mr president, has lived and developed for 20 or 30 years without patents. the software was copyrighted and that was enough. then came the idea of extending patentability in this area from the united states, which has no law on the subject. at the outset, the intangible is not technical and everything that connects to the material world, involves matter or energy or involves tools, is patentable. what is patentable must be new, inventive, capable of industrial application and have a technical contribution. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the environment in the event of accidents at work. and then software was incorporated indissolubly into an invention where sensors, software and effectors were all together again and were inseparable. then, there were inventions in which only the software is new, sensors and effectors remain old. we have also seen the drift of some courts, some national patent offices and the european patent office to classify the whole thing as technical, with the result that 200,000 or more such patents have been granted in the united states and some 30,000 granted by the european patent office, despite article 52 (2) of its basic charter which states that software is not patentable. the abuses are well known, and we must remember them: educational methods, commercial methods and even surgical guides for the hand of a surgeon have been patented. in all these cases, the free software would have made it possible to benefit all of africa immediately, for example, in education or medicine. but they are patented in the united states, and as a result, they are very expensive and out of reach in today's world. we have all condemned these abuses, including by the european patent office, but its drift does not set clear boundaries. it is proposed that you, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, return to principles and law. but some of the flower children of our great industry have not understood us. they are afraid of losing their protection, which we understand in the short term, because the lack of protection will change some of the balances. how do the biggest companies do it today? they trade patent assets with each other to get rid of the disadvantages that patentability brings to those who cannot enter the game, that is, anything smaller. legal costs are increasing very steadily in all the research and development budgets of these companies, to a level now exceeding 20% in some places. two thirds of the patents in force in european territories are american or asian but not european. finally, when siemens, gem plus or alcatel sell mobile phone divisions, it is these divisions, including patents, that go to asia, leaving no chance for europe to develop in these areas. we therefore believe, mr president, that in the long run the defence of our european industry is better achieved by freedom, by open access than by patents. and china is training two and a half million computer scientists a year! how can we resist this battle? better to be free. our big industrialists should have understood this, but instead they sought ridicule, not to mention that this debate has given rise to some insults. for example, you are a "man of the middle ages" talking to you. this shows the fragility of a position. our industrial friends should admit that just because there has been a drift, it does not mean that the principles and the law have to be adapted to that drift. the last problem is that the trips agreement allows both. or all software is patentable, in which case there is no problem: they all fall under the trips treaty (adpic) and wto panels, but that is not what we want. or if no software is patentable, it is subject to international copyright laws. they also fall under the wto panels, but under different rules. in the second case, we are also in line with the trips treaty, but we know that the only thing that is prohibited by the trips treaty is the grey area. if there is a dispute about the reasons why a particular software is patentable, the boundary is no longer valid: "anything patentable" is possible or at least allowed. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. mr president, can software be patented? for information technology giants like the americans ibm, microsoft, there is no doubt about it. for most innovative smes, but also for professionals in the software industry, such as programmers, researchers and independent developers, software patentability will certainly mean their death. the heavy file has been shuttling between the european parliament and the council of ministers for over two years. the outcome of this parliamentary marathon could lead to the approval of yet another bolkestein directive on software patentability. the european patent office, contrary to the letter and spirit of the law, has granted more than 30 000 patents on mathematical calculation projects or methods of processing or displaying data. often these patents are as extensive, trivial and harmful as their counterparts in the united states. i think that software should not be patentable for a number of reasons, the first of which is that computers use languages and you cannot patent the words of a language, which would prevent others from using it freely. the specific combination of these words is protected and this protection is exercised by copyright, just as copyright protection is exercised in music in respect of a score and not musical notes. this is exactly the principle that was laid down in the munich convention. why revisit this positive right? why remove that copyright? that would make it impossible to write new software. how can we imagine living in a country where we allow a company to have the exclusive right to present a document with bold type and italic subtitles, the progress bar, the use of double clicking, the electronic shopping cart which have already been patented in the united states? we must deny the commission and the council the right to kill the innovation of small computer makers.

member of the commission. mr president, through many plenary sittings such as this and the unflagging work of its committees, your institution has always played a decisive role in the development of european cohesion policy. the commission appreciates the farsighted ways in which you have helped to bring into being and develop a policy which, besides its economic objectives, forms such a secure link between the european union and its citizens. this debate in which we are discussing the policy’s medium-term future is just the most recent example of these efforts. whilst expressing the commission’s recognition of your role and its gratitude, may i, on a more personal note, thank the four rapporteurs – mr hatzidakis, mr fava, mr andria and mr olbrycht – for the outstanding quality of their reports. my thanks also to mr galeote quecedo, who has steered the work of the committee on regional development so efficiently. together they have set the stage for a fruitful discussion today. in replying now to your proposed amendments i hope i can be as clear and convincing as the reports themselves. as i said, we are discussing the future of cohesion policy until 2013. in the years between 2007 and 2013 cohesion policy can build on its present results, but we have to look and move forward. we can secure a growth dividend by involving regions more closely in our economic and social modernisation. this is what is at stake in the present discussions on cohesion policy. the commission and parliament see the advantage of having our regions and cities on side and it can only be beneficial if their role as key actors in lisbon and göteborg is enhanced. it is with these overall objectives in mind that i would like to give you the commission’s reactions to the proposed amendments, a reaction inspired by our common goals. the commission is grateful for your support on many key points. i will list some of them. we have a common view on the architecture of the policy, one built around the objectives of regional competitiveness and employment, regional cooperation in a number of forms and of course convergence. it is vital to boost the growth of the poorest regions and close the wealth gap between them and the rest of the union. here eu cohesion policy has a starring role to play in raising aggregate productivity growth in the union as a whole. we have a common view on the imperative of concentrating finance on the poorest regions. i fully share your opinion that the national strategic reference framework should be the object of the agreement between the member states and the commission. this agreement should provide the basis for the final decision of the commission, in line with article 26 of the draft general regulation. we also have a common view on the essential role of cohesion policy in the drive towards a modern knowledge-based economy. that is why it is important for the council to adopt strategic orientations for the union as a whole and why we propose that member states should draw up national strategies for the pursuit of these objectives. the report before you supports this view. however, i must tell this house that the battle is not yet won. we still have some way to go, therefore, to transform this part of the commission proposal and the views of the european council into a political reality. the commission and parliament also have a common view on the importance of territorial cohesion or, to put it another way, the understanding that economic modernisation will benefit if special attention is paid to particular places in europe. the present urban initiative that was added to cohesion policy at the insistence of this house is a major success and the commission wants to build on it by creating a special place not only for cities but also for rural areas. we have proposed a special programme for the outermost regions and welcome your support. these are some of the points where the resolutions before parliament offer firm support for the commission’s proposals. others suggested by your rapporteurs will be taken on board by the commission. perhaps i can give one or two examples. your resolution suggested that cohesion policy will be strengthened by better cooperation between erdf co-financed operations and other community policies. i fully share your view and i am working to bring this about. however, we all need to understand that the pursuit of this goal and the requirement that we concentrate our scarce financial resources mean that some kinds of project can no longer figure amongst our priorities. you also suggest the maintenance of a specific strength for inter-regional cooperation within the objective for european territorial cooperation. the commission accepts this. you have proposed that the interoperability between the regional and social funds be increased from 5% to 10%. this gives greater flexibility to regional and national programme managers and thus ensures a close link in some cases between investment and training. the commission believes this to be very useful and accepts the proposal. in the particular case of mr olbrycht’s report on european grouping for cross-border cooperation, i am pleased to be able to tell you that the commission accepts most of parliament’s amendments. most important is the proposal that the registration of european groupings should be subject to national laws and associations. discussing the amendments that the commission cannot accept is always a more delicate matter. here i will refer to one or two cases and hope that my explanations of the reasons behind the commission’s approach will convince the house. i have already spoken of the need to focus cohesion policy on economic modernisation. i have also said that this is especially important for the regional competitiveness and employment objective. in this branch of the policy financial resources are particularly limited and, furthermore, we need to be able to demonstrate the added value to the overall economic situation. in that light, i am worried by the amendments that seek to enlarge the scope of the policy, especially the regional competitiveness objective. i understand why members might believe the door should be opened a little wider here and there, but i would ask you to accept that, if we do not take great care, the policy will lose its ability to address key issues and key areas. we have to find an appropriate balance. for example, i do not believe that it would be appropriate to widen the scope of the policy generally to cover operating aid, or to soften the conditions covering land purchase. this is not because of a lack of sympathy; it is an acceptance of the overriding need to concentrate the policy on the main challenges. there are two particular points i should mention in this connection: vat and housing. the vat and housing discussions arise from an effort by the commission to simplify the regulation by clearly listing elements of expenditure that are not eligible for funding. with regard to vat, the discussions in the council and the amendments put forward by honourable members demonstrate that this part of the commission’s proposal creates some problems, especially in new member states. we want to avoid a position where erdf cofinance goes straight into member states’ budgets by cofinancing vat payments. that position is, i am sure, shared by this house. at the same time i hear from you about problems: the cost for some beneficiaries, for example voluntary organisations and local governments, because the vat they are obliged to pay is not recoverable. in the coming weeks the commission will therefore reflect on its proposal with a view to finding a solution to your concerns. much the same is true about housing, although the solution to the problem might not necessitate a change in the commission’s proposal. again, the commission does not consider that housing expenditure should be eligible for co-financing under cohesion policy. that is not a change from past practice. it is merely a clarification. it is clear today from the amendments proposed by members and from discussions in the council that what was intended as a clarification might lead to confusion, thus complicating the lives of programme managers. the way out appears to be to make a common declaration with the council that spells out the sort of investments associated with housing that are eligible for erdf co-financing. thus we would make clear, for example, that investments to improve the energy efficiency of housing are eligible for co-financing and that the same is true for investments to improve the environment around social housing. another area covered by members’ amendments is the automatic decommitment rule known as the n+2 rule, which will become applicable to the cohesion fund after 2007, since the commission is proposing to move from the present project approach to the programme approach. this is the discipline that lies at the heart of the present high-quality performance of official policy programmes and is having beneficial effects on the ground. it turns out to be a strong incentive to efficient and rapid implementation of the programmes. we recognise, however, that the application of this rule for the cohesion fund could bring difficulties, especially in the new member states, as the major focus of this fund is on large infrastructure projects where the investment cycle and public procurement procedures are considerably longer and more complex. we do not underestimate these problems. for this reason, we have been working together with the presidency and the member states in order to reconcile the requirements of proper financial management and discipline with the specific nature of the cohesion fund. the commission cannot accept some suggestions by honourable members that aim to alter the conditions for the implementation of the policy. here, of course, we have to remember the importance of achieving sound financial management which leads us to maintain clarity and a clear distinction between the general regulation and the erdf regulations. we have to remember the importance of decentralised management and the role of the regions and member states in defining development strategies. we also have to ensure that the regulations that emerge can be clearly understood and followed by programme managers and that they do not contain political messages or statements of intent. it is on those grounds that the commission is unable to accept a number of amendments. you are fully aware of the difficult conditions under which the debate on the future financial framework is taking place. the commission needs your full support to ensure that an ambitious cohesion policy to achieve lisbon and göteborg objectives can be implemented by 2007. by adopting your reports, you are giving a clear signal to the council of your determination to take up this important challenge. by choosing to discuss its position on the future shape of cohesion policy now, this parliament is sending the message that there is no time to lose. you are signalling that you want to secure a medium-term future for a cohesion policy before the end of the year. the commission supports you in this. we are doing all we can to ensure that the necessary decisions are taken as soon as possible under the british presidency, so that the member states and regions have new cohesion policy programmes ready to come into operation at the start of 2007.

exclude any instrument, directive or free market organisation, or any model, with or without separation of activities, for the consolidation of post-market activities. it seems to me, however, likely that legislation will be needed to remove legislative and fiscal obstacles, possibly to adapt the european competition rules to these activities and finally to ensure the transparency and accounting separation necessary for the exercise of healthy competition. i conclude by saying that it is time to move forward in this area because european consolidation is under way, without control, and that after having achieved market harmonisation, post-market harmonisation is an urgent need if we are to reap the benefits of all our work in the framework of the financial services action plan.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the european parliament, in particular the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy and the rapporteur, mrs isler béguin, for their detailed and constructive report. i would also like to thank my colleagues from the committee on budgets and the committee on financial perspectives for their contribution to the report on life+. life+ is the instrument proposed by the commission to finance the implementation of community environmental policy for the period 2007-2013. in parallel with implementation, the programme provides funds to support better environmental governance and funding for information and communication actions. the proposal is a positive measure for financing the environment. as the reports prepared by the commission for the council show, life+ provides for an average annual increase in funding of 21% compared to current levels. in addition, it is envisaged that the new programme will move from a project-based approach to one based on national programmes. this gives member states greater flexibility to meet their most pressing environmental needs. this approach implies even greater subsidiarity than today. regional and local actors, who are often on the receiving end of environmental legislation, will thus be able to have a say in the design and implementation of the programme. i am aware of parliament's assessment of the commission proposal. however, the commission considers that the main environmental costs could be better financed by financial instruments with high economic power, i.e. the structural fund programmes and the rural development programme. to date, we have had three notable developments in our efforts to secure integration policy: first, the adoption on 21 june of the regulation on rural development; the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the creation of a european network of national networks for the protection of the environment, the creation of a european network of national networks for the protection of the environment, the creation of a european network of national networks for the protection of the environment, the creation of a european network of national networks for the protection of the environment, the creation of a european network of national networks for the protection of the environment, the creation of a european network for the protection of the environment, the creation of a european network for the protection of the environment, the creation of a european network for the protection of the environment, and the creation of a european network for the protection of the environment. the commission is therefore implementing a policy of integration in the field of the environment. life+ would be unable to undertake projects of the scale and scope envisaged in these programmes. life+ is therefore called upon to complement these programmes by focusing on the development of environmental policy, as parliament has often called for, on supporting the implementation of policy, a point on which parliament has often expressed its interest, on improving environmental governance with the involvement of civil society and on disseminating information so that the european citizen can understand the purpose and impact of environmental legislation. the commission's proposal is therefore in line with the wishes expressed by parliament and, through it, by the european citizens.

with natura 2000. moreover, it is entirely possible for member states to focus an even bigger share of their national envelope on natura 2000 financing if they so wish. two days ago the commission networking, awareness-raising and ngo financing. in addition, certain aspects, such as eco-innovation are clearly covered by other programmes, in this case by the competitiveness and innovation programme. to contain this in life+ would introduce the risk of the double financing of projects, something the court of auditors feels very strongly about. secondly, on procedure: the commission commission can accept amendment 25 in part, as amended by amendment 43. the commission cannot accept any other amendments. in conclusion, the life+ proposal offers a flexible financial instrument for the environment. i hope that we can find common ground in the short term to take this proposal forward.
