the rapporteur. mr president, the first aim of this recommendation is the protection of minors on the internet. the internet is a great tool, without borders, open to all, and which makes available to everyone a wealth of knowledge, documentation and a capacity for exchanging information that has never been equalled in the history of our humanity. in a few short years, the internet has changed the face of the world. but it is the duty of the legislator to prevent this formidable communication tool from becoming a harmful, even dangerous, tool, especially for minors who are using it more and more frequently. in fact, young children today spend more time in front of the computer than in front of the tv. they don't know it, but they're not always safe on the net. they are faced with new dangers that can cause deep and irreversible trauma. i would like to give some figures on this situation, which is becoming increasingly worrying. more than one in three children has unwittingly come across violent, pornographic or pedophilic images on the internet. there are currently about 260 million pornographic web pages and 470 pedophile web sites on the web. it's been estimated that there are over 1.5 million images identified on the net of children, very young children, being sexually exploited or abused. between 2003 and 2004, child pornography on the internet increased by 70 percent. an average of 30 seconds is the time it takes for a teenager to be sexually assaulted by a predator - an adult posing as a teenager just to get the teenager's picture, address, and a date. the pedophile trade generates $20 billion a year worldwide. in france alone, it represents a turnover of 50 million euros a year. in view of this, we must not, we cannot, remain inactive. it's time to protect children and the most vulnerable from all harmful content, legal or illegal. it's time to hold all actors accountable for the reality of the internet. the need is all the greater now that new technologies are ubiquitous, most often freely accessible in schools, homes, internet cafes and, in the future, on mobile phones. these are new ways of giving young people a way out of the control of the authorities. today, self-regulation is no longer enough. we must go further and call on all actors to take responsibility, politicians, industry and educators. responsibility for policy, first. it is up to governments and education ministers to implement specific internet education programmes for all children, teachers and parents. they also have to organise information campaigns to finally alert public opinion to the dangers of the internet. they also need to extend the use of telephone hotlines to enable harmful content to be reported and to encourage the establishment of a european green number accessible to all. finally, we propose that the commission should consider the creation of a .kid domain name exclusively for children's content. industrial responsibility, then. the existence of charters, codes of conduct and quality procedures is no longer sufficient. it's time for web hosts to offer easy-to-use parenting software, subscriptions to access services specifically for children with automatic filtering at the source. it is also time for creators and producers to make an effort to describe their sites so that they can be classified. the responsibility of educators, that is to say, parents and teachers. children are exposed to information and images on the internet at an increasingly early age. only an educational approach, including in school curricula, will allow better use of the internet. this of course requires training and information for teachers, but also for parents. that is the essence of our proposals. but this recommendation also aims to allow the use of a right of reply in all online media. this right of reply already exists satisfactorily for print and audiovisual media, but not for online media. at present, in most member states, there is no provision for this. it is therefore appropriate to establish the minimum principles at european level for the exercise of this right of reply for all new electronic means of communication. this recommendation will, with the support of our parliament, which i thank for the quality of its work, improve the use of the internet and will, i hope, help to restore confidence. europe is now facing a serious crisis, a crisis of its institutions, its functioning, its budget, its identity and its values. but i want to make a vow that at least when it comes to our children's future, we can regain the ability to act and bring about the changes that are necessary to protect them. it's the least we can do.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. i am very pleased to be able to present to you this evening the commission's proposal for a regulation on paediatric medicinal products. it is a very important proposal which will improve the health of children in europe and will avoid suffering in many families because of children who have to die prematurely. at present, more than 50% of medicines used in children in the european union are not tested on children or approved for children. this means that we can't always be sure that these drugs are effective or safe. that is a risk that i think none of us are prepared to take any longer. the commission proposal directly addresses this aspect of public health. it will stimulate high-quality research and achieve the development and authorisation of high-quality, high-safety and high-efficacy paediatric medicines. the proposal not only addresses this important aspect of public health, but also aims to stimulate innovation and competition and contribute to growth and employment in the european union. i would like to thank and congratulate mrs grossetête, the rapporteur for the committee on the environment, for her work and efforts in completing this report. you have done a wonderful job! i would also like to thank mrs toia, the rapporteur for the committee on industry, and all the members of both committees for their support of the proposal. i would like to come straight to the specific point which i know has been the subject of very intense debate in parliament. i am referring to the commission's proposal for a six-month extension of the supplementary protection certificate for the products in question. this is one of the most fundamental provisions of our proposal. without this provision, the proposal is of little value. let me first explain why we prefer a fixed extension of the supplementary protection certificate to a variable extension. a fixed extension is easy to use and predictable. it creates a low administrative burden and is compatible with existing patent law. in contrast, a variable extension of the supplementary protection certificate would be contrary to the principles of patent law and would not promote innovation. such a provision would be impracticable in practice, since it would require a precise economic analysis of each medicinal product. i also doubt the justice of a variable solution. a solution like that is based on sales figures. we should remember one thing: the success of a drug does not tell us anything about the innovation that a drug represents; it also does not say what research costs have been incurred. i would like to make it clear that the commission is very firm on this point and i do not think that the commission sees any possibility of compromise here. the commission has already proposed a six-month extension of the supplementary protection certificate. on the basis of our impact assessment, which we have carried out very thoroughly, we believe that this period ensures that the objectives of the proposal are proportionate to the costs and benefits to public health, industry and public budgets in health. the commission can in principle support the amendment which calls for a review of the paediatric regulation so that the consequences, and above all the financial impact, of bonuses and incentives can be properly assessed. we need to ensure that any review also takes into account the intended public health benefits of this regulation. finally, the financial impact of the regulation should be assessed only when sufficient data are available. i have not, for obvious reasons, commented on every amendment. the commission's position on all the proposed amendments has, however, been forwarded to parliament's services. the commission's position is set out in the annex. the proposal for a regulation on paediatric medicines is an important proposal for children's health, for innovation and for competitiveness. i am sure that today's debate will show that we are on the right track here. i would like to conclude by saying with all the urgency that we are talking about the welfare and health of children who have not been helped so far. this is more important than the interests of any pharmaceutical industry lobby groups!
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i have been waiting for this moment for a long time, because for several years our parliament has been calling for this specific european regulation in favour of paediatric medicines. commissioner, you have explained it very well: it seems inconceivable that our children today cannot have access to a therapy adapted to their needs. it is a reality. in 2005, a very large number of medicines that were given to children were not developed for them. often the products used for the youngest are the same as those prescribed for adults. use only in decreasing doses. however, the metabolism of a child differs from that of an adult. children therefore need a specific form of medication that is adapted not only to make it better tolerated but also to make it more effective and safer. that is the subject of this regulation and i thank all the members who have taken part in it. my report makes great progress and is supported by many members. the aim of the proposals is to make the work of the paediatric committee, which will be set up within the european medicines agency, more readable, to prevent additional clinical trials being carried out on children when they are not necessary, to promote the transparency of devices, to reduce administrative delays, to strengthen pharmacovigilance, to introduce a requirement for paediatric research for each new medicinal product for adults, provided that this system does not delay the marketing of the innovative medicinal product, to ask the paediatric committee to draw up an inventory of paediatric needs, and finally to create a european research fund to finance studies on medicinal products which no longer have intellectual protection but which could be very useful for children. however, the central point of this text is still the one related to inducement. i've been working on this a lot. i have listened to a lot and, after discussing it with all of you, i think that the proposal for a fixed incentive, namely a six-month extension of the supplementary protection certificate, is the best possible solution. this is the most fair and pragmatic timeframe we can find. i said six months, not five. the united states has a recognized system with a six-month delay. why should europe not do the same? i admit that i do not understand this amendment suggested by mr maaten very well. mr maaten, we always ask the european parliament to look for the best solutions through benchmarking. well, the united states has a good practice in this; since they got that regulation, about 100 pediatric drugs have benefited american children. why should we not be able to give the same support to pharmaceutical research in europe? i feel that this is a carpet salesman's discussion between us, and i regret it, because it is a public health issue for children. i am sorry, mr maaten, that we cannot agree on this six-month deadline. research is by definition random and if the european union wants, as you all want, to develop this strategic sector, we cannot create a watered-down system or introduce vague measures. some colleagues have put forward a proposal based on a proportional reward. but this system is too restrictive. i asked my colleagues some important questions, public health questions. i am still waiting for the replies of those who advocate this proportionality. in fact, i wonder why the commission has been silent for so long, as we have been waiting for information which has never come from the authors of these amendments. this is about saving children's lives, not keeping a book. proportionality puts the number of products sold in front of the column "lives saved". under the proportional system, three months plus three months, or four plus four, the second part would be granted according to whether or not a sales volume or turnover was achieved. the danger of this system, in my view, is that we are moving from a health logic to a market logic. why would you do that? there is no european price for the drug. each member state sets this price and, as we know, there are very wide variations. with the logic of sales revenue, the laboratories will take their calculators, choose countries based on the prices they charge and not on health needs. secondly, who will be able to verify sales figures? some colleagues suggested the use of an independent audit, but did not specify the procedures to be followed. there is no evaluation, no cost, no additional time involved in this bureaucratic procedure, and no possible recourse in case of conflict. the european medicines agency itself tells us that this system is unrealistic, that it cannot afford it. so what's the advantage of this proposal? the proportional system is not good, it is not applicable. the quotation i am proposing is not based on the drug itself but on studies conducted under the authority of the paediatric committee. i ask you to evaluate this condition carefully. as regards the impact of this measure on the public health budgets of our states, a study presented to the council estimates that with six fixed months, the increase in health expenditure would be small, between 0.7 and 1%. finally, i wanted to include in the amendments a revision clause on incentives. the commission will have to take stock of the situation in six years' time, stating precisely under what conditions the six months were granted, with what costs and what benefits. we have the opportunity to turn this text from speeches into action. let us stop being philosophers and be pragmatic. let's not make a mistake. the failure to establish a stable framework for promoting research in europe is to favour american and asian industry. this would be a political, scientific and health hazard. what is europe for? this regulation can demonstrate to our fellow citizens how useful it is. this is a matter which affects everyone and which can only be resolved at community level. no member state can support research policy in the pharmaceutical industry on its own. your vote will be decisive. if we say yes to a six-month fixed incentive, our children will soon be able to benefit from appropriate and safe medicines thanks to the european union.
we have wanted this text, we have been waiting for it for a long time and we are all very pleased to know that it will soon allow children to be better cared for. but we must be demanding. we will have the opportunity tomorrow to improve this draft regulation so that it best serves children and public health, and we will improve it if we vote for the amendments which guide the research and marketing of medicines with greater added value, offering real therapeutic benefit; how can the aim of limiting clinical trials on children be achieved without limiting the number of medicines that will be placed on the market? if the added value of the medicinal product were taken into account, it would avoid unnecessary trials on children. tomorrow we can also improve the text by voting on amendments which propose greater transparency of pharmacovigilance data and their public access. the financial question is also important for the balance of our social security systems and the guarantee of access to health care for all. it is upstream, when it comes to finding the right financial incentive for the pharmaceutical industries to take a greater interest in paediatric medicines. it is for all european citizens, because it is public money that indirectly finances these financial incentives in the form of an extension of commercial exclusivity. that is why, in view of the results of the impact studies, in view of the enormous gaps between 1 and 4 million euros, it seems to me that we should at least be able to offer the industries a two-tier system: a fixed incentive of three months and a three-month extension depending on the level of profit generated by the marketed medicine. we all want what's best for the children as soon as possible. but no hypocrisy. those who spoke of urgency did not want to support the proposal to reduce the time between the marketing authorization, which is two years, and the marketing. that is why we will have further meetings and we will really see what we can do for the health of european children.

mr president, there is a growing and very worrying number of situations around the world in which states use the argument of the fight against terrorism to impose a policy of repression on other groups, not terrorists, or to violate the most fundamental rights of suspected terrorists. there are many examples in pakistan, china, morocco, saudi arabia, tunisia, yemen, kenya and many other countries, and in many cases, as the un rapporteur, mrs jilani, has pointed out, human rights defenders are among the first victims of the fight against terrorism. in tunisia, for example, the government passed an anti-terrorism law in 2003, a law purporting to support international efforts to combat terrorism, which in fact infringes on the basic rights of citizens, the peaceful activities of civil society, trade unions and political parties. as regards the united states, we know of the abuses committed in guantanamo bay and abu ghraib, where hundreds of non-us citizens are held indefinitely without being prosecuted and without any prospect of trial. we cannot ignore the very serious allegations, particularly in the united states, reported by international ngos such as amnesty, that a number of individuals arrested in connection with the war on terror are being held in unknown locations. they are backed up by official reports of the situation of ghost prisoners, held in secret prisons and transferred from one place to another to hide them from the attention of the international committee of the red cross. equally serious are the accusations made by ngos such as human rights watch against the countries of the european union - the netherlands, the united kingdom, germany, austria, sweden - which do not hesitate to send alleged terrorists back to countries such as syria, egypt or uzbekistan, where the risk of torture and ill-treatment is very high. such practices are contrary to international human rights standards, in particular the principle of non-refoulement. the member states of the union, as we see, are not left behind. there is also cause for concern about a draft recommendation from the european commission to the member states on non-profit associations, mr frattini, which states in its introduction, i quote: 'there is evidence that non-profit organizations have been exploited for the financing of terrorism and other criminal activities.' such a generalization, such a lack of nuance in a commission document is particularly unforgivable and worrying.
mr president-in-office, commissioner, it is obviously necessary to rethink our fight against terrorism. we must eradicate terrorism from its roots, punish the perpetrators severely and pursue the leaders relentlessly, we agree. but it is essential that we stop with the "orthopedic" measures and consider a thoroughgoing treatment and new means of control. and let us repeat that these means of struggle must be in accordance with our legal rules, our rule of law and our democracies. we have raised the question of the abduction of european citizens and residents by the cia on the territory of the european union itself. some member states have initiated legal proceedings to clarify why these citizens may have been abducted and transferred to third countries where they were tortured. the commission acknowledges that this is a violation of fundamental rights but refuses to address this issue. the european union has a duty to protect the fundamental rights of its citizens. what can we say to their legitimate concern? the second point is that the european union must not be left to the mercy of the united states, which is the only country in the world that has a policy of combating terrorism. we must find in our societies, but also in the less developed countries, the means to combat exclusion and we must fight against all the injustices in the world. all advanced civilizations have understood that justice and fairness are the most effective ways to fight violence. on the other hand, it is necessary to teach, to educate, to provide critical equipment, to fight blindness when beings are capable of self-destruction, to end their lives when, for example, they have just given life as was the case with one of the london terrorists, we understand that it is absolutely necessary to act upstream. only early and effective integration into our societies can end this mental manipulation. it is necessary to understand that integration must not remain superficial and integration is not assimilation. every citizen of our states must feel truly recognized as a citizen, valued as a person. i repeat, where there is a sense of injustice, there is violence, there is hatred. and if you add to that climate the manipulation and the enslavement of weak minds, then you have terrorists. the range of measures is vast, but it is by activating all the levers that we will win. in conclusion, i would like to return to what you said, mr minister. we support you when you say that we must have deeper cooperation. we can certainly achieve more by sharing our experience, information and resources. we will only succeed at european level, but the european parliament wants to be fully involved, we will work together, so we will move forward.
in writing. i have recently received many letters from professionals in the hotel, catering and building industries expressing their legitimate concerns about a council common position on the exposure of workers to optical radiation. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. if it is understandable that the safety of workers exposed, for example in industrial environments, to artificial optical radiation should be improved and better regulated, why should we also be interested in so-called "natural" optical radiation? why would we want to regulate the working conditions of people who are more or less exposed to the sun? these proposals with unverifiable results, besides being ridiculous, obviously promise an increase in constraints, especially for small and mediumsized enterprises. against the background of the economic, social and identity crises and the international insecurity that is shaking our countries, this kind of incredible proposal once again demonstrates the inadequacy of the reality of these europeans who want to control everything. that is why i opposed this new gadget which risks "overshadowing" many of our companies by this administrative over-billing and financial suffocation.
in writing. this relationship that starts with a good feeling quickly becomes an unlikely catch-all. the explanatory statement started well, however, and the interest was obviously to consider greater protection of minors against the scourges of pornography, paedophilia, violence in images and content, but also - and this was forgotten - the provocation to use drugs or dangerous behaviour, recruitment and enlistment in fanatical and terrorist companies. the subject was broad enough and our policies unfortunately weak enough to take a more serious look at these very serious facts and try to respond to them in order to protect our children. instead, the report is misleading, scattered and mixes everything and anything, pornography, of course, but also the fight against discrimination, teacher training and finally the right of reply, which we really do not see how it can be of any help to minors. the report's usual technique in this house is to drown the political fish in a sea of good intentions. it makes the text once again more obscure, abstract, ideological and therefore totally ineffective.

in writing. i support the report in its main lines. however, i would have some reservations about its approach to tourism development, which is too focused on environmental and consumer protection. the voice of consumers and environmentalists is already being heard in full in the european institutions: consumer protection and environmental protection are the subject of specific titles in the treaties and entire directorates-general of the commission are concerned with these two poles respectively. so why would you want to outbid in these areas? i believe that any tourism policy should be focused primarily on the economic activity generated by the tourist industry and that a balanced approach to the different poles can only be achieved if the interests of tourist service providers (hotel operators, restaurants, tour operators, crafts of all kinds, private transport services, etc.) are fully protected. the rapporteur is right to say that tourism is a factor of growth, but in order for it to be fully so, it is also necessary to enable our national economic players to be competitive and to avoid over-regulation and over-taxation, as is the case in france.
in writing. as early as 1957, europe set up private schools to educate the children of staff of the european communities together with accepting, for a very limited number, children from outside. what was the spirit of this policy of exception, applying a principle of corporatist preference, which is condemned in other areas by the same europe? do what i say, but don't do what i do! this system of european schools thus promotes the concept of european citizenship which is for europe what the concept of national preference should be for france and the other free nations of europe. but the development of these schools is not intended to build the europe of nations to which we aspire, but to promote european integration; the commission has also adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of accidents. these schools are not only discriminatory towards non-european civil servants but also towards all children in europe. they also create a system of exorbitant privileges for the sole use of officials of the european institutions in order to reproduce a single and obligatory european model: a federal europe through integration.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating my colleague mr bowis, as has been done before, on his excellent, comprehensive and balanced work on serious and neglected diseases. the report is a hot topic on the eve of the united nations summit in new york, where the millennium development goals will be the focus of debate. we need not remind you that we already know that these goals will not be achieved within the time limits we set ourselves and that they are about to be added to the list of promises broken by the rich countries. because three of the eight major objectives of the millennium development goals concern health issues, my colleague mr bowis's work must allow for a better reflection of this reality. i hope that the european parliament will not only raise awareness but also send a strong and clear message to the member states to revive the objectives. the health problems faced by the poorest countries are fuelling the spiral of underdevelopment. the simple fact is that those who need treatment the most today do not have access to it. why would you do that? either because they are expensive or because basic research and development of research is insufficient or non-existent for some serious and neglected diseases. in addition, where these medicines exist and are affordable, they may not be available to the population because they are not adapted to the specific health conditions of those countries. the problem is more serious and structural; while most basic research is carried out by the public sector, drug development is almost entirely in the hands of the private sector. without a guarantee of profits, the pharmaceutical industry sees no point in investing in the development of new molecules. the commission has therefore decided to grant a number of patents to the companies concerned. the problem is that the majority of the population with little purchasing power in the countries targeted by the millennium development goals cannot afford to buy the vital medicines. this logic also leads to artificially high prices. in the era of globalisation, colleagues, everyone's health must be everyone's responsibility. as far as medicines are concerned, it is the needs that must determine our strategy for action in response to the global health and development problem. we must also encourage and support developing countries to spend at least 20% of their budget on health policies, investment in research and development or adaptation of intellectual property rules, since the financial resources of these countries are not sufficient on their own. there can be no progress in today's world on the major health challenge without a joint commitment from the public and private sectors. the pharmaceutical industry must abandon its exclusively profit-oriented approach and reassess its commitments and priorities, particularly in the area of research and development and marketing. the public authorities, on the other hand, must define a legal framework, set guidelines and offer prospects that guarantee the general interest while respecting the interests of each individual. i therefore draw the attention of the council and the commission to the need to take initiatives: to draw up a new international treaty on medical research and development, to include in the 7th eu research framework programme a specific reference to research and development for neglected diseases which would be guaranteed funding, to ensure that the doha declaration on compulsory licensing is not called into question by bilateral trade agreements, and finally to promote the early entry into force of the community regulation currently being discussed between parliament and the council, so as to enable the generic drug industry to produce treatments which will avoid catastrophic health effects on a large part of our planet.

president. - mr president, commissioner, on 28 august mr annan said: 'we are all responsible for the famine in niger.' should we do the same? i myself wrote to you in april, asking you to take account of the threat of famine in niger. i should like to take this opportunity to thank you for your reply. but we still have to wait for the horror images to appear on our screens before we intervene. it is true that until june the nigerian government, which has long denied the seriousness of the crisis, refused to distribute free food rations, saying that it did so to avoid destabilising the market, when we know very well that these moderately priced and subsidised foodstuffs were unavailable and unaffordable for the poorest. so we always come back to the same question: what are we doing for this dying, sinking africa? the world has finally given some thought to the fate of niger. help is finally here. donors realized that this crisis was a real famine, affecting a third of the population of nigeria, or 3.6 million people, which is huge. what we can still ask in our resolution is that the aid to these populations be commensurate with the demand and that, of course, it reach the most vulnerable without exception. but i'm not going to tell you anything about that either. i am thinking in particular of the nomadic populations, for example, who are not necessarily on the world food programme's lists and who have lost almost all their livestock, which is also starving. for example, there have been a number of suicides among the peuls, a proud people who cannot stand begging. this famine also reminds us that we must have a genuine development aid policy. i know very well, commissioner, that you know how to put figures and actions behind words. so what is the commission's sustainable development plan for niger? member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the food crisis in niger is unbearable. it is unbearable because populations, especially children, are in nutritional distress and in vital need of help. but the way in which this crisis has been exploited, to criticise the slowness of the donors and accuse them of not assisting people in danger, calls for a few comments on my part which are simply intended to present an objective analysis of the situation in niger and to give correct information, at least on european aid. niger is one of the poorest countries on the planet. it is one of the driest areas in the sahel, where food balance is still precarious. food security is extremely fragile and malnutrition is a recurring problem. the slightest climatic disturbance, such as insufficient rainfall, or crop destruction by predators, whether birds or locusts, the slightest disturbance in market prices immediately cause food safety problems. people are using up their stocks too soon, the granaries are empty as early as april, food is scarce in the markets or is offered at skyrocketing prices. people have to wait until the next harvest, in september, october, provided, of course, that the rainy season is going well. the crisis we are facing is, however, more severe than in previous years. the locust infestations in late summer 2004 and the lack of rainfall in several parts of the sahel, and particularly in parts of niger, resulted in a very poor harvest. as early as september 2004, the commission has allocated €25.5 million for locust control in the sahel countries most affected, i.e. senegal, chad, mauritania, mali and niger, and funds have been allocated to the fao (food and agriculture organization of the united nations). in february and march 2005, the first signs of a severe food shortage began to emerge in niger. there has been a rapid increase in the price of grain, a fall in the price of livestock, a massive and premature transhumance of herds and a shortage of local food in the markets. in march, the nigerian government, using data from the national food crisis prevention and management facility, largely supported by the commission, released money for the purchase of 42 000 tonnes of cereals sold at low prices and distributed food in exchange for labour-intensive work. the world food programme, which supports the national scheme, launched an appeal for eur 2.3 million, to which the commission immediately responded by allocating eur 1 million. at that time, no one, not the government, not the wfp, not the ngos, could assess, in the absence of precise overall data, whether this was a slightly more difficult weld than in other years or a serious food crisis. the commission then contacted aid organizations to find out their analysis and, above all, their plan, since no request for funding had been received at that time. no ngo, no operator with whom we are currently working has contacted us to ask for help, as is normally the case since, as you know, the commission does not intervene itself in this type of intervention operation. it was only in late may or early june that nutritional surveys conducted in certain parts of the country revealed the growing crisis. that's when the humanitarian partners came forward. the commission then took two emergency decisions, via echo, for a total amount of eur 6.3 million. that's the timeline. what about today? a recent echo evaluation mission concluded that nutritional needs are now being met satisfactorily, although implementation is lagging behind. the commission is of course prepared to step up its assistance if additional needs arise. what is needed now is good coordination of the partners on the ground, so that relief can be targeted and accelerated. the european commission also provided €2 million for mali, €4.6 million for eritrea and €4.5 million for ethiopia, which is also facing a food and nutrition crisis. this crisis is a challenge to us and it deserves that we collectively learn all the lessons from it. at my level, i see two main ones. firstly, with regard to niger, it is imperative, beyond humanitarian efforts, to find a lasting solution to the country's vulnerability by strengthening the food security strategy. this is exactly the policy that the commission has been pursuing for years, in its attempt to provide a lasting response to this crisis. i am thinking in particular of irrigation projects, the construction of reservoirs, etc., which are financed by the community. the nigerian national early warning and nutritional detection mechanisms must be supported and strengthened. rural development and market organisation programmes are part of this objective, as are school canteens. the commission is niger's largest donor. the ninth edf has provided the country with a financial envelope of almost eur 400 million, including eur 60.6 million for the development of food security. the food security budget line allocates eur 15 million to a programme (2004 to 2006) to support the national food crisis prevention and management system. the commission is, however, almost alone, with a few european countries, in helping this country. discussions on the post-9th edf allocation, which will begin next year, will certainly take into account the lessons learned from this food crisis. but it must be said that whatever the commission does for niger, the challenge is immense. it will be difficult to raise it without greater development aid from the international community as a whole. the increase in development aid is, as you know, the commission's priority and that is the message we will be delivering in new york. secondly, as regards the response of international aid organizations, i regret to say that it could have been better coordinated, better coordinated with the nigerian government, between aid organizations, whether ngos or un agencies, both in the alert and detection phase and in the crisis response and needs targeting phase. the commission is ready to support an independent evaluation to identify ways of improving aid coordination in such a situation. a word about the action of the donors. i am not hiding the fact that i am disturbed by the statements made by some humanitarian organizations. as a donor, the commission could have acted more quickly if it had found humanitarian organizations on the ground last spring, as it sought to do. but i can see that once the media machine got going, there was no problem finding partners willing to come to niger. i have always praised the expertise and commitment of the humanitarian organizations that are our partners, but the comments i have heard from some of them about the food crises in africa, whether in the sahel, the horn of africa or southern africa, saying that the problem is inadequate donor response, surprises me. it's an intellectually limiting argument. the food crises in africa - as you know very well - are complex phenomena, the result of many factors, the climate, the demography, the health of the population - just think of the disastrous effects of aids in southern africa, for example, because of the lack of physical resistance - political governance and economic governance. i do not think it is entirely fair to say that the aid of donors will be enough to prevent these crises. i also reject a somewhat paternalistic and moralistic attitude. i can assure you that the commission will remain extremely vigilant and i hope that in future, when we become aware of a problem and an appeal is made, we will find operators and partner organisations to enable us to work more quickly.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am going to speak on behalf of my colleague, mrs benita ferrero-waldner. although significant progress has been made on human rights issues in china in recent years, notably in the area of economic and social rights, the european union remains concerned about the human rights situation in general in the country and in particular about the restrictions on civil and political rights that have been implemented. respect for human rights is indeed an essential factor in the union's external policy. the commission has regularly raised this issue frankly and openly with the chinese authorities, both through political dialogue - including at the highest level as was recently the case at the last bilateral summit held in beijing on 5 september - and through the bilateral dialogue specifically devoted to human rights. in the framework of the euro-chinese dialogue, the issue of freedom of belief, religion, expression and association has always been at the forefront of the european union's priorities. the union has repeatedly expressed its deep concern in particular at the situation of individuals who are persecuted or deprived of their fundamental rights for openly practicing their faith, whatever their religion or belief. a number of the imprisoned religious mentioned by the honourable members are included in the list of individual cases which the union systematically transmits to its chinese partners in the framework of the human rights dialogue. in addition, the european union has made several formal approaches to the chinese authorities through its representatives in beijing. tenzin deleg rinpoche and pastor zhang rongliang - to cite recent examples - are among those who have been targeted. the abolition of the death penalty, or at least the introduction of a moratorium on its application, china's rapid ratification of the international covenant on civil and political rights and cooperation with un mechanisms are also among the priority topics regularly discussed with the chinese authorities. in the latter case, the european union made particular efforts, at the last session of the human rights dialogue held in luxembourg on 24 and 25 february, to ensure that the un special rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief could visit china as soon as possible. the european union certainly intends to continue and deepen the dialogue with beijing in the field of human rights through seminars on these issues which, in addition to the dialogue, also raise awareness among some important actors of chinese civil society. we hope that the next session of the specific dialogue on human rights, to be held in beijing on 24 and 25 october, will make significant progress.

mr president, the wine market is facing major challenges. the united states remains a priority market for the european union with 60 million wine consumers and an average increase from 8 to 13 litres per capita per year over the last ten years. last year, the us market grew by 5.6% in volume. france is the third largest transatlantic exporter after italy and australia. in this context, the agreement on wine between the european union and the united states, which concludes the first phase of negotiations begun 20 years ago, should be welcomed. the united states threatened to blackmail european exporters by subjecting them to a heavy certification procedure. so, this autumn's new beaujolais would have been front and center. it would have been subject to additional analytical and certification checks. the agreement also made progress on the aspect of oenological practices. however, european producers consider these control protocols to be insufficient. they are opposed to practices such as flavoring, which is intended to give the wine fruit flavors. it's about the evolution of the definition of wine. they also insist on the protection of geographical names. the commissioner, in the second phase of the negotiations, will therefore have to ensure that the commitments made by the us authorities are respected: to stop using semi-generic wines such as burgundy, chablis, champagne and porto, to improve the protection of geographical indications and labelling. in this global wine market, often carried by the great american merchants, the grape variety has become a brand. i am not against the globalisation of the wine market, but i am against copies, i am against the standardisation of taste, i do not want a chardonnay mcdo. wine accompanies the cuisine, it is the trademark of the region where it was produced, it has the taste of the culture of the land, it symbolizes conviviality and living together. the diversity of appellations reflects the diversity of wines, our cultural diversity. the mutual recognition of geographical indications, that is to say the designation of the place of production, will help to preserve our respective cultural identities, to stimulate our trade with the united states, but above all to encourage european winegrowers who have for years been constantly improving the quality of their production to meet the demands and the pleasure of consumers like us.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to present my report on the role of territorial cohesion in regional development in a few minutes. it should be recalled that the inclusion of this concept in the policies of the union has been the subject of a recurrent and insistent request from a large number of european regions for several years. the accession of ten new member states, which has resulted in a widening of regional disparities and the emergence of new territorial inequalities, has given a particular expression to this major need. the drafters of the draft constitution for europe understood this well, since article 3 of the draft treaty mentions economic, social and territorial cohesion as one of the union's essential objectives. the problematic fate of the treaty would lead some regional policy makers, particularly at the level of the european commission, to exercise the greatest caution at the mere mention of a necessary territorial cohesion. we do not think that this is justified and i hope, madam commissioner, that you will share our view. the very great geographical, human and cultural diversity of the union's territory, in a relatively small area, represents a unique wealth on our planet, but if we are not careful, it can lead to serious risks of intolerable distortions for those who consider themselves to be its victims. this has unfortunately proved to be true, beyond all our fears, in the referendums in france and the netherlands on the draft european constitution. it is likely that public consultations on the same basis in many other member states would produce the same results. i therefore wanted my report to help answer the questions raised. how can citizens be reconciled with the european project? what is the future of europe? for our europe. one of the answers is provided by cohesion policy, the policy of solidarity which is the original model of the union and distinguishes it from a simple free trade area. in addition to having the necessary resources, which means that it must be taken into account in the financial perspective for 2007-13, it will be important that it takes into account the territorial dimension in all its aspects. territorial cohesion will thus represent an explicit basis, understandable to all europeans, for a coherent approach to the territory of the union. more specifically, for the implementation of territorial cohesion, i would like to indicate some principles and concrete measures. the principles are: the principle of equity between citizens throughout the territory, which implies in particular appropriate accessibility of services of general interest and services of general economic interest; the integration of the territorial dimension in the lisbon and gothenburg strategies; the polycentric development of the european territory; the role to be played by small and medium-sized towns and the connection with the rural world; strengthening all dimensions of territorial cooperation; decentralisation based on the regions that know best the needs and potential of their territories; multi-level governance and the involvement of non-public partners. one of the concrete proposals we are making to the commission is to set up three schemes. first, a mechanism for linking sectoral policies which have a strong impact on the development of territories with regional development policy. secondly, new territorial indicators, alongside gross domestic product, to measure the development of the regions and objectively assess the obstacles to this development. finally, a system for assessing the impact of the various community policies on territorial cohesion. another proposal concerns the preparation of a white paper on the territorial cohesion objective and in particular on how it should be integrated into the national strategic plans of the member states which they are currently implementing. i hope that tomorrow's vote will reflect the broad support of this house for an ambitious territorial cohesion policy.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of myself and my colleagues in the liberal and democratic group, i would like to say to mr guellec and mr marques that we have had the pleasure of working on their report, which is of course very much to our liking. i would like to focus on one of the points raised in mr guellec's report, which has some bearing on mr marques' report, since mr guellec has dealt with the role of urban centres and the surrounding areas. we have been talking about the concept of life pools for a number of years - i myself have been elected as a city councillor in reims, in champagne. the basins of life are the territories that encompass a city, whether small, medium or large, and all the rural territories that surround it at 5, 10, 15, 20 or, in the case of our capital of paris, france, up to 200 kilometres in the outskirts, where a number of people are found who, every day, travel from their place of work to their place of residence. it was therefore essential, in order to achieve the objectives of lisbon and gothenburg, that the european union should place the bulk of its interventions within the framework of harmonious, coherent territorial development. these pools of life, in particular, must play their full part, which is not the case at present. i was talking about traveling; it is clear that in all these areas of life, housing problems arise. housing is more expensive in the city centre, cheaper in the outskirts; people choose to live in the suburbs because it's quieter or because it's cheaper. all this leads to problems of daily commuting. we see villages depopulated a few kilometres from our cities, when in some of our neighbourhoods there are abominable concentrations of people. we find security issues, and i'll pass them along. it is therefore only natural that, in order to achieve our lisbon and gothenburg objectives, we must ensure real coherence in these pools of life, between the city centre, the immediate periphery, the near periphery and the far periphery. these difficulties, can we overcome them without too much effort? the answer is obviously no, given the multiplicity of actors involved. these are housing agencies, employment sector decision makers, and of course policy makers, operating at local, regional and national levels. we know how difficult it is to harmonize the positions of the various political organizations. in this respect, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam commissioner, i believe that the european union has a central role to play at the moment, to act as a catalyst, to ensure in the coming years that all these territories are truly brought into coherence, that they develop harmoniously in these pools of life. finally, mr marques, i said that i had great respect for your report and that we were very much in favour of it. i hope that in all our outermost regions, whether in small towns, in large cities or in any other area, the 1 100 million euros which we hope will be available will enable us to ensure the harmonious development that everyone is hoping for.

mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, while i welcome the work of mr marques, i would like to speak more specifically about the report on the role of territorial cohesion in regional development. i would first like to congratulate mr guellec on his excellent work and his relevant reflection on the concept of 'territorial cohesion', which seems to me to be the heart of community regional policy, which is more and more often called cohesion policy. the constitutional treaty makes territorial cohesion the objective of the european union alongside social and economic cohesion. so even though the ratification process has been difficult, as we know, it is an official recognition of the relevance, timeliness and importance of the territorial features of regional and cohesion policy. the latest enlargement confirms its imperative character. in my view, regional policy is primarily aimed at reducing disparities in development at regional and local level and is thus an indispensable counterweight to the policy of convergence and economic competitiveness. but cohesion is not opposed to convergence and competitiveness, which must be and remain complementary. while ensuring that the development of europe's most dynamic regions is not hindered so that they can play their role as the driving force of the european economy, cohesion policy is primarily intended to help the most disadvantaged and backward regions. the reformed regional and cohesion policy must also be integrated into the lisbon strategy, but above all it must ensure solidarity and equity between the territories and visible continuity of the efforts made previously in the former member states. so, for a harmonious and sustainable development of the european territory, territorial imbalances must be tackled. the diversity of the european area and the handicaps, often cumulative, of certain territories, whether natural, historical or demographic, such as the low population density or the imbalance in the age pyramid and the working population, must be taken into account. the additional costs faced by these regions must be measured and assisted so that these territories have the same opportunities for development as others and the people living there are not penalised. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i hope that the council will take them up.

regions, their importance for a better understanding of climate phenomena or their contribution in terms of cultural diversity. the great distance from the continental whole to which the outermost regions are integrated and the geographical proximity of other continents with which the european union has agreements are also sometimes sources of contradictions. i would like to conclude, mr president, by saying that this dual ownership offers a real prospect for the sustainable co-development of these areas, all of which are facing major challenges. the union's ability to respond to the question of the development of its ultraperiphery will be a testament to its capacity to be a decisive player in a controlled and fair globalisation.

on behalf of the ind/dem group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the railway issue is of interest to all the people and member states of the european union. geography has long shaped the transportation and politics of peoples. today, technology and the construction of major infrastructures are enriching the field and in turn conditioning the future of economic and cultural exchanges. in this area we have a role to play: to build bridges between nations, to promote trade. but not just any exchange! we need an exchange which enriches national specificities, because it is the complementarities which justify and underpin the usefulness of the exchange. we are glad to have texts which promote such free trade between sovereign peoples. yet, when we read the three reports before us, three simple principles that govern the order of nations, we seem to be mistreated. first, the principle of subsidiarity, which does not always seem to be respected. in transport, as elsewhere, we believe that whatever can be done at the level closest to the action should be done at that level. and only the strictly necessary will be reserved for the upper level. we do not understand why the sterckx report, which correctly quotes the international convention, cotif, is so quick to clutter the text with details of inflation which should be dealt with under that convention. we should be reviving this convention. in this case, the increase in the rights of persons with reduced mobility is an exception and is necessary. however, this requirement could be the subject of a simple injunction in principle addressed to cotif. in addition, why is there not a clearer distinction between the training of drivers and that of flight attendants in the excellent savary report, which also deals with the training of personnel at the same level? why not stick to different qualifications, since the jobs are so different? the second principle that we feel is being abused is respect for sovereignty. we cannot allow a necessary international transport organization to become a trojan horse to invade national law. the amended sterckx report systematically substitutes the term 'all passengers' for the term 'international rail passengers'. we cannot accept this subordination of national standards to international standards. a third principle that is abused is that of caution. it is imprudent when, in mr jarzembowski's report, amendment no 8 proposes a time limit of only three years for the introduction of major changes. you have to give time to time. to go too fast is to fail. it is also imprudent in the sterckx report to try to cover everything in one file, disability, ticketing, compensation in the event of an accident, penalties for poor service. it's not relevant to deal with everything. it is unwise not to state clearly that the railways must be subordinated first to freight and first to long-distance freight. it is unwise not to include these proposals in the report on highly competitive modes of transport beforehand. in conclusion, we acknowledge the commissioner's hard and worthwhile work but we remain once again doubtful in the face of such an avalanche of standards and the effectiveness of the methods of this parliament.

member of the commission. mr president, thank you for those remarks, of which i have taken due note. we will take them into account in our future work. i will begin by responding to the questions from members mohácsi, de groen-kouwenhoven and kallenbach. there are three camps of internally displaced persons in northern mitrovica for roma ashkali and egyptian people. these sites suffer from major lead pollution as a result of the activities of the former trepca mining complex and this poses a serious health risk to the inhabitants. in july 2004, the world health organization released a report on elevated platelet levels in those communities and recommended a set of emergency measures, including the evacuation of the centres. an agreement was signed in april 2005 by unmik, unhcr, osce and the president of the mitrovica municipal assembly, creating a framework for the return of former residents of the roma mahala to their homes in southern mitrovica. unfortunately, however, this process has not yet started. in the case of the roma mahala, we could not easily make funding available and so have communicated the request to all eu member states through the management committee, asking them to consider making sufficient funds available. we will continue to raise this issue on the ground through our eu liaison office and the european agency for reconstruction, which works in that area. i would also like to respond to mr posselt's question concerning minority rights in different countries, in the eu, in accession countries and in our partner countries. it is true, as mr posselt said, that there are many violations inside the european union. the minimum rights of minorities are set out in the relevant documents of the council of europe and the convention on human rights. some countries inside the european union stick close to the minimum standards, while others go beyond that and have a very high level of minority rights and protection. as the commissioner responsible for enlargement, i am faced with difficult situations, because it is hard for us to go beyond what some eu member states practice. nevertheless, we must practice what we preach when we are dealing with our partners, whether they are accession countries or countries in the wider world. that has to be taken into account, nevertheless. i agree that there is a case for working towards a more uniform definition of minority rights. in my view, human rights in general and the rights of minorities are at the heart of the european idea and of the european union. therefore, we should not see it as a static product but as a dynamic process which develops these rights at ever higher levels inside the european union and throughout europe. finally, concerning the questions raised by several members on the future of kosovo and its standards and status, there is clearly an urgent need for the economic and social development of kosovo. the level of unemployment depends on which statistics you look at. however, it is at least 40% and often more than 50%, and the situation on the ground is extremely difficult. people have no hope at the moment. therefore it is high time to move from stability and reconstruction towards defining the status and working for economic and social development and for the real needs of citizens. that is why it is time for the european union to move from a policy of standards before status to a policy of standards and status so that we move forward in the status talks, ensuring that they can start soon and be conducted and concluded without unnecessary delay. in that context, it is worth noting that the council has reached an agreement at working group level on the negotiating guidelines for the stabilisation and association agreement with serbia and montenegro. that is important because it enables us to open the negotiations on the stabilisation and accession agreement around the fifth anniversary of the democratic transition in belgrade and, moreover, because it will make serbia and montenegro's european prospects concrete and tangible and will also pave the way for a genuine dialogue on kosovo and a resolution of the question of its status without undue and unnecessary delays.

the agenda calls for debate on the report by ari vatanen on behalf of the committee on transport and tourism on the commission communication 'european road safety action programme - halving the number of road fatalities in the european union by 2010: a shared responsibility' (a6-0225/2005).
rapporteur.– mr president, it is a pity that this debate is taking place so late, because when you drive home on an empty stomach that can be a safety hazard too. debate on traffic safety is a question of attitude. it is a question and a test of how we value human life. that is what it amounts to: is human life precious to us? the figures regarding traffic safety are as bleak and grim as the weather outside tonight. there are about 50 000 deaths per year, about 2 million people are injured. it is the main cause of death in the under-50s age group. it costs about 2% of gnp, equivalent to eur 200 billion. but that is only money. we have to realise that what is at stake is the human suffering. why do we do so little? it is because it is not the concorde which crashes, it is not the pride of the uk and france which crashes. when that happened, all concordes were grounded immediately. no stone was left unturned in seeking to remedy the problem. but when it comes to traffic safety, it is just one family crying here, another family crying there. their lives are shattered, amputated. you do not recover from it. you have to live with it. and perhaps only those people who have experienced that know what the grief of a family means. when i was a small boy i was with my entire family in a motor car when my father was killed. i remember him leaning against the steering wheel, that anxiety in my chest. i am sure that experience has left me with a bigger internal handicap than i dare to admit. there is still so much that we could do and can do. first of all law enforcement. okay, that is not an eu matter, it is not within our competence, but that is by far the most efficient way to get things done - through law enforcement, just abiding by and obeying the current rules. on the way here tonight i saw the french police carrying out an alcohol check. when more radars appeared on french roads, immediately fatalities came down. sometimes i think that, although it is a matter for subsidiarity, eu citizens should be protected from their respective governments. i am sorry to say that, but that is how it is, because we do not seem to realise the magnitude of the problem. there are incredible discrepancies between different states. it is up to eight times safer in the uk or in sweden than in some of the new member states - eight times - imagine that incredible diversity! we have to learn from one another. from now on we must carry out a systematic scrutiny of what is going from country to country. we have to render that transparent, so that people know about it, so that they make a noise about it, so that they create political pressure. we must coordinate our actions and we must disseminate our best practices. if we make mistakes, why should those mistakes be made in those countries which are still on the road to development? we have to name, shame and fame. that leads to action. when people have been woken up they will demand action from the politicians in their various member states. at an eu level we can promote new technology, we can promote new cars with fiscal incentives. at the moment a chinese car is coming onto the european market, with no eu approval. that should be stopped, because it is downright dangerous. we must invest more money in infrastructure. we should have an infrastructure directive on ten roads. europeans are mobile thanks to the european road network. it is not justified, or fair on european competitiveness, that we should spend so much money on railways, which serve so little purpose compared to the road network. we have to be just in that allocation. yet things are not so bleak. traffic has grown threefold since 1970 and yet fatalities have been halved. so cultures can be changed. we must believe in the new generation. at the end of the day, whatever we do, responsibility always lies with the individual. at the end of the day we are responsible. mr president, i know my time is up. the eu must act decisively. when our time really is up, hopefully it will not happen on a road. there are still many small boys out there waiting for their fathers.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place on thursday at 12 noon. the competent authority shall inform the applicant of the reasons for the refusal.
member of the commission. mr president, the european textile and clothing industry is, and will remain, an essential part of the eu's industrial and social fabric. the figures speak for themselves: around 2.5 million employees, about 4% of eu gnp. there has been a significant reduction in employment in the sector over the past years. that is unavoidable in an increasingly open world economy, but this fact is of no consolation to the worker who loses his or her job. the role of the commission and the european union as such is to provide a predictable framework for the european producers and importers in the context of an open economy. however, this framework must be a compromise between widely differing objectives. on the one hand, we must and will ensure continued protection of our industry against unfair trade practices. also, if there are genuinely unforeseeable and major surges in imports, the european commission should be ready to provide temporary relief to the european textile and clothing industry without neglecting other interests at stake, such as those of importers, traders and distribution or of industry that is sourcing abroad. on the other hand, we must respect our commitments to china and help it to become a responsible wto member. china, provided it avoids unfair trade practices, is entitled to enjoy the benefits of its comparative advantages and its wto accession, while managing its integration into the global economy in a way that avoids trade disruption. this is what we have called the 'smooth transition'. as far as the textile and clothing sector is concerned, the scene for what is happening today was set a decade ago. it was agreed during the uruguay round that we would gradually abolish the remaining quantitative restrictions on imports in the textile and clothing sector by 1 january 2005, after a decade of transition. however, few anticipated the scale and speed of china's rise in this sector. there is a need to create a positive environment in international trade for textiles and clothing after the end of the textile and clothing agreement. the european textile and clothing sector has already proved that it can adjust to difficult situations and that it has the capacity to compete. one fact is often ignored: the eu remains the world's second largest exporter of textiles and clothing. this fact contradicts the view of those who see globalisation and the rise of china, and india in particular, as a swamping of european markets by low-cost producers. the truth is that the eu can compete globally but it involves a process of restructuring and adjustment playing to our strengths, not to the strengths of other countries. we should focus on innovative, high-tech, valued-added textiles in which we are strong. it also requires that other countries, not least the most competitive textiles and clothing exporting countries, should open their markets to competition too. that is why the current negotiations in the doha development round are so important and china has to fulfil the commitments it made when it joined the wto. when china joined the world trade organization it accepted a formal commitment that allowed the importing countries to apply special textile-specific safeguard measures if imports from china were to increase very rapidly and cause prejudice to the industry of importing countries. it did not apply unilateral measures. the eu and china reached a reasonable and balanced memorandum of understanding on 11 june 2005. this agreement was the result of months of patient and difficult negotiations aimed at dealing with this problem in a negotiated way with china, rather than through unilateral safeguard action which would inevitably have had unwelcome repercussions. above all it enables the european union and china to focus on a more positive overall trade agenda and to continue building a solid trade and economic partnership in the textile and clothing sector as well. let me recall that this memorandum of understanding gives a breathing space to the european industry, giving it extra time to adjust. it also provides a predictable and sure trading environment between the eu and china for the textile and clothing sector enabling businesses, including both the manufacturing industry and importers, to plan their investments with more time and to adjust. it affords temporary protection to the current position of many vulnerable and poorer countries in the eu market and avoids a wide-ranging trade dispute with the eu's second largest trading partner. what has been agreed is the maximum we could have extracted from china in terms of an agreed limitation of their exports, against the background of their and our wto obligations. on 5 september the eu and china decided through agreed minutes to fine-tune the implementation of the memorandum of understanding. these agreed minutes aim to unblock as a matter of urgency goods shipped after 13 july, the day following the entry into force of the regulation implementing the 11 june memorandum of understanding, in excess of the agreed levels set out in the memorandum of understanding. these agreed minutes entered into force on 13 september enabling from that moment the issuance of the necessary import licences and the release into free circulation of the merchandise which had been blocked on entry to the eu because of the exhaustion of the quantitative limits. through the agreed minutes, and in the spirit of close cooperation set up with the chinese since the june memorandum of understanding, both parties decided to share the burden of the agreed solution. half of the blocked amounts were unblocked by advance transfers from the 2006 agreed limits, plus transfers between different categories for 2005. the other half was unblocked through a unilateral increase by the eu of the import for 2005. the lucas report, which we will be discussing later, expresses concerns about the way the memorandum of understanding has been implemented, causing disruption to retailers and importers. in the implementation of the memorandum of understanding, the commission has acted diligently and transparently. we have to remember that, in this case, we are dealing with unprecedented volumes of trade in clothes, which are creating unforeseen circumstances. the difficulties arising from the transitional phase of the implementation of the memorandum of understanding should not recur due to an improved monitoring and control system applicable from now on. should implementation problems arise in the future, the commission will take expeditiously the necessary measures to ensure full respect of the memorandum of understanding as complemented by the agreed minutes of 5 september. but we insist that from now on, importers need to make sure that they conduct their operations in compliance with current eu regulations and that they verify that the quantities are available from the agreed limits. looking to the future, european industry now has an additional two-and-a-half years of predictability ahead, at least with respect to the product categories covered by the memorandum of understanding. the challenge for european industry now is to use this time to the maximum extent possible, in order to adjust to the new competitive situation that began to emerge regularly ten years ago. the difficulty of the challenge that faces the industry should not be underestimated, especially in those sectors where china's advantages, arising out of cheap labour, make it exceedingly difficult to compete. the commission, aware of the difficulties that the sector is experiencing, will continue its work in several other trade policy areas to provide the best possible environment for the industry to thrive in the current competitive environment. among our priorities will be: securing better and effective market access in third countries, notably through the doha development agenda negotiations, but also through bilateral contacts; fighting fraud, counterfeiting and piracy; and acting on allegations on unfair trading practices where justified. these and other measures are being examined in the context of the high-level group on textiles and clothing. the commission is determined to take the necessary steps to give new momentum to those measures, which are destined to help the industry overcome successfully this transitional period.
