member of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by expressing my gratitude for the congratulations and also for the understanding that has been shown for the difficulties of the situation. i am also grateful for the concerns and critical remarks that have been voiced. i have already addressed some of these in my introductory remarks. the commission is prepared to learn from the situation and to take on board all relevant concerns and criticisms. when we deal with china, we of course take into consideration the geopolitical aspects and the important role china plays in the world. however, in this particular case, we are giving preference to the aspects of trade policy, the interests of our textile industry and even to the possible social consequences of the situation. our trade policy vis-à-vis china – the memorandum of understanding and even the agreed minutes – are aimed at establishing a sustainable future for the european textile and clothing industry, which is basically competitive. we are very strong in upmarket products, for instance, and we are the second largest exporter of textile and clothing products in the world. the memorandum of understanding has given our textile and clothing industry additional time to prepare for the challenges it faces. measures are also aimed at protecting the interests of the maghreb states, as well as those poor developing countries which export textile and clothing products. the work on the reform of the rules of origin and origin-marking, which is being considered by the commission, is also intended to help the developing countries. concerning the problems of implementation of the memorandum of understanding and the question of whether the commission acted too late and lost time before may 2005, i would remind you that we first had to evaluate the situation and examine the quotas. some member states were late in submitting or providing the necessary information. it is true that there has been a huge stockpile of textile products and there were many reasons for that. one of the reasons is that it occurred in a short period between the signing of the memorandum of understanding and its entry into force, and some importers even put in orders in an attempt – ultimately unsuccessful – to block the system. at the end of the day, we had to apply a flexible solution, which was the advance use of the quotas for 2006, but of course this did not result in any increase in the quantity of the textile products which china will be able to export. the agreed minutes and the monitoring will prevent similar problems, similar bottlenecks, and the commission regularly makes the quotas public in order to inform importers. many speakers referred to the burning issue of counterfeiting and there is no question that the commission is firmly committed to combating it. i want to refer to the customs cooperation agreement we signed with china, which entered into force this spring and for which we have high expectations. as far as the prospects for the european textile and clothing industry are concerned, several questioners asked whether the industry needs protection. my answer is 'yes' and the measures concerned appear to be good enough, although we are prepared to review them. one measure, for instance, is the ongoing anti-dumping investigation on footwear. in reply to another question raised, chinese garments are subject to the same provisions as eu products. of course, we cannot extend the quotas after 2008, but as far as other solutions like outsourcing are concerned, my answer is 'yes'. however, the real solution is to further strengthen the competitiveness of the european textile industry through research, innovation and investment, but certainly not at the expense of environmental protection and environmental standards. but we will urge, encourage and help china to respect these same standards, as well as urging it to respect ilo standards. so, we understand the situation in its full complexity. these were the most important points raised during the debate. in the limited time available, of course, i cannot answer all the questions raised.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, before i begin, i would like to express my sadness and indignation at the events that took place this weekend in darfur. the loss of two soldiers and two civilians serving in the african union peacekeeping mission in darfur has been a shock to us all. the european commission condemns this cowardly and cruel act in the strongest terms. i would like to express my sincere condolences to the african union and to all the soldiers in the mission and tell them that europe is more than ever at their side in the quest for peace. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with the adoption today of a proposal for a european strategy for africa, the european commission is taking a giant step towards a new political partnership between europe and africa. a sound and rational strategic partnership between an enlarged europe on the one hand and a reborn africa on the other. for too long, europe's relations with africa have been disparate, between policy-making and implementation, between the policies and actions of some member states and those of the european commission, between the approach in sub-saharan africa and the approach in north africa, between trade cooperation and economic development cooperation, between traditional socioeconomic development initiatives and strategic policy measures. neither europe nor africa could tolerate this situation going on any longer. the new strategy for africa which i am presenting to you today therefore aims to provide the european union with a single, comprehensive and integrated framework for the long-term management of its relations with africa. for the first time, europe is addressing africa as a whole in a coherent way from cairo to cape town. although africa has many faces, many histories and different needs, it has now collectively embarked on the path of political, economic and cultural integration of the entire continent. this commitment has been concretised through the efforts to integrate regional economic communities, the launch of the african union and the new partnership for africa's development, nepad. these organisations are now the hope of the continent. i also remember the scepticism surrounding the creation of the african union three years ago. today, however, there has been remarkable progress in all areas, especially in the areas of peace and security. the african union is a major strategic player, i would even say, for us, an indispensable player on the african continent. it is europe's duty to respond to this call from africa which is on the move. for the first time, too, this strategy creates a framework for action by europe as a whole. it is not a question of eliminating the various national policies. i will not stop repeating that these national policies have their own specificities and added value. no, it is rather a question of creating a coherent framework for strengthening collective action at european level. together we are more efficient, together we weigh more. the enlargement of the european union to ten new member states has reinforced this need because it has brought the number of potential individual partners to twenty-six: twenty-five member states plus the european community. it is not enough that the european union's aid is increased, it must also be made more effective. in the past, the lack of coordination and complementarity between donors has often prevented development policies from delivering concrete and effective results. the european union has already done much to improve this situation, notably in the context of the high level forum on aid effectiveness held in paris in march 2005. but i think we need to go further. that is why i propose that next year we draw up an action plan for aid effectiveness, a plan which we will apply as a matter of priority in sub-saharan africa. this action plan will contain concrete tools, such as the creation of an operational and interactive atlas of eu donors, the harmonisation of national road maps, the adoption of common programming documents and the development of common procedures. some may feel that this is an exceptional initiative. the only question is to implement what we have all decided. i also think that the european union should expand budget support both in general and in sectoral terms. this would not only give the european union greater transparency, predictability and sustainability, but also a much greater collective influence on its action. finally, for the first time, the european union has a comprehensive and integrated framework of its various policies for managing its relations with africa. as i have said many times here, all the decisions we have taken in terms of increasing the quantity, quality, efficiency and consistency of aid will be implemented in sub-saharan africa as a matter of priority. let's go back to the consistency. until now, there has been little or no trade policy, security policy, so-called development policy or environmental policy in relation to africa. it must be admitted that these policies were not always articulated, and sometimes even contradictory. europe's security policy, for example, has long coexisted with its development policy, sometimes with some difficulty. recent experience, particularly in the area of the african peace facility, shows how closely security and development are linked and how important it is that european policies in these areas be closely coordinated. the central objective of the european union's strategy for africa, ladies and gentlemen, is to facilitate the achievement of the united nations millennium development goals in africa. i think that these should be our starting point and our reference point. the commission therefore proposes a three-pronged strategy. first, strengthen policies in areas which are considered to be prerequisites for achieving these objectives. for example, peace and security, good governance. second, strengthen policies that create the economic environment necessary to achieve these objectives. for example: trade, private sector development, interconnection. finally, strengthen policies in areas directly linked to these objectives, such as health, education, employment and the environment. together, these measures constitute a common, comprehensive and coherent response of the european union to the challenge of development in africa. these measures are ambitious and obviously have a huge scope, but to fundamentally change the course of history, we need more, we need to clarify our basic approach, the spirit of our relationships and maybe also sometimes our mindset. the communication therefore proposes to adapt the principles governing relations between europe and africa to a new african and european reality. this is achieved by three key principles: equality, ownership and dialogue. we're gonna have to replace guilt or charity as the determining factor in our partnership. the first principle is equality. the emergence of the african union and regional economic communities on the one hand, and the consolidation of european integration on the other, have created a more symmetrical and equal institutional framework. europe has more to offer than development aid. it has a unique experience of integration, dialogue and building supranational political institutions, although integration has sometimes been slow and has never been easy. the second principle is partnership. the european union and africa share the same values and objectives. we believe in a much more multilateral world order, a more equitable development and the promotion of diversity. more than ever, our two continents must be strategic allies within the international community. the third principle is appropriation. development policies and strategies cannot be imposed from outside. the african union and nepad's vision of good governance, respect for human rights and democracy deserves the support of the european union. this purely african initiative has given a new dimension to the concept of ownership as a basis for dialogue and cooperation with each country, with each region and with the continent. the very drafting of the strategy for africa is the first example of the application of these three principles. i would also like to thank the regional organisations and the african union for their comprehensive, constructive and judicious contribution to the preparation of the document. too often, strategies were written "about" or "for" our african partners rather than with them. ladies and gentlemen, when i asked for the portfolio of european commissioner for development and humanitarian aid almost a year ago, i knew that africa would remain at the heart of my action and commitment. i cannot hide my satisfaction at seeing the whole european commission engaged in the same effort today. the joint meeting with the african union commission has demonstrated the motivation and commitment of my colleagues. europe now has an unprecedented opportunity to build a new continent-to-continent partnership. the commission is presenting you with a plan, a vision, a coherent and integrated set of concrete and ambitious proposals. it is now up to you, members of parliament, and to the council, to take up your responsibilities. five years after the cairo summit, i believe that the time has come to turn our dialogue into action. we must work together to break the current impasse and enable the lisbon summit to take place. a successful lisbon summit will be a moment of great symbolic value, a moment when we will confirm the ever closer partnership between our two continents, a moment when we will conclude a new and ambitious euro-african pact. on behalf of the alde group. mr president, we are talking about economic and social development and not cultural or spiritual development: africa does not need us for this, it could even give us lessons. we have therefore set up the millennium development goals. i would draw your attention to the fact that these objectives should not be sacralized, because if they are not achieved, there will the rapporteur. mr president, i would first like to briefly recall the context in which i wrote this report, then outline the six priorities that guided me in drafting my report, and finally draw your attention to six key proposals in this report. as regards the context, it should be recalled that the purpose of this report is to alert the council to the delays in the implementation of the lisbon strategy by the european union in the field of education and training. as you know, ladies and gentlemen, the spring european council of 22 and 23 march 2005 set itself the objective of making the european area of education and training a reality. however, member states must move from grand declarations to concrete measures. this report therefore identifies priority areas for action. in a very recent working document on progress towards the lisbon objectives in the fields of education and training published on 11 april 2005, the commission services analysed the performance of thirty education and training systems. on the basis of the analysis of the very precise data available in this document, i would therefore like to remind you of the six priority areas in which it seems to me that member states must act urgently if we want education to remain at the heart of the lisbon process. the six priorities, which i have already set out in the committee on culture and education, are as follows: reducing the high number of young people leaving school prematurely; to meet the need for a sufficient number of scientists; implementing coherent lifelong learning strategies that are conducive to social inclusion; attract more than one million people to the teaching profession over the next decade; to combat the fact that most pupils in the european union do not achieve the target of at least two foreign languages and, finally, to strengthen the open method of coordination and the exchange of good practice in the field of education and training. i would therefore like to draw your attention to six proposals contained in this report, based on these six priorities and on the comments made by my colleagues in the committee on culture. firstly, in order to develop skills in line with the needs of the knowledge society, it is crucial for member states to take swift initiatives to accelerate the mobility of students, trainees, workers and their families, researchers and to develop social inclusion policies for disadvantaged young people affected by poverty. secondly, the report calls on the commission and the member states to encourage young people to take up technical careers that will lead to employment and integration. in this context, i think it is useful to propose that the european union launch a communication campaign to promote excellent technical courses among young people in order to remedy the often negative social image of young people. thirdly, the report stresses the need for parliament to reiterate its support for the initiative of a pilot project to develop an erasmus-type programme for apprentices, in order to facilitate access for apprentices to the community's 'new generation' education and training programmes. fourthly, in the context of the budget debate, i think it is useful to also recall the need for the european union to ensure sufficient funding for the new integrated action programme in the field of lifelong learning. it is also necessary to ensure that the european social fund can continue to be available after 2006 in all member states of the european union. fifthly, the report asks the council to provide adequate budgetary allocations, in the context of the next financial perspective, for all actions relating to lifelong learning, on which the achievement of the objectives will largely depend. finally, sixthly, the report warns the member states of the need to implement without delay more coherent national training policies aimed at improving the conditions of access for jobseekers and workers. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that we are at a crucial moment for the european union. recent political events have made it clear that the education of citizens and the fight against unemployment must be placed at the centre of all public policies. we cannot have a competitive economy without an adequate and competitive education and training system. i would also like to say to you and to our colleagues in the commission and the council that unless a substantial budget is allocated to education at european level, there will be no real european citizenship and it will always be difficult to agree on a common political project to be carried out by the twenty-five. i therefore count on your support, ladies and gentlemen, so that we can send a strong signal to the member states to put education back at the heart of the lisbon strategy as a matter of urgency.
member of the commission. mr president, i want to thank you for the many interesting contributions and for the discussion you have given us. whether we call education a cornerstone or a central or a key, it is clear that without better, higher quality and more accessible education and training, there can be no better economic and social answers to the lisbon strategy or to the current problems in europe and in the member states of the union. i believe that education should be a central priority here too, and - of course - especially in the policies of the member states. perhaps i should respond directly to one comment - on mobility and the european year of mobility 2006. in my view, the best contribution to the apparent increase in mobility would be for many older member states to lift the moratorium on labour mobility from the new member states, which is precisely what the 1 may 2006 deadline would do as a two-year first start-up period. in conclusion, lifelong learning is neither a luxury nor a hobby, it is a necessity to maintain one's ability, whether it be digital literacy or language or otherwise. the same is true of teachers who multiply these skills in their students. lifelong learning - this should be both a principle, a policy, a strategy and a programme. on the one hand, we are concerned about the lack of results that we have agreed with the states, but on the other hand, we have the encouragement that it is possible. if you look at lisbon or the pisa studies or the benchmarking, you see good results, but on average, it's not satisfactory. but what i'm saying is that we must not be guided by mediocrity, but by excellence, by the best examples. it shows that european countries can be the best in the world in terms of science, skills or literacy, many important conditions for competitiveness. the goal, but also the answer, is to invest more and better in education. better - that is reforms, adaptations - very necessary, sensible and timely. it's more about really needing to add in state budgets (some are very good examples) but also here in the union. i want to thank you for this approach, for this support, also in financial terms, and i look forward to this type of policy and cooperation for the good of education in europe.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam commissioner, i would first of all like to thank all those who have helped me with the preparation of this own-initiative report at the level of the commission, parliament and also the council with which i have had contacts. i hope that this report will be adopted soon. so what is the point of the european parliament being concerned with urban actions which are not in our texts and are not normally within our competence? i think that in order to understand the situation today, it is interesting to take a quick look back. over the past half century our institutions have devoted much of their attention to such vital central problems as coal and steel at the outset, the common agricultural policy, the single act which was a founding element of our european organisation by allowing people, capital, goods and services to move throughout our countries and then, more recently, the single currency. in parallel with these great moments, our european organization has taken hundreds and thousands of measures concerning the lives of our fellow citizens. but, with all this, we have not seen coherence develop at the level of the places where 3,700,000 people are concentrated, the 80% of the population who now live in urban and peri-urban areas. i insist on the terms urban and peri-urban. nevertheless, a number of decisions have been taken in the last 15 to 20 years. the first, which is probably the most significant, dates back to 1988, since article 10 of the erdf specified the need for urban pilot projects. then, in 1990, two years later, two documents were published: a green paper on the urban environment and a report on urban neighbourhoods in crisis. in 1993, jacques delors organised a european crossroads in the city. the first urban programme, which we are now discussing, was launched in 1994, followed by a second programme in 2000. finally, in 2004, the urbact data exchange programme was launched. we can thus see that over the course of some 15 years a number of programmes and decisions on urban matters have been gradually, very slowly and very modestly introduced. it should also be noted that, in parallel, in recent years there have been numerous conferences, symposia and other events on the subject. in recent months, however, things have accelerated considerably. on 30 november 2004, an informal council meeting of the dutch presidency was held in rotterdam, which focused on the subject and devoted a very good text to it. i would also like to highlight, together with my colleagues in the urban intergroup, the creation of the urban housing intergroup in 2005. many articles on urban policy appeared in all the texts on regional funds prepared by the commission in 2004. the uk presidency is planning a meeting on sustainable communities in bristol next december. so we see that the urban business has developed considerably. what is the question today? well, we see a certain amount of mess in our urban and peri-urban sectors. one of our colleagues, who is here, told us the other day that, for example, in leipzig, 30% of the renovated dwellings are unoccupied. isn't that a huge waste? we are not seeing that, thanks to our regional funds in particular, but also thanks to national funds and local budgets, a school is being built here and there, without the housing being rehabilitated or, on the contrary, housing is being rehabilitated without the public transport being rebuilt, etc. it's time this mess ended. it is time we really had a policy that was much more coherent. my report, which has been the subject of a long debate, is not intended to set new objectives. we have goals. the report is intended to provide the means to achieve the lisbon and gothenburg objectives at the urban level. what are these ways? i think you have all read this own-initiative report. i would like to draw a few essential points from this, in particular the fact that our three institutions - the parliament, the council and the commission, which prepares and implements - must organise themselves internally in order to be more effective in their decisions on urban issues. we are witnessing a power struggle between the state, the region, the city and possibly the european union, and these different powers must now work much more coherently to be ultimately much more effective. we must achieve an integrated urban policy at both spatial and thematic level. i have spoken of this with the unfortunate examples quoted earlier. we cannot carry out an action without it being coordinated with other actions. in conclusion, i would like to stress the importance of good practice. i have always said that knowledge and the implementation of good practice that has been proven elsewhere is often much more productive than a small grant. our parliament has no competence in urban policy. our parliament, let us not be deceived, will not allocate fabulous sums of money in the financial perspective to finance new urban prospects. it will all depend on our ability to organise ourselves better to be more efficient, and that is the proposal i make to you in the various articles of my report.

for the gue/ngl group mr president, my group naturally supports the socialist group in its dispute with mr mccreevy and the commission in general. how could the left accept a conception of europe based on the competition of workers and the organization of social dumping? this is exactly the kind of policy we have in mind when we say 'no' to liberal europe. the point is that the brutal and provocative mr mccreevy and all those who think like him can unfortunately rely on the rules in force in the european union to support a latvian company which claims to ignore swedish collective agreements and apply more restrictive social standards. the provision to which the latvian service provider and its brussels sponsors refer in this case is called mutual recognition, which was introduced into community law by the court of justice's case-law as early as 1979 with regard to the free movement of goods and then extended to services some 15 years ago. it's a strategic move. instead of legislating for social harmonization upwards, we are letting the market and competition drag social achievements downwards: this is what we call in community jargon better regulation. the commission published a very explicit communication to parliament and the council in 1999. i quote: 'the application of mutual recognition is fully in line with the philosophy of the internal market, according to which the rules of the member state of origin normally prevail and the member state of destination may derogate from this rule only under very strict conditions involving imperative requirements of general interest, such as health, consumer protection or the environment.' with the latest enlargement, this rule has become explosive: the more social disparities increase between member countries, the more they reveal its diabolical implications. the court's decision will now depend on what it considers to be 'overriding requirements in the general interest'. it is therefore not only mr mccreevy's zeal that must be attacked, but also the pernicious provisions of the community acquis itself that must be opposed. let us think about this now, in the light of the forthcoming mr president, the scale of mass population movements is greater than any that have occurred in the past. regulations have been introduced to put an end to undeclared work, which denies any worker the right to benefit from the law. the continued presence of people without rights, in the most complete precariousness, forced to supply the lucrative illegal labour market or to give in to crime, raises inevitable social, moral and legal questions. the reasons for migration are many, but economic and social factors often predominate. it is worth recalling the four areas identified in tampere, which should be the best way of controlling migration flows and responding to the contemporary economic and demographic challenges. the first is to manage migration flows in a comprehensive way, to strike a balance between the humanitarian and economic aspects and the repressive aspects of illegal immigration. secondly, fair treatment of third-country nationals, guaranteeing them rights and obligations as close as possible to those of national citizens. thirdly, the development of a genuine partnership with the countries of origin, including co-development policies, in the management of flows. fourth pillar: a common asylum system in all the member states of the union. there are many fears that, with the recent rise of populism, so symptomatic of a fear of foreigners, the common approach to the question of immigration will take on a dangerously repressive tone, when it is well known that this policy will not solve the problems and that, on the contrary, it may accentuate them.

in writing. once again, the practices of the european patent office are being debated in this house. a few months ago, it was software and inventions implemented by computers. today, in a much more serious way, and one that touches deeply to our moral principles and to the essence of our humanity, it is about the technology of living. it is true that european legislation, its inadequacy and the legal vagueness it allows, are partly responsible for the current situation, which has made it possible to grant a patent on human germ cells or to render ineffective an opposition to a patent on embryonic stem cells. this legislation must be revised quickly. but the epo cannot be fully exonerated in this case. it has been said time and again that living things cannot be patented, that human beings, in whole or in part, at any stage of their development, cannot be patented. it is high time we put it in writing in a binding text.
in writing. issues related to human genetics should not be addressed in emotional and reductive terms. the european union cannot afford to lag behind its international partners and leave many questions unanswered. in view of the great fundamental principles and universal values which we defend, it is essential to exclude completely the risks of eugenics and reproductive cloning. but it is equally important to define what is possible and acceptable in genetic research, particularly in the context of therapeutic cloning and stem cell research to promote human health. we know that the framework for patenting biotechnological inventions is the essential foundation for developing new therapies which, for many patients, represent an unexpected opportunity.
in writing. this report, which is a response to the european commission's green paper on economic migration, is just one in a long line of dangerous and suicidal aberrations for the nations and peoples of europe. the most immigrationist and third worldist proposals are intertwined: recognition of the right to vote in local and european elections for non-european immigrants, relaxation of entry and residence conditions for economic migrants, approval of mass legalisation as a means of creating future prospects for illegal immigrants, launching awareness campaigns on the positive impacts of immigration policies and integration in school curricula of the history of migration, reaffirmation of the right to a large family reunification, possibility for economic migrant workers to benefit from social contributions of the host country after returning to their country or elimination of bank charges when funds are transferred from the host countries to the home country by migrant workers. finally, as a cherry on the cake, this report refuses to give priority to citizens of the european union before appealing to nationals of third countries. it's the eternal recurring: foreign preference, yes! preferably not european !

madam president, this report states that the european union can make a significant contribution to the process of globalisation by promoting its social model and promoting it at international level. but with 20 million unemployed in europe, what social model are you talking about? the lisbon process is a failure? the debt of states on the verge of bankruptcy, social insecurity, crushing taxation, the new poverty of the european quarter of the world? and all of this, in your view, constitutes an exportable social model? if you want to get a concrete picture of the social dimension of globalisation, i invite you to come and tour the 300 french cities which have been the scene for the past 18 days of social unrest, ethnic riots and anti-french hatred, with cars being burned, schools, nurseries, gymnasiums and hospitals being destroyed, not to mention the systematic and widespread attacks on firefighters and police. you will thus be able to see the concrete and visible consequences of the ultra-liberal, ultra-globalist and ultra-immigrationist economic policy pursued for the last twenty-five years by the european institutions and the member states, with france at the forefront. your social model of integration is actually a total model of disintegration: economic and industrial disintegration, social disintegration, cultural disintegration, institutional disintegration. in addition to the relocation of firms to countries with low social costs of production, there is also the relocation of people from poor countries to countries with a high level of social protection. the widespread social dumping due to globalisation is a real economic bonus to social regression. your economic globalisation is in fact the globalisation of social dumping and the globalisation of migration. foreign populations are entering europe en masse, while companies are leaving europe en masse. we must now endure not only the suburban breakdowns but also the economic breakdowns of our industries, to which must be added the political and institutional breakdowns of our national identities, our national units, our sovereignty and our values of civilization. economic globalisation and forced migration will eventually impose on the peoples of europe a multi-communal and multi-ethnic society, positive discrimination, compulsory ethnic mixing and the level of social protection of communist china. this is clearly not our model and it is vital today to stop this infernal machine. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to thank our colleague mr brejc for his report. it comes just in time for the opening of the wto in hong kong. the form of globalisation we know today has always been presented to us as positive and wealth-creating. it has its winners, but to plagiarize the former french prime minister, it is a new aristocracy of money and power that today accumulates profits and leaves out a majority of losers. not only do we see a worsening of inequalities in north-south relations, but we find that these inequalities are now reflected in south-south relations and within a western society itself where the gap between the richest and the poorest has increased dramatically in recent years. the search for social globalisation has resulted in endangered social rights, undignified working practices and dangerous imbalances. this new situation requires us to look at the world with a different kind of detachment. we must take note of the concern of our fellow citizens about this process of liberal, non-transparent and uncontrolled globalisation. but who can blame them for fearing for their jobs, their future, their democracy and the environment of the planet on which they live? no one did. for what have we done to respond to these legitimate concerns? if i were to take the most recent example, the recent united nations summit in new york, the results have been disappointing. disappointing in terms of concrete commitments to the poorest countries, disappointing in terms of reform of international institutions. europe must act in a coherent and credible manner. it is an example to be followed in this respect at the multilateral level. that is why it is a priority to integrate high social and environmental standards into trade rules and to ensure that they are respected in the bilateral agreements we sign. europe must also set an example internally. to do this, it must improve its model, implement social harmonization from above, stop the dismantling of public services and reject a market europe. europe is an opportunity, a hope. it must be the main actor in another globalisation.

the agenda calls for the commission's statement on 'secret detention centres' in europe.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, following reports in some reputable newspapers about the allegation of the existence of secret prisons run by the cia in some member states of the european union and also in some candidate countries, the commission would point out that a considerable number of member states and candidate countries have already made public statements categorically refuting the allegations. so far, the alleged facts have not been corroborated even in terms of judicial evidence. it is important to be absolutely clear that such events, if they had actually occurred, would have been a serious breach of the principles of the european union, apart from any reference to the member states' legislation, including criminal law, which punishes events and incidents similar to those described. the commission would point out that, according to article 6 of the treaty on european union, the union is founded and lives on the principles of democracy and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms and, of course, the rule of law, principles which are also common to the national legislation of the member states, which provide for criminal law to punish violations of fundamental rights and the rights of the human person. it is therefore clear that the member states are bound by these principles, but they are also bound by international legal obligations, in particular those deriving from the european convention on human rights and fundamental freedoms and those deriving from the convention against torture. it is also clear - as we all know - that when the enlargement process of a candidate country is completed, that country must have acquired a level of institutional stability to ensure full respect for democracy, the rule of law and human rights, as well as the protection of all fundamental freedoms, in order to become a member of the european union. this is a principle established by the copenhagen european council back in 1993 and is therefore a pillar of the so-called copenhagen acquis. in the light of these principles, it is clear that we consider it necessary for the member states and the applicant countries to verify the accuracy of such news reports by all the legal means at their disposal and in the appropriate forms. the commission welcomes the recent decision of the committee on legal affairs and the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe to address the issue of the accusation of the establishment of secret prisons in europe and we have already asked the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe to be informed of future developments in this extremely important and sensitive matter. the commission will continue to follow closely all developments concerning these allegations. we will do so at member state level, in compliance with european legislation, and at international level, with particular reference to any action that the authorities of the united states of america may decide to take on the whole matter. in conclusion, i can assure you that i and the commission will keep parliament informed and in constant dialogue with it on the developments in this matter.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, mr vice-president, major newspapers have indeed dealt with this problem, in particular the washington post, which recently announced in its columns that secret prisons, run by the cia, would be located on the territory of the european union, particularly in eastern europe, to be precise. the newspaper did not name the countries involved for security reasons, but it should be noted that an investigation by human rights watch indicated that in 2002, some "ghost" prisoners were indeed held by the cia. it should be recalled that the us congress also published a report which mentions questionable practices used by the united states in the transfer of prisoners to third countries in order to be able to use torture in interrogations. in addition, the recent allegations that the bush administration is seeking to have the us congress grant the cia an exemption from the prohibition on ill-treatment of prisoners is of the utmost concern to us. we need all the light we can get on these revelations. we cannot accept, as you have said, areas of lawlessness in europe and the world. we have always opposed in this house the use of a legal vacuum for the treatment of prisoners at guantanamo. we cannot therefore allow such prisons to exist in europe. if the facts are established, they must be stopped immediately. if they're false, we need to gather evidence to finally shut down the rumors. we therefore ask the commission to investigate these allegations, as you have recently promised to do in the press, mr vice-president. the results of this survey should be presented to the european parliamentarians; i think you'll agree. what measures does the commission intend to take to ensure that the european convention on human rights, the european convention for the prevention of torture and the european charter of fundamental rights, in particular article 4 thereof, are properly respected throughout the european union? member of the commission. madam president, the commission, together with the entire international community, is following very closely the development of the electoral process in the drc and its organization by the independent electoral commission. i personally carried out a mission to supervise the registration of voters at the end of august this year, to see under what conditions this registration was taking place. despite the state of the country's dilapidated infrastructure, the number of registered voters to date has exceeded 21 million. this figure is broadly in line with the demographic projections made on the basis of the last general population census which remains, at present, the most reliable statistical basis to work on. voter registration is governed by a specific law which sets out the conditions for voluntary registration. in addition, arrangements were made by the electoral commission to ensure that all registration centres were treated equally and that no region or area was penalised by a late opening of the centre. to give you a simple idea of the scale of the technical difficulty, i must tell you that we had to distribute more than 10,000 recording kits throughout the territory of the congo, knowing that in some places there are no runways, there are no roads, and we had to use helicopters. so you can imagine the scale of the work. furthermore, in order to avoid as much as possible the risks of double registration and massive fraud as mentioned in question the electoral commission has opted, with the endorsement of the international community, for the registration of voters on the basis of biometric data, the immediate issuance of the voter card, the daily display of the lists of registered voters in each registration office, the european parliament, in particular those in its committee on transport and tourism, for the hard work they have put into this important proposal. i would also like to thank the drafting committee from the three institutions which has made the agreement today so much easier. the council attaches the highest priority to aviation safety. it shares your determination that initiatives should continue to be taken to ensure that aircraft carrying europe’s citizens around the world are safe. we were all shocked by the number of air accidents that occurred in august and september this year, in which too many of our citizens lost their lives. in light of those events, parliament seized the opportunity to amend the proposal from the commission. you proposed amendments aimed at strengthening the scope for community-wide action on the safety of airlines. although the council had agreed a general approach in april on the principle of information sharing, ministers expressed support for this new objective at the transport council on 6 october. the council believes that the procedures for assessing the safety of carriers set up by the regulation are the most appropriate. we considered whether a role might be given to the european aviation safety agency but decided that this would be premature: the agency is still consolidating its structures and procedures and recruiting the staff necessary to carry out its present responsibilities. we should therefore be cautious about giving it new responsibilities too soon. the expertise and experience in dealing with the safety of air carriers currently exists in the member states and it is important to draw on this expertise so that it can be applied fully for the safety of our citizens. the process of banning air carriers and publishing this information is important, but we should not lose sight of the extra rights to be given to consumers. the council agrees that passengers should be given information about the identity of carriers they may book to fly with and that they be kept up to date on the changes in the carriers once bookings are made. the text today makes important contributions to both of those important safety and consumer objectives. i am delighted that a deal has been reached and that it will allow concerted action to be taken in a timely, transparent and well-organised way. it will identify carriers that do not meet acceptable international safety standards and ensure that action is taken to ban them throughout the community and that information about such action is published. it is a measure of the importance that we all attach to those objectives that parliament, council and the commission have worked so constructively together to prepare the text. credit is due to everyone concerned, especially to the rapporteur for her inclusive approach to reaching early agreement. i understand also that the recently established drafting committee contributed to the swift and efficient way in which a first-reading deal was arrived at. clearly, this is a valuable tool for future negotiations. i would like to finish by saying that i am looking forward to the debate and the individual contributions and i am pleased to be here this evening.

examples, but we often discuss topics in the middle of the day which interest almost no one, and when it comes to texts which concern a large number of our fellow citizens, such as the one we are fruitful and, why not say, sympathetic cooperation. we have all worked quickly and efficiently to reach an agreement at first reading and thus to deliver a positive message to our fellow citizens. as you said, the tragic events of last summer have increased our responsibility to adopt new measures to strengthen the safety of air passengers and their information. and that responsibility, we all took on together. we are talking about air safety; i would like to say that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. at the same time, we must be realistic and realise that there is no such thing as zero risk and that the sharp increase in air traffic in the coming years could lead to an increase in the number of plane accidents. to avoid this, we must address the shortcomings of the present system by providing for a european mechanism which, in addition to icao, goes further in strengthening aviation safety and this is the view with which this report has been drawn up. when we compare the starting point of the european commission, namely the publication of the national lists, with the text we have today, we see that we have come a long way and that this did not seem possible a few months ago. thanks to parliament's initiative, we are on the verge of having a single community blacklist, drawn up on the basis of common criteria and applicable throughout the union. this will ensure that our citizens are guaranteed the same level of safety, regardless of the community airport they use, and why not say that this text is a great victory for the european union. i should now like to try to go into the proposal for a regulation in a little more detail and tell you how the initial establishment of this list will be done. member states will have one month from the entry into force of the regulation to transmit the list of air carriers banned from flying on their territory, drawn up on the basis of the common criteria annexed to this text. this may concern any airline with a right of traffic in the union, as well as those without such a right but whose aircraft are likely to be chartered in the european union. the commission will then have to convene the committee of experts within one month and decide whether or not to include the carriers concerned on the list. and all airlines on that community list will be banned from flying throughout the union. this community list will be updated at the request of a member state or the commission, whenever necessary. the list will also be made public and widely and effectively communicated to passengers, including by electronic means and by means of display. finally, passengers will be entitled to reimbursement or re-routing in cases where their operating carrier is included in the community list after booking or if it has been replaced by a banned carrier. that is the blacklist part, but there is also the part dealing with passenger information and this regulation places an obligation on ticket sellers to tell passengers the identity of the airline with which they are actually going to travel. and this information should also be given to passengers if there is a change of airline. finally, the regulation leaves it to the member states to implement sanctions in cases where the passenger's duty to inform has not been respected. as regards procedure, the text should be ready for approval by the council by the end of november, after verification by the legal linguists of the two institutions. finally, mr president, i should like to say a few words about the european aviation safety agency, since this regulation is, in my view, part of an overall strategy to improve aviation safety in europe. the next step in this process will therefore be to extend the powers of easa, particularly with regard to the certification of aircraft from third countries, and i am very pleased that you have put forward this proposal today, commissioner. for the time being, the regulation we are discussing tonight will make the european blacklist available to citizens from the beginning of 2006, and i welcome this result. europe is moving towards a stronger aviation safety. she's making good progress.
mr president, i welcome the report by my colleague, christine de veyrac, who has the great merit of clearly stating the principle of adopting a blacklist of unsafe and even dangerous airlines. in view of the recent and repeated occurrences of accidents caused by defective aircraft, it is essential to take action to list and ban such aircraft. it is essential for the safety of all air passengers to know the identity of the airline which is transporting them and, moreover, to know whether or not it is considered dangerous. this right is an absolute right. it cannot be restricted because it is the life of millions of people who travel by air all over the world. however, i will make one reservation. what will be the scope of the community list of these carriers which do not meet the european safety criteria? at the moment, it seems that no common criteria for establishing a community list have been set by the commission. are we afraid of diplomatic repercussions with some sensitive countries? should we be afraid, for example, of the reaction of the turkish authorities to the recent flight ban on onur air by the netherlands, belgium, france and switzerland alone? why have the other european countries not joined in this ban? the text before us proposes, among other things, to increase the powers of the european aviation safety agency. why not, if the objective is to strengthen common criteria for inspection, prohibition and restriction of flying rights? however, have there been any control measures for this agency and any appeals against its decisions? the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the adoption of a provisional constitution by the iraqi people is a major step forward for us. the high level of citizen participation in the electoral process is a factor of optimism for the nascent democracy. the developments in iraq are of course opening the way to a future partnership between iraq and the european union, particularly in the context of its neighbourhood policy and a peaceful mashreq, and in this respect i thank mrs ferrero-waldner for the commitments she has made on behalf of the commission. the challenges of this partnership are many: democratic stabilisation of the country, the construction of a real and no longer formal state governed by the rule of law, respect for fundamental freedoms and the rights of minorities, but also the transition from a war economy to a peace economy, from an economy governed by a market economy, the allocation of oil resources to diversification in favour of agriculture, industry and services, and finally the reconstruction of the education and health systems destroyed by so many years of authoritarian power, embargo and war. but there are a few prerequisites to this partnership. the uncertain developments in iraq deserve our utmost vigilance. we cannot ignore the losses and gains of the use of white phosphorus bombs if the information proves to be accurate by the americans in fallujah. there must be an investigation. the replacement of foreign forces by a un-led peacekeeping force is one of our objectives. the elections in december must enable the iraqi people to elect a government and a parliament that reflect the human and political balance of the country. the federal institutional framework seems particularly suited to this. the european union must set itself the objectives of reversing fundamentalism, of combating the so-called clash of civilizations and of building the mashrek based on shared values.

president-in-office of the council. mrs president, there is now almost universal acceptance that climate change is a serious and an urgent problem. the ipcc predicts that global temperatures may rise by as much as 5.8°c by the year 2100. according to one insurance company, the estimated economic costs of global warming could double to usd 150 billion each year in the next 10 years, hitting insurers with usd 30-40 billion worth of claims. there is good evidence that the 2003 european heatwave was influenced by global warming and that, as members will recall, resulted in 26 000 premature deaths, as well as costing usd 13.5 billion. those events and their associated price tags bring very close to home the reality of what unchecked climate change would mean for us. it is clear that the scale of a climate change problem is enormous and that it is pressing, and that is why the uk decided to make climate change a priority for our presidencies of both the g8 and the eu. 2005 has been a critical year for international climate change policy. the kyoto protocol has entered into force. the eu emissions trading scheme is up and running and we are due, at the end of the year, to begin discussions on further action beyond 2012, something to which i will return. the g8 represents only a small – albeit key – group of countries, but the progress we have made there will, i hope, have a major impact. the g8 summit discussions in july concluded with an ambitious communiqué. it included agreement from all members, including the united states, on the role of human activity in global warming and on the need for urgent action. there was also consensus on a package of actions to combat climate change through a diverse range of avenues: energy efficiency, cleaner power generation, research and development, financing of cleaner energy, managing the impacts of climate change, as well as combating illegal logging. the g8 countries have engaged with the world bank and other development banks to improve the harnessing of funding for clean technology and, crucially, they also agreed to begin a new dialogue between the g8 and other countries with significant energy needs on climate change, clean energy and sustainable development. the first meeting of that dialogue took place in london on 1 november. mexico has offered to host a second meeting next year. the member states of the european union were some of the first in the 1990s to recognise the dangers of global warming, the link to human activity and the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. as long ago as 1991 the commission issued the first community strategy aimed at limiting co2 emissions and improving energy efficiency. in the light of the eu’s commitments under the kyoto protocol, it soon became clear that more needed to be done. so, in 2000 came the launch of the european climate change programme. today the eu is taking the lead, for example in focusing on emissions from aviation, and we warmly welcome the commission’s recent communication on reducing the climate change impacts of aviation. its announcement of support for the inclusion of aviation emissions in the eu emissions trading scheme is highly encouraging and we look forward to fostering progress in that area as a priority for our presidency of the european union. within europe there is a clear recognition of the importance of energy efficiency in meeting the challenge posed by climate change and work is already under way to deliver energy efficiency savings throughout the community. the energy services directive which we hope to agree by the end of the year is expected to provide a challenging first step, while the commission’s green paper on energy efficiency published at the end of june should set the future blueprint for europe’s energy efficiency strategy to 2020. but despite all this work and effort, it is clear that emissions in the eu are not being reduced as quickly as we want and that urgent action is needed in all sectors, at both national and eu level. so i applaud the commission’s decision to launch a new phase of the european climate change programme to look at what more can be done. alongside this, the commission and council are developing an eu medium- and long-term strategy for tackling climate change and will report on progress so far to the december european council. parliament’s input in this will be crucial, so the resolution that you have recently produced is an extremely valuable contribution to this process. the uk presidency has set out to create a fresh momentum in the wider international process in which the eu plays such a crucial role. that is why we put climate change on the agenda of our eu summits with china and india. these two countries are particularly important partners for the eu in tackling climate change. both summits included useful bilateral discussions on energy security and efficiency. a key element of the partnership with china is a new initiative on near-zero emissions for coal, with carbon capture and storage, to address the vital challenge of tackling the increasing greenhouse gas emissions from coal. we also agreed a new partnership with india. the eu-russia summit too was an excellent chance to consider what experiences we can share with regard to the implementation of the kyoto protocol, to ensure its mechanisms are up and running as soon as possible. in september, for the first time, ministers from the agriculture council met environment ministers to discuss the impacts of climate change on agriculture in the eu. we also put climate change on the agenda of the energy, transport and competitiveness councils. all this activity is leading to the first meeting in december of the parties to the kyoto protocol in montreal, where, under the protocol, parties will begin discussions on the next period after 2012. let me make it quite clear that the eu and the uk remain absolutely committed both to the kyoto protocol itself and to the united nations framework convention on climate change. as our prime minister tony blair said this week at the lord mayor’s banquet in london, the world needs a framework with the necessary targets, sensitively and intelligently applied over the right timeframe, that takes us beyond 2012. perhaps i could ask colleagues to take particular note of the use of the word ‘targets’, because the uk has repeatedly stated that formal agreements with targets are absolutely essential in any international climate change regime, not least because they give incentive and certainty to the business community. the informal g8 process is also hugely important, but it is complementary. it is not, and was never intended to be, a substitute for the kyoto protocol or for the united nations convention. i hope the work we have done this year through both presidencies will in fact be built on at montreal. montreal will primarily be the celebration of a massive achievement: the entry into force of the kyoto protocol. there were times when it looked as though that might never happen, but the eu continued doggedly to work for such an outcome, and now here we are, with the world’s only credible, binding international agreement on controlling greenhouse gas emissions. the eu set out our negotiating position for montreal at the october environment council. first, we want to agree the marrakesh accords – the decisions that will form the rulebook of the protocol. secondly, we want to agree a compliance mechanism to ensure that parties to the protocol keep to its rules. thirdly, we want to seek to improve the way the kyoto mechanisms – and here i am talking mainly about the clean development mechanism – work. emissions trading, the cdm and joint implementation are all crucial elements to the protocol and will remain essential in the years to come. finally, the montreal conference will look to the future and begin to discuss what happens when the first kyoto commitment period ends in 2012. this last issue is likely to be by far the most delicate, as well as the most important, element. there is no question but that we want to build on the kyoto protocol post-2012 and that we have to launch a discussion under article 3(9) of that protocol to consider future commitments of the eu along with other kyoto parties. however, it is also quite clear that for a global climate change regime to be truly effective, we need broader participation than the protocol currently offers. at montreal we will be looking for pathways towards a framework post-2012 which builds on and learns from the kyoto protocol as it stands and can include as many countries as possible. the eu will clearly have to back our political ambition for the montreal conference of the parties with real evidence that we are taking a lead in tackling climate change. the kyoto protocol also stipulates that, by the end of 2005, parties must demonstrate their progress in meeting their kyoto commitments. this will be the ideal time for the eu to reaffirm our commitment to kyoto, to meeting our emission reduction targets and to our obligations to assist developing countries. in preparing for the conference, we are assembling data, facts and figures to show the practical application of our political commitment. we know that we need to do more and we all stand ready to do more. today’s debate here in strasbourg will allow us to take stock of the current situation and offer us a further opportunity to demonstrate to the rest of the world that the eu takes this problem very seriously and is committed to delivering results. together we have already achieved a great deal; we have shown leadership and made a real difference. we need to continue to do that and not falter as the environmental stakes get higher. we will not see a resolution to the problem at montreal, nor under the current uk presidency of the eu. we need future presidencies – both of the eu and of the g8 – to carry on this work, keeping climate change high on their agendas and tackling the major threats it poses to our economies, our society and our environment. there are encouraging signs that the next g8 presidencies – russia and japan – fully intend to do so and i have every confidence in the eu’s continued determination to tackle this vital issue. (applause)
member of the commission. madam president, i am particularly pleased to have the opportunity to discuss with you the recent developments on climate change and how to strengthen the european union's policy on this matter and to ensure the active involvement of all partners in effective international cooperation in this field. today's debate is of particular importance in the run-up to the upcoming meeting of the parties in montreal, which will mark the entry into force of the kyoto protocol and the discussions on the post-2012 climate change regime. we are all concerned by the recent spate of theocratic events. we have had a severe drought this year in the iberian peninsula, we have had floods during the summer in central europe, we have had a series of hurricanes - katrina, rita, wilma - and other minor events. 2005 already set an unprecedented record, as 2005 was the year with the most named tropical cyclones since records began. although specific weather events cannot be directly linked to climate change, the increasing droughts and floods, as well as more severe and frequent hurricanes or tropical storms, are confirming scientific warnings about climate change. the earth has probably never in its history warmed as rapidly as it has in the last 30 years. the 1990s were the warmest decade on record, with nine of the 10 warmest years on record occurring between 1995 and 2004, with 1998 the warmest. scientists are expressing fears that 2005 may finally be the warmest year on record. it is known that when the planet warms, the sea warms, and when the sea temperature exceeds 26°c, then tropical cyclone formation is possible. the global sea surface temperature has increased by 0.6 percent over the past 100 years, which means that we're likely to have much more frequent and intense cyclones in the future. however, more important than determining whether hurricane katrina or other weather events were caused by human activities is learning from these weather events to win the battle against climate change. i would like to refer in particular to parliament's resolution on the communication 'combating climate change successfully' and i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr wijkman, and the members of the committee on the environment, the committee on development and the committee on industry, research and energy for their valuable and specific suggestions. the draft resolution stresses that the community strategy to limit climate change must be based on an approach that includes: making use of the key elements of the kyoto protocol; drastically reducing greenhouse gas emissions in the european union; involving other key countries, such as the united states; developing strategic cooperation with key developing countries; actively promoting research and innovation; and improving energy efficiency in the european union. i agree with and support this approach, and the initiatives taken by the commission this year in the field of climate change are largely in line with parliament's proposal. let me make a brief general reference: in october, the commission marked the beginning of a new era in the european climate change agenda with a major conference in brussels attended by the main players in the sector. the new european climate change programme will provide a new framework for our climate change policy with a purpose and a perspective beyond 2012. we are tackling a number of new issues, such as aviation, and we are also working on new technologies - such as carbon sequestration - which offer opportunities for cost-effective measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. as a first step, the commission sets up a number of working groups. these include: the working group to review progress to date in implementing climate change policies; the group to investigate carbon capture and storage in geological formations as a climate change mitigation measure; the group to assess the integration of aviation into the community's greenhouse gas emission allowance trading scheme; the group to prepare the review of the community strategy to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from light commercial vehicles; and the group to identify the necessary policy adjustments to be made by the european union. each of the above groups will identify specific new areas where the european union can step up its action to tackle climate change. the first of these groups is expected to start submitting its final reports in the first half of the following year. the commission has also adopted, as mrs beckett said, a green paper on energy efficiency. i would also like to refer to the commission communication entitled 'limiting the impact of aviation on climate change'. air transport is an increasing contributor to greenhouse gas emissions. the communication concludes that the best way to reduce these emissions is to integrate the aviation sector into the community's emissions trading scheme. after consulting stakeholders, the commission intends to present a legislative proposal by the end of 2006. the commission's initiatives are not, of course, limited to the development of actions within the european union. we are actively engaged in discussions with third countries, seeking their views on the next steps to be taken in future climate negotiations and on the creation of new structures to strengthen our political dialogue and technological cooperation. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the programme to include the following areas: in this area we are working closely with the british presidency, which, as mrs beckett said earlier, put climate change very high on the agenda at the gleneagles summit of the eight, and which is continually putting climate change as one of its priorities. the results are encouraging. the eu-china partnership agreement on climate change and energy provides the political framework for closer cooperation and dialogue on these issues. the eu-china partnership has as its main objective the development of advanced, near-zero emission carbon technology based on carbon capture and storage in bioforms. it also intends to promote other clean energy sources, as well as energy efficiency, energy saving and renewable energy sources. the european union-india clean development and climate change initiative provides for various initiatives to develop the dialogue. it emphasises cooperation on the development and evaluation of clean technologies, the necessary adaptations to global warming and the clean development mechanism of the kyoto protocol. at the end of this month, in montreal, canada, the two-week united nations climate change conference will begin. the commission has actively participated in a number of informal preparatory meetings for the montreal conference. our activities, both in the european union and on the international stage, have played a major role in creating the conditions for the success of this conference. what are our goals in montreal: first, the meeting will mark the entry into force of the kyoto protocol by establishing the rules and procedures required for its implementation. in this context, it is important to demonstrate that the european union is living up to its commitments. secondly, the intense dialogue that has taken place in recent months has created an important momentum for the montreal conference to start the debate at international level on the shape of the future international regime on climate change. the achievement of these objectives is not, however, a given. a small number of countries, led by the united states, remain reluctant to engage in the debate on the future global regime on climate change. the commission has the following is the proposal from the chairman of the sitting. we are dealing with rule 170 (1) of the rules of procedure, which says in the second paragraph: 'the intention to request the adjournment of a debate must be notified at least 24 hours in advance to the president, who shall inform parliament without delay.' it is clear that this condition is not met: the postponement is not requested twenty-four hours in advance. i am therefore obliged to proceed with the debate, especially since our rapporteur wishes it to proceed. i admit, ladies and gentlemen, that a debate of this importance would have deserved a wider audience. but i must point out two things. firstly, in general our debates rarely fill the house, whether on a thursday afternoon, a monday, a tuesday or a wednesday. secondly, our calendar is set up in such a way that our parliament meets on thursday afternoons. there can therefore be no discrimination between those who make the effort to stay and those who prefer to take care of other matters. we shall therefore proceed to this debate by giving the floor to our rapporteur, mrs martens, immediately.

member of the commission. mr president, the commission is extremely concerned by the retention of the death penalty law in the philippines and the omission by president gloria macapagal-arroyo to reinstate the moratorium on the death penalty lifted on 1 january 2004. the eu stance against the death penalty is based on the firm belief in the inherent dignity of all human beings and the inviolability of the human person. the member states, together with the commission, have strengthened their international activities in opposition to the death penalty as an integral part of eu human rights policy. they have also adopted eu guidelines laying down the basic principles to be followed in this respect. we know that there are currently more than 1 000 inmates on death row in the philippines. of these, 165 death sentences have been affirmed by the supreme court and can be stopped only by a presidential stay of execution. we are calling again on the philippine president to reprieve death-row convicts. we are particularly concerned about the supreme court’s sentence of 3 february 2004 condemning the spanish-filipino citizen francisco larrañaga to death and the refusal to reconsider the case in july 2004, thus ending all judicial channels for appeal. on 5 july 2004, the eu troika – consisting of the netherlands, the uk and the commission – handed an amicus curiae brief to the philippine department of foreign affairs in support of the motion for the reconsideration of the case. since then, the spanish embassy in manila has had the lead on that specific case, while the commission is dealing with general issues related to the support of the campaign against the death penalty by various actors in the philippines. the uk embassy, in cooperation with the uk organisation reprieve, has sent a lawyer to the philippines for three months, starting in october 2005, to investigate the case. we also support the various internal parliamentary initiatives on the revocation of the death penalty law that are currently being debated in the philippines congress, and we encourage the efforts by civil society to work towards that goal. it is important to insist on the reconsideration of the larrañaga case, as he has not had a fair trial according to international legal standards. so, even if parliament ruled in favour of the abolition of the death penalty in exchange for life sentences, the larrañaga case would remain flawed. the eu should continue to insist on the right to a fair trial for mr larrañaga.
