member of the commission. mr president, i wish to begin by saying that the commission fully shares the concerns regarding the situation in burma/myanmar, as expressed here today by honourable members of the european parliament. there is no doubt that several issues are of serious concern, in particular the proceedings of the so-called national roadmap, the human rights and forced labour situation and many more issues that have been mentioned today. in this context, let me emphasise that the commission continues to call for the unconditional release of aung san suu kyi and other political leaders who remain in detention. in the past, the commission maintained contacts with most of the shan leaders who have now been sentenced, and it goes without saying that the conduct of these politically motivated trials was unacceptable according to democratic and legal standards. the commission continues to urge the regime to engage in a real dialogue with all political actors, including the national league for democracy and ethnic groups. we are convinced that only a transparent and constructive dialogue between legitimate stakeholders can lead to national reconciliation and a return to democracy. probably, the regime will deliver on its roadmap. it will probably formally accomplish the national convention later this year and organise a referendum on the draft constitution in 2006. the result will certainly fall short of our expectations in terms of real democracy. it should nevertheless be considered a small step in the right direction. burma/myanmar is partly isolated from the western world and partly isolating itself. however, we must understand that the country continues to enjoy a comfort zone in the region, especially with regard to its neighbours. there is a degree of intra-asean solidarity, despite the position of individual political leaders in asean. i mention these issues because they illustrate the difficult background against which we operate. without any doubt, we must voice our concern for the people in the country. the eu is called upon to help the people of burma/myanmar. the commission therefore strongly supports a significant increase in humanitarian aid and assistance. the commission maintains that our common position generally reflects what should be done. we should continue voicing the union’s criticism of members of the junta and policies pursued by the regime. this can be done only if we continue the agreed eu policy by keeping communication channels open and using high-level asem and eu-asean meetings, or the margins of such meetings. an update of the common position needs to be discussed with and agreed by all eu member states, bearing in mind the possible positive or negative developments in the country, and reflecting our values and political interests. this would also apply if the eu were to nominate a special envoy. a year ago, in october 2004, we strengthened the eu common position. we introduced a more comprehensive visa ban and prohibited support for international financing. any further change in the common position – apart from the fact that we would need all the partners to agree – would need to ensure the legality of such a measure under international law and ensure that the people of burma/myanmar did not become the victims. the people of burma/myanmar should not pay twice: once for living under a repressive regime and twice as a result of the economic sanctions imposed by the west. then there is the question of whether the un security council should discuss burma. most of us have seen the recent report, endorsed by vaclav havel and archbishop desmond tutu. the report concludes that the un security council should deliberate on the burma/myanmar issue. however, we are all aware that it will prove very difficult to pass any resolution on this subject given the reluctance of some permanent members, notably china. i assure honourable members of parliament that the commission will continue its work on burma/myanmar, stepping up its assistance for people in need and, at the same time, pressing for democracy, human rights, the release of political detainees and for democratic reform and political transition. without a doubt, the overarching goal of our dealings with burma is the transition towards democracy.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, mr president of the council, mr commissioner, we are on the eve of a wto conference which was to make it possible to take a decisive step in implementing the doha work programme, the development programme, adopted in 2001 and which was to make it possible to put the rules of trade at the service of development. unfortunately, as you have told us, commissioner, it is now clear that the hong kong conference will not be able to produce the results expected in the main areas of the negotiations. progress since the framework agreement concluded at the wto on 1 august 2004 has been insufficient, sometimes almost invisible. much valuable time has been lost and the level of ambition for the hong kong meeting is now being revised downwards, with the real decisions being deferred to a later conference in 2006. i would like to stress at the outset, on behalf of the socialist group, that this must in no way lead to a downward revision of the ambitions of the doha round itself in terms of development objectives. any reduction in the commitments of the developed countries in relation to the implementation of the doha agenda would lead to a substantial reduction in the potential benefits for the developing countries. as you know, commissioner, the world bank has carried out a study which shows that if the probable scenario based on the proposals made today by the united states and the european union were to come to fruition, the benefits of the doha round would again, as in previous rounds, go mainly to the major trading powers, the developed countries, while the benefits for the developing countries would amount to less than 0.2 cents per capita per day, which would reduce the number of poor people in the world by just 1%. i also believe that insisting on the idea of reciprocity in the commitments required of the developing countries in return for the efforts made by the developed countries, particularly in terms of opening up markets, risks blocking the negotiations and, from this point of view, we must not forget what happened in cancún. we are convinced that if the doha development round negotiations succeed, while maintaining the priority of rebalancing in favour of developing countries, rather than reciprocity, they will ultimately bring tangible benefits to all, including the european union, which will share in the benefits of new global economic growth and the development of new markets for european products. it is therefore essential that the doha round be a success. to this end, the rules and agreements negotiated in hong kong must aim at a more equitable sharing of the benefits of globalisation; they must take better account of differences in levels of development; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. they must not weaken the most sensitive economic sectors and the nascent industries and must, on the contrary, contribute to economic diversification. they must recognize the right of developing countries to control the pace of their trade opening and their national development strategies. we are calling for more flexibility from the various actors, including the european union. i think that in the field of agriculture you still have some room for manoeuvre. for example, our group tabled an amendment to ask for a commitment, with a timetable to support it, to abolish export subsidies by 2010. we are asking that in the field of industrial tariffs, a formula of the swiss formula, which you are supporting today and which does not respect the principle of 'less than total reciprocity', should not be applied. we must accept that a certain level of protection in the industrial sector is maintained for developing countries. in the area of services, we insist that the european union's demands on market access for service providers preserve the right of all wto member countries, including developing countries, to regulate their services and in particular their public services. we are asking that health, education, audiovisual are clearly excluded from the negotiation, but also that public services such as water and energy are not dismantled or weakened in the framework of the gats negotiations. finally, you noted the strong reluctance of the developing countries to your proposal for a benchmarking, which it would be more reasonable to withdraw. we support you on the development aid package. we need a lasting solution for access to medicines which includes a revision of the agreement on intellectual property itself. the rules on special and differential treatment must be strengthened. finally, there is a need for a financial facility to support technical assistance and capacity building for poor countries. finally, our group believes that sensitive issues such as social and environmental issues cannot be excluded from discussions within the wto. it is also a condition for public support for the multilateral system, which can only be saved if it is reformed.
for the gue/ngl group mr president, we must not despair of anything or anyone if even mr mandelson comes to the conclusion that, and i quote, whatever we offer is not enough for the very competitive and aggressive producers and exporters of brazil, australia, new zealand and the united states. it is therefore not too late for the twenty-five to seriously review the mandate of their negotiator, which dates, for the most part, from 1999, i.e. before the double failure of seattle and cancún. in this context, my group would be happy to submit to you ten proposals for new and closely linked priorities, which i shall call the ten commandments of an alternative vision of europe's ambition on the international scene. firstly, as we are on the eve of world aids day, i would mention the need to find a permanent solution to the problem of access to medicines in countries lacking pharmaceutical production capacity. the persistent blocking of intellectual property by industrialists is criminal and unacceptable in this respect. secondly, i would like to mention the official priority of the doha round which has been completely sidelined in practice: development. europe has gradually economies of the south and increase their dependence, and the choice of full liberalization in order to open up access to land, seeds, water and the market for goods and services to multinational groups. the time i have is not enough for me to discuss our other priorities in telegraphic style. fourth, the wto must ban the patenting of living things and protect the biological resources and opposed to the gats and in favour of designating global public goods, excluded from the scope of the market. sixth, the cultural exception: no wto rule should prevent a state from defending what it considers to be its cultural heritage. the commission's proposal for a directive on the harmonization of the laws of the member states relating to the protection of employees in the event of the insolvency of their employer is a very good one. eight, social and environmental standards. in contrast to the obsession with lowering costs, binding and constantly evolving minimum standards are needed, with compensatory aid to be given to the countries in the greatest difficulty. nine, it is urgent to democratize the wto, to ensure that each member country has the effective means to participate on an equal footing in the negotiations, to guarantee the transparency of the debates, to involve parliamentarians in the decision-making process. finally, the wto must be integrated into the united nations system and a hierarchy of international law standards must be established giving priority to fundamental rights and, in particular, to international conventions on the rules of international trade. mr president, may the union be inspired by this type of approach and i think that its existential crisis will begin to be nothing more than a bad memory.

mr president, commissioner, the judgment of the court of justice of 13 september 2005 recognises the exclusive competence of the community to adopt criminal sanctions to ensure the effectiveness of community law. it thus enables the union to reaffirm that the protection of its citizens is one of its fundamental principles. it also gives us the opportunity to put an end to a recurrent conflict between the european institutions by clarifying the division of powers between the first and third pillars. the case before the court of justice concerned a directive on environmental protection which included criminal sanctions, and that was the di lello report of the committee on civil liberties. we agree with the european commission's analysis. the consequences of this judgment go far beyond the protection of the environment and are likely to affect all community policies and the fundamental freedoms recognised by the treaty. serious violations of citizens' fundamental rights must be punished by effective, proportionate and dissuasive penal measures. this is what we want for the data retention directive, for example, because it will have a major impact on the privacy of european citizens. one of the major consequences is that the codecision procedure will apply in areas which were previously subject to a procedure of voting by unanimity with the european parliament's simple opinion. the judgment gives the european parliament a decisive role and this strengthening of democratic control is a step forward for democracy as a whole. the commission identified several framework decisions adopted on the wrong legal basis. the definition of such sanctions should be based on community provisions relating to the protection of fundamental rights. i would therefore like to end my remarks by asking the commissioner a specific question: has the commission considered that the framework decision on racism and xenophobia could also benefit from this review?
vice-chairman of the commission . mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank mr roure and mr buitenweg for raising this question, which is of central importance in europe in terms of the legal space in criminal law. i share the approach of both speakers and i assure them that the commission will work to give full effect to this important decision of the court of justice, implementing the principle that, where it is necessary to ensure the effectiveness of community rules, a criminal penalty may be introduced by the community legislator through the codecision procedure, and only with it. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission will of course have to adhere to two main principles when formulating proposals to introduce criminal sanctions: firstly, the need for the criminal law, because criminal penalties can only be introduced when they are necessary; it is a universal principle of law; secondly, the coherence of the various provisions, because once again we must avoid conflicts between criminal provisions which could theoretically lead to serious legal uncertainty if there were no coherence. we have identified some areas where the court's decision can be applied in practice. you will probably be aware that we have decided to bring an action before the court of justice in connection with the framework decision on marine pollution. we did so a few days ago because the time-limits for appeal were not yet expired and we thought it appropriate to give an immediate demonstration by challenging the framework decision on marine pollution before the court of justice, considering it one of the matters in which, instead of the framework decision, a directive containing criminal sanctions should have been adopted. we have also proposed a method for extending this modus operandi to other fields. for example, when a framework decision has already been tabled, without changing the substance of the text, an agreement between parliament, the council and the commission could adopt the correct legal basis and at the same time avoid opening a debate on the substance. such a solution would greatly speed things up. a final answer on the two issues of racism and non-discrimination. i am naturally in favour of legislation which criminalizes at least incitement to racial hatred, and therefore the commission of acts of racism. in this respect, a criminal sanction is certainly necessary, although you will be aware that there is unfortunately still no agreement on the framework decision either. i promised that at the beginning of 2006 i would propose a new initiative on racism and xenophobia to overcome the deadlock that has arisen in the council. article 13 of the treaty can be used to introduce criminal sanctions in cases of discrimination based on race or nationality. the instrument exists, in particular article 13, which is clearly a directive, and therefore a community matter in the first place. in such cases, the commission may also adopt proposals for criminal legislation.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am glad that we can finally decide on mr gollnisch's immunity, because this succession of postponements of our vote has gone on for too long. we have had ample time to assess the facts. i will not go into these specific facts here, but i want to stress that it is entirely right to support mrs wallis' report, which proposes to waive mr gollnisch's immunity for a number of reasons. first and foremost, mr gollnisch did not make the alleged statements as a member of the european parliament. the immunity enjoyed by every member of the european parliament is intended to protect freedom of expression in the exercise of his duties, which is not the case here. immunity is not irresponsibility, just as freedom of speech cannot justify the intolerable. the second reason is that in this case the values of the european union, which we meps are supposed to defend, have been flouted. far from these humanist values, far from them, mr gollnisch, a good pupil of jean-marie le pen, tried to match his master in provocation by the remarks he made at that conference. we must therefore condemn them strongly. finally, the third and final reason is that there is no fumus persecutionis in the argument put forward by mr gollnisch. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the application of the principle of subsidiarity. it is a little short in the face of the extremely shocking words he uttered with full awareness - i am sure - of the blows to our democracy.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament has been calling for a ban on cadmium and a limitation on the use of this heavy material since 1988. in every piece of legislation, for example on end-of-life vehicles or electrical and electronic products, parliament has stressed a simple principle: the use of cadmium must be banned and it must remain where there is no alternative. this is the principle of substitution from the outset, the principle which underlies the reach directive proposal which we mobilised some time ago. as in other sectors, the reach directive excludes batteries, on the grounds that a proper directive must precisely allow parliament's action to be calibrated. i therefore strongly urge that we apply the principle of substitution to cadmium batteries. mr blokland has spoken of the difficulties he has had in making an ambitious point of view prevail and his willingness to compromise is to be commended. we support it. nevertheless, it seems to me that our parliament should be able to accept a simple principle. if there is a technology on the market which offers an alternative to nickel-cadmium batteries or to batteries containing cadmium - whether portable batteries or industrial batteries, for that matter - then we must ban cadmium. mr blokland tried to list what was already available on the market. there are emerging technologies, including nickel-zinc technology for industrial batteries. i therefore propose that you accept amendment no 4 by the socialist group in the european parliament, which proposes that if an alternative technology for industrial batteries appears on the market, a revision of the directive should be initiated. this seems to me to be the minimum minimum to be true to environmental ambition and, above all, to the will to promote technological innovation in the european union.
mr president, i find it attractive to ban nickel-cadmium batteries outright at first sight, but a more detailed analysis leads me to advocate genuine exemptions for the industrial use of these batteries. in particular, the application of accumulators is found in the security and transport sectors, for example aircraft and trains. these batteries are sought after for their reliability to operate under critical conditions, making it difficult to introduce replacement products. the regulations are already very strict. the risks associated with the end of life of these types of batteries are controlled, in particular by ensuring that producers take charge of collection and recycling. i would draw your attention, ladies and gentlemen, to the definitions adopted by the committee on the environment, which give priority to the physical characteristics of the battery over the nature of its use. certain batteries would then de facto fall under the ban, such as those used in respiratory assistance systems for intervention in toxic atmospheres, individual or collective lamps in the mining sector, etc.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the mild climate, the beautiful scenery, the attractive prices and the warm welcome of the people have for years encouraged thousands of europeans to become landlords in the valencia region of spain. to cope with the rapidly growing demand and to combat speculation, the autonomous government of valencia passed an urbanisation law in 1994, the lrau. it is precisely against the application of this law that thousands of petitions are being sent to the european parliament. the petitioners complain about what they believe is an unfair challenge to their property rights due to urban development. criticism is directed both at the substance - the legal, economic and environmental legitimacy of such a project - and at the form - lack of information, transparency, too short a time limit for appeal and too low a compensation amount. they feel helpless in the face of an otherwise very complex situation, since - it should be remembered - the legal and political responsibility in this case is shared between the spanish government, as regards the land law, the autonomous community of valencia, as regards the local legislation on town planning rules, and the municipalities, which, relying on both spanish and regional legislation, implement the programmes they consider legitimate. in order to be better informed of the situation on the ground, the committee on petitions sent a delegation twice, in 2004 and 2005, to inquire about all the parties concerned. as rapporteur, i was part of the second delegation and was very impressed by the large number of petitioners and touched by their speech but also by their confidence in the european response. i also appreciated the attention of the authorities in valencia and their willingness to cooperate. the community of valencia, aware of the problems, is also working on a new law, the luv, which will take into account the demands raised by the petitioners. in the interest of openness, the valencian government has invited the european parliament to make any suggestions it considers necessary. europe is often accused of being far from its citizens, and we have here the opportunity to demonstrate the opposite: the european parliament, through its committee on petitions, is listening to the citizen. the problem is that we cannot go beyond our competence, because we must avoid creating expectations among the citizens that can only be disappointed. as regards the facts and community competence, we therefore ask the european commission to continue to ensure that the tendering procedure is respected and to monitor any breaches of the environmental directives. it has also begun to meet our expectations by opening infringement proceedings against the kingdom of spain on 21 march for failure to comply with the directive on public procurement. we urge the regional government and municipalities to provide all those affected by the lrau with assistance to consider a possible correction and compensation process. we call for the environmental issue, which is crucial for europe's future, to be taken into account in all projects. i thank my colleagues who have been passionate about this subject and who have enriched my initial report, but i remind them that we can only act within the limits of our community competence and that our margin of manoeuvre is narrow. we all react and have reacted according to our temperament and our commitments. some people tend to do a lot, others not enough, i have tried to adopt a middle-of-the-road heard them, that we deplore the situation and that we are not here to judge, but to try to put pressure on them so that they are all heard, respected and that finally a just and fair solution is found. i hope that this report will be successful, that the situation will finally be fair for all and that the committee on petitions will once again prove that we are an important link in the relationship between the citizen and the european parliament.

member of the commission. mr president, the european union can be proud of its achievements in the field of non-discrimination, which place it amongst the most advanced regions in the world in this respect. in 2000, we adopted two key directives: one which outlaws racial discrimination, and another that bans direct and indirect discrimination in employment on the grounds of religion or belief, disability, age or sexual orientation. however, legislation alone is not enough to counter discrimination effectively. many member states are falling behind with their transposition schedules, and where national legislation complies with the european directives, it is unfamiliar to the general public and not properly implemented. the commission has therefore proposed, inter alia, to declare 2007 the european year of equal opportunities for all. it is intended to make the public aware of the benefits of a just society that offers everybody the same opportunities, irrespective of sex, ethnic or racial origin, religion or belief, capacity, age or sexual orientation. it will highlight the benefits of diversity as a source of social and economic vitality, which europe must acknowledge and make use of. this diversity enriches the social fabric of europe and is a vital component of its economic prosperity. the discussions and activities during the year will be organised around three main topics. firstly, the right to equality and protection against discrimination. a key element will be to make the general public aware of the fact that equal treatment does not necessarily mean identical treatment, but that, sometimes, different treatment is required in different situations. secondly, recognition of the positive contribution that everybody, whatever their personal characteristics, makes to society. the aim will be to make the public aware of the rewards and advantages accruing in europe through diversity. thirdly, better representation in society of disadvantaged groups: a debate will be initiated on ways to rectify the underrepresentation and underparticipation of certain groups in society. fourthly, respect and tolerance vis-à-vis and among the various communities that make up european society. civil society and the social partners will be fully involved in implementing the european year. one of the key principles of implementing the year will be that activities will be decentralised at member state level. to get this message across effectively, the year must be implemented as closely as possible to the citizens. finally, it must be ensured that, during the year and in all the member states, equal importance is attached to all the grounds for discrimination set out under article 13 of the treaty, namely discrimination based on sex, ethnic or racial origin, religion or beliefs, disability, age or sexual orientation.
the rapporteur. mr president, there are no institutional barriers between one group and another, and there is nothing to prevent anyone from proving their worth and receiving the prize. specific systems, in the form of examinations or competitions, with diplomas, have been set up to ensure the ability of each individual. access to the most important functions is in principle open to all, without distinction. however, men are not always equal in law. at least, equal opportunities do not seem to be achieved. despite some examples of spectacular social advancement, which are claimed with all the more complacency because they are more exceptional, the chances of success are not equally distributed among all, and if the social organization does not allow everyone to manifest his abilities, it fosters serious germs of frustration and tension. neither efficiency nor justice are involved in this situation. if this is the case, nearly two centuries after the declaration of human rights was adopted, it is not hard to understand why. should we consider that we have no way out? are democratic principles a mirage, or an ideal, that moves further away as we get closer to them? we reject that approach. it is true that inequalities tend to pile up. individuals from modest families are on average less likely to achieve a high level of education. those with a low level of education are less likely to achieve high social status or to pursue a well-paid profession. the number of women in senior positions, whatever they may be, is still very limited, if not insignificant. the predominance remains, as a rule, the prerogative of men. disabled people still do not have the right to a fair place in our societies. homosexuals are still too often discriminated against and some still consider this fact to be normal. the colour of their skin, their ethnic origin, leaves many men, women and children stranded on the roadside. do we have the right to accommodate ourselves to this situation? is it right to consider that nothing can be done to bring reality closer to the democratic ideal? the obstacles seem to be great, inherent in the social organization itself. but it's not by denying them that we're going to overcome them. we must face the truth and expose it. thus, discrimination often leads to unskilled and unstable jobs, which are almost always accompanied by low pay and, consequently, a low standard of living. people who suffer from them have great difficulty in accessing decent housing and health care. they have virtually no chance of promotion through continuing vocational training and their leisure time will be reduced to a minimum. in these circumstances, their children's education is mortgaged from the start. they are deprived of the material, social and emotional conditions which make it possible to build a life project. and there is a great risk that they will end up in the same situation as their parents. in a word, disability calls for disability. if you experience the effects of social inequality in one way, you are likely to experience it in other ways. this phenomenon of cumulative disability, which is intuitively perceptible, has, however, so far been little studied. i would therefore like to ask the council and the commission to make a strong commitment to the fight against all forms of discrimination in all the countries of the union, particularly in the context of the year of equal opportunities. we ask you for that strong commitment, commissioner. we heard what you said earlier. we are pleased with this, but you will understand that we will be very vigilant about the application, and i will conclude by recalling that on 28 august 1963, in washington, in his famous incantation speech i have a dream, martin luther king expressed with emotion the hope, the dream of a world of freedom and justice for all. i have a dream, he said, that my four children will belong to a nation where they will be judged not by the color of their skin, but by their qualities. let us dream together that by the end of the decade we will finally have a union without discrimination, a union which gives every child a chance. let's have a dream together, commissioner.

in writing. the proposed procedure reveals significant legal shortcomings. the procedure is divided into two stages: 1. the first, after an application has been made, the court draws up a european order for payment which is served on the debtor and the latter has a period of three weeks in which to lodge a claim. 2. the secondly, if no claim is made, a european order for payment is issued. the authors justify this double relaxation by the risk that an irreversible security would have to be issued from the outset. it would then seem more appropriate, in order to simplify the procedure and to guarantee the rights of the debtor, to maintain only one stage, that is to say to provide for the issuing of the european order for payment from the outset and to make it enforceable. in return, the opposition period should be extended and run only when the debtor has actually been affected by the notification. that is why we reject amendment no 12, which allows a person to be sentenced without being informed of the decision. finally, the choice between the notary's certificate and the postal delivery as proposed in amendment no 20 must not exist. the act of the bailiff must be imposed in view of the failures of the post office in some countries, such as france.
mr president, parliamentary immunity is intended to protect the freedom of expression of members of parliament. therefore, according to the consistent case law of the legal affairs committee of the european parliament, it is established as a fundamental principle that when the acts of which a member is accused are part of his political activity or are directly related to it, immunity is not waived. this includes, according to the same case law, the expression of opinions, deemed to be political activity, which are expressed at demonstrations, public meetings, in political publications, in the press, in a book, on television, and even in court. in the case of mr gollnisch, there is no doubt that this well-established case law has been circumvented in a partisan way in this house. bruno gollnisch is legally wrong because he is a political minority. your conception of law is one of variable geometry. what are you doing in this place of democratic and legal values and principles? the fact that the parliamentary immunity of our colleague bruno gollnisch has not been defended today means that this house is unworthy of the principles it embodies, unworthy and unjust!

in writing. strangely enough, a fundamental point in the case of our colleague bruno gollnisch, which was present in the first three versions of mrs wallis' report, has disappeared in the last one. this is the fumus persecutionis. it is the presumption that the criminal action is inspired by the intention to harm the political activity of the member. the european parliament has a principle that immunity is not waived when there is a suspicion that the criminal action is motivated by the intention to harm the political activity of the member. however, the evidence of this fumus persecutionis is abundant in this series. this is not a matter of mere conjecture. the intrusion of political power is evident in the person of the then minister of justice, mr perben, who is a direct political opponent of mr gollnisch, since he is a declared candidate in the municipal elections in lyon. he will personally order the prosecution, even though the investigation had cleared mr. gollnisch. the public prosecutor of lyon acknowledged this in a statement published by the press at the time. it is therefore not clear why the rapporteur has excluded this fumus persecutionis. however, it is clear from the facts and circumstances of this case that the measures taken by the judicial authorities are intended to impede the political activity of this member of parliament.

president-in-office of the council. mr president, i shall begin by thanking the european parliament for proposing this timely debate on tunisia. i would like to record our appreciation of tunisia’s recent hosting of the united nations world summit on the information society from 16 to 18 november. we welcome the summit’s agreement to the tunis commitment and the tunis agenda for the information society, an important contribution to the global effort needed to bridge what is known as the digital divide. at the same time, it is right for us to consider more generally the issues of human rights and freedom of the press in tunisia. the council shares the concerns of members of this house about the human rights situation in tunisia and is well aware of the shortcomings in tunisia’s performance, particularly with respect to acts of intimidation and harassment by the authorities against civil society and human rights activists. the meeting convened on thursday, 1 december, involving meps, certain committees and other eu institutions involved in the summit, specifically to discuss human rights concerns in tunisia, further highlighted the importance of these issues. human rights is an essential element in the eu’s relationship with tunisia, as set out in the eu-tunisia association agreement, which came into force on 1 march 1998, and the european neighbourhood policy action plan which came into force on 4 july this year. under its action plan, tunisia has signed up to commitments in the area of democracy, good governance and human rights. implementing these commitments will be an essential element in developing eu-tunisia relations. they include, for example, the establishment of an eu-tunisia subcommittee on human rights. to this end we continue to urge the tunisians to establish and hold a first session of a human rights subcommittee as soon as possible. in addition to this, the euromed tenth anniversary summit on 27 and 28 november in barcelona represented an important opportunity to help the eu’s mediterranean partners, including tunisia, to address the challenges of the 21st century, including in relation to good governance. at the euromed summit, leaders endorsed an outcome-oriented five-year work plan. that plan included the creation of a governance facility to help those countries that make progress on good governance, allowing them access to additional funds to spend on their priorities. tunisia is a state party to the six core united nations human rights treaties. tunisia scores well on most socio-economic indexes of multilateral institutions, and social and economic rights are recognised and protected. tunisia plays an active role within international human rights institutions and was elected to the united nations commission on human rights in april 2004. tunisia has not yet, however, signed the rome statute of the international criminal court. the eu welcomes tunisia’s record of promoting reform in the arab world, notably on the position of women and the right to education. however, the eu remains concerned about the human rights situation in tunisia, particularly in relation to freedom of expression and assembly and the independence of the judiciary. this debate has raised in particular the issue of the freedom of the press in tunisia. all books and publications, with the exception of newspapers, are still subject to censorship. until may 2005, all newspapers had to clear articles with the ministry of the interior in advance of publication. whilst this is no longer the case, we remain concerned that the fear of reprisals appears to have resulted in some self-censorship, as no newspaper offers any political criticism or opinion on domestic issues contrary to the government’s view. access to foreign television, however, is common, as most tunisian households have access to satellite television. as i already made clear, the eu welcomes the agreement on the tunis commitment and the tunis agenda for the information society reached at the world summit on the information society in tunis. the eu looks forward to working with all stakeholders to ensure the full and effective implementation of both stages of the summit process, both on substance and on follow-up. a number of incidents involving freedom of expression and freedom of assembly were reported in the run-up to and during the summit itself. the tunisian human rights league, the oldest human rights body in tunisia, claimed police harassment of its activists and says that it has been prevented from functioning properly. a court decision in september 2005 postponed its congress. the eu consequently made representations to the tunisian authorities and issued a statement reminding the tunisians of the eu’s expectations of its human rights responsibilities. during the summit itself, the eu troika made representations to the tunisian authorities following an incident at the goethe institute, where ngos were prevented from meeting to discuss plans for an alternative ‘citizens’ summit’. the eu is also concerned about a number of other incidents involving freedom of expression and freedom of assembly, also reported during the summit. these include the disruption of the activities of a belgian tv crew, as well as the disruption of the european commission workshop for meps to meet members of civil society in the summit’s conference centre. tunisia’s constitution provides for freedom of association, but within certain defined limits. the law provides for freedom of assembly, as long as a permit is obtained from the minister of interior. however, some ngos experience difficulties in renting space and the control of funding. a number of associations have applied for legal status and have been refused, for example the national council for liberties in tunisia. ngos also report that internet access is routinely blocked and e-mails addressed to certain e-mail accounts never reach the intended recipient. during the presidential campaign of october 2004, the electoral code prohibited tunisians from discussing politics in the international press, and opposition parties were given little opportunity to campaign. whilst recognising that the election law safeguards female representation in parliament as well as the representation of minority views, we noted that the overall process leading to the elections did not provide a level playing field for contenders. we therefore encourage the tunisian authorities to continue to improve the framework for elections and to take the necessary steps to ensure that the next elections fully meet international standards. the eu is also concerned by reports from ngos, including amnesty international, about prison conditions in tunisia. these reports state that overcrowding in prisons and discriminatory treatment of political prisoners continue as well as a lack of basic medical care, poor hygiene, torture and ill-treatment. we therefore welcome the fact that since june 2005 tunisia’s authorities have allowed the international committee of the red cross access to prisons. earlier this year, the tunisian authorities announced their intention to allow human rights watch representatives access to prisons in a similar way to that of the international committee of the red cross, although no timeframe was specified. the minister for justice and human rights also announced that the practice of detaining prisoners in solitary confinement beyond 10 days, the maximum allowed under the constitution, would cease. the eu welcomes these announcements and hopes that both undertakings will be put into practice. i should also like to say a few words about the judiciary in tunisia. under its constitution, it is independent. however, amnesty international and others report that the authorities interfere in the judicial process. the trial in april 2005 of a lawyer and member of the national council for civil liberties in tunisia, mohamed abou, who wrote an article criticising tunisia’s president ben ali, seems to support this contention. the tunisian magistrates’ association has complained of increased intimidation by the government after its board issued a communiqué criticising the attack on abou. the public prosecutor closed the tunisian magistrates’ association’s office in august. a law passed on 12 august 2005 making provision for the statute of magistrates does not take into consideration earlier calls by the tunisian magistrates’ association concerning terms and conditions of service and would appear to weaken its position. we also note that despite several requests to visit, the united nations special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers has yet to receive an invitation from the tunisian government. the eu wishes to work with tunisia to support the modernisation of its judiciary. the eu has provided money through meda to fund a project that will support this work and hopes to see progress on this. i am sure that the commission will want to say something about this. in conclusion, the eu welcomes the agreements reached at the world summit on the information society as an important contribution to the global effort to bridge the digital divide. in terms of the eu’s relationship with tunisia itself, we wish to see tunisia maintain and develop its security and prosperity. we regret the serious restrictions on freedom of expression and association and the incidents which occurred prior to and during the world summit on the information society. the council should like to assure honourable members that the eu will continue to express its concern over specific human rights violations and to impress on the tunisian authorities the need for full respect for human rights and democratic principles. it is now time for us to look forward to the implementation by the tunisian authorities of the commitments made by president ben ali on democracy, good governance and human rights set out in the european neighbourhood policy action plan. implementation of these commitments will be an essential element in developing eu-tunisia relations.

this adjustment phase and has therefore proposed accompanying measures. before drafting the proposal for a regulation on accompanying measures for sugar protocol countries, the commission had produced strengthening alternative economic activities. social and environmental litigation measures are also included. i congratulate the rapporteur, mr lehideux, on his commitment and very constructive president-in-office of the council. mr president, i welcome the informed and thought provoking-debate that has taken place this afternoon on this important issue for the european union. the interventions we have heard have reinforced the importance of enlargement in my mind and underlined the benefits it brings to candidate countries and indeed the wider member states. as in our previous debate, honourable members’ points and questions went to the heart of the issue and raised some interesting issues for us to consider about romania and bulgaria’s accession processes and the wider policy of enlargement. given the constraints of time, i shall limit my concluding remarks to a few of the points that were addressed directly by honourable members. mr tannock and mr belder mentioned the issue of corruption and, in particular, concern in relation to border guards and the security thereof. both countries certainly face major challenges in tackling corruption, and bulgaria, in particular, must step up the fight against organised crime. the new governments have demonstrated a real commitment to tackle these problems and we have seen some progress, but there is still a long way to go. it is right to acknowledge that before this house today. in romania examples of progress include: a new head of the anti-corruption department in the general prosecutor’s office; 11 new senior prosecutors removed for ineffectiveness; and 22 cases of corruption by former and current senators and deputies now under way. in relation to the further work that romania has undertaken, border police and customs have dismissed large numbers of senior border and customs officers at several posts for ineffectiveness and corruption. but let us be very clear: there is considerable and important progress that needs to be made on these important points. mr beglitis and mr tannock also mentioned the issue international adoption, a point that was then touched upon by ms mcguinness in a later contribution to the debate. corruption in international adoption has been clearly a problem. recent measures have been introduced to protect the interests of the child, as we have heard from a number of speakers, to improve domestic child protection and family facilities and to reduce the numbers of institutionalised children, in line with the united nations convention on the rights of the child and european union norms. in relation to the specific question as to why the romanian government is blocking pre-arranged adoptions, for example to the united states, a number of the so-called pipeline cases, which have been mentioned in the course of contributions to this debate, relate to requests made during the period of the 2001 to 2004 moratorium on international adoption. the romanian authorities set up a group of experts in june 2005, who are working through the files of the children concerned, to analyse each specific case and to look for solutions within the context of the legislation currently in force. ms mcguinness, ms sbarbati and ms de groen-kouwenhoven also mentioned children in the wider sense and asked what is being done in relation to the treatment of children in both of these countries. we are certainly concerned about the plight of institutionalised children whose living conditions are generally inadequate in both of these countries. more work is needed to improve conditions, but we are encouraged by both governments’ recent actions. for example, in the case of bulgaria, the government has established six regional offices of the state agency for child protection since early 2005 to take forward improvements. it has started to implement a new action plan to close old state care homes. in the case of romania, the government is working hard to take children out of care homes and move them in with foster parents or relatives. it has closed almost all of the 85 large, old-style institutions for children and replaced them with modern child protection alternatives. since 2000, it has reduced the number of children in care homes from 37 000 down to the present figure of 32 000. mr piotrowski suggested – on a different matter entirely, but one that it is apposite to respond to, not least given the timing of this debate – that the presidency’s proposals on the financial perspective for 2007 to 2013 could not accommodate romania and bulgaria and failed to meet the criteria for solidarity. i do not accept either charge. on romania and bulgaria, our proposals fully respect their allocations under the accession agreements and provide for a historic shift of spending towards the new member states and accession states and offer them greater flexibility as to how to distribute those european union funds to the greatest possible effect. that historic shift in funding, which includes significant cuts in receipts for the united kingdom, shows why our proposals are all about solidarity, which featured prominently in his remarks. there is no virtue in repeating the word ‘solidarity’, while avoiding the difficult challenge of finding the common ground on which both net contributors and net recipients can meet in the course of the coming hours and coming days. in relation to both bulgaria and romania, i would recognise that significant progress towards european union accession on 1 january 2007 has been made, but more work needs to be undertaken. the commission, under the capable leadership of commissioner rehn, will continue to monitor progress closely and will produce a follow-up report in april or may next member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the members for the substantive and substantive debate and the weighty speeches. it is also good that the speakers emphasized that we are now talking about completing the last, the fifth, round of enlargement. this is in addition to the historic breakthrough that was triggered by the fall of the berlin wall more than 15 years ago. i believe that the commission and the european parliament and the presidency, in view of the weighty speech by mr alexander, are looking at the accession preparations for bulgaria and romania in much the same way and with the same emphasis. in particular, the reform of the judiciary is absolutely necessary. it is essential for the legal security of citizens in bulgaria and romania, it is essential for the economic dynamics and foreign investment, and it is also essential for the implementation of eu law in these countries. we have a responsibility to assess objectively and fairly whether these countries are ready in this respect to join the union in 2007. the same applies to administrative reform, in particular the fight against corruption and crime, and the elimination of problems in the field of agriculture and food security. the coming months will be very crucial for both countries. both countries have the opportunity to join in 2007, but only if both countries do their utmost and take the challenge fully seriously. i trust there is no ambiguity in this matter, but in case of any confusion, i will repeat my message. the key is not a charm offensive in the capitals of the eu countries, but a determined practical action to bring about reforms in the judiciary and administration and to fight corruption and crime in a very determined way. i would not like to be in a position in the spring to have to propose security clauses on behalf of the commission, but it should be noted that they have not been included in the accession treaties for the sake of entertainment. this possibility should be taken seriously in bulgaria and romania, and every effort should be made to achieve membership eligibility so that both countries can join in january 2007. we will assess this capacity in the light of the facts in a completely objective manner. the commission will support reforms in bulgaria and romania, monitor developments and present to parliament and the council in due course an assessment of this progress. it is important to stress that we need a regular dialogue, as the chairman of the committee on foreign affairs, elmar brok, among others, has said. i suggest that we come back to this during the spring, when we will have a more precise picture of how bulgaria and romania have progressed in their efforts to achieve membership eligibility at the beginning of 2007.
in spring 2006, the european commission will present to the council its final opinion on the accession of bulgaria and romania in january 2007. these accessions will depend on their ability to fulfil the commitments entered into in the accession treaty. if not, the safeguard clauses providing for the postponement of accession to 2008 may be activated. although the reports on the level of preparedness of romania and bulgaria respectively underline the importance of the progress made, particularly in the area of market economy, it is clear that the pace of reforms needs to be stepped up, particularly for romania, in order to strengthen the administrative and judicial system, the fight against corruption, roma integration and border control. there are also worrying delays in the implementation of the acquis communautaire in the fields of agriculture, public procurement and the environment. this enlargement will present the european union with a double challenge: not to disappoint the romanian and bulgarian citizens who have high hopes for this accession, and at the same time to explain to our citizens, at a time when the european union is going through a major political and budgetary crisis, the justification for this enlargement - rejected by a large part of public opinion.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the machinery directive we are discussing here is a revision of a directive, as you said, dating back to 1998. this is a highly technical subject, but one which will have a major impact on the european machine industry and on the european economy as a whole. i would like to recall the figures mr verheugen has already quoted, which are even better than the ones i had. i cannot help but recall that the annual turnover of the profession is 402 billion euros, of which 113 billion euros are exported to third countries. the first reading reflected a reasonable compromise reached after years of debate. the very definition of a machine and a quasi-machine, as i recall, required a strong mobilization during the previous mandate. in the second reading, i focused on the provisions of the directive on ce marking, as i felt that the wording was not legally clear. i thank the council for accepting my amendment, but i am glad that the commission is working on this subject, which still needs further study. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the way he has conducted the negotiations. we have made considerable progress towards a common position thanks to an informal trilogue bringing together the chairman of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, the fictitious rapporteurs, the representatives of the european commission and those of the council. we have reached a consensus that all professionals expect. there are still some points to be clarified, particularly with regard to tractors, but i remain optimistic and hope that the problems will be solved by the effective application of this directive. as a result, the alde group will vote for the compromise.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, fisheries - like agriculture - is not a sector like any other. fisheries play a part in shaping the quality of life at european level, coastal safety and environmental protection. in many cases, when it is small-scale, fishing even helps to boost tourism. it should be stressed that the fishing community plays a major role. their passionate work is demanding, hard, dangerous, and their pay is subject to too many uncertainties. often in debt, victims of the continuous rise in gasoline prices, fishermen and their families live in fear of not being able to make ends meet and losing their jobs. the community's fisheries policy has not helped to relieve them of their anxieties. on the contrary, it has contributed to the disappearance of the activity of thousands of artisanal fishermen and to the social insecurity of fishing seamen, without obtaining any clear results in terms of conservation of resources. worse, this policy has often given the impression of being subject to the law of lobbies, more concerned with cultivating their media image and chasing subsidies than working seriously on environmental protection. that is why, commissioner, fishermen are tired of being constantly suspected of being sea-dealers by a european commission which, on the contrary, is very complacent about the real sea-dealers, the flags of complacency. mr commissioner, contrary to the prejudices of your scientific circle, no one is more committed to the preservation of fisheries resources than fishing seamen. it is their livelihood, their heritage and the future of their children. it is more than enough that quotas for fishing quantities and days are set, often without any real scientific basis, and that the states sell each other, despite common sense, in establishing fishing zones. the commission must no longer favour fishermen of certain nationalities to the detriment of others. everyone must be on an equal footing within europe. i am sure that your text makes some progress in this area, and that it is formally intended to involve all the parties concerned, but i think it is vague and timid. we cannot save fisheries and fishery resources without fishermen and their professional and trade union organisations. the fishermen, through their representatives, must be fully involved in all decisions affecting them. the union must also provide financial assistance to member states to protect their territorial waters against piracy. i am thinking in particular of the territorial waters in the peripheral regions of the union. while there is a real problem of financing a fair, sustainable and bold european fisheries policy, let us not forget that one of the threats to resources is pollution caused by maritime transport. behind this pollution is the flag of convenience system. so let us put the blame for this permanent ecological disaster on the shoulders of those responsible and we shall have the means to embark on a truly ambitious policy.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to confirm the withdrawal of amendment no 9, which called for the amount of 40 million euro to be increased to 80 million. not only do i want to confirm this withdrawal, but i want to take responsibility for it. the committee on development unanimously adopted this amendment and i thank the members of the committee very much for their foresight and support. but the council has refused to make any gesture towards the acp countries, despite the positive position and action of the british presidency, to which i can testify. the commission, for its part, has not moved a hair. the system, which was blocked by the budget debate in this parliament, did the rest and carried the bottleneck. but, mr president, for imperative reasons of timetable, this regulation must be adopted at first reading. so we took our responsibility and withdrew the 9th amendment, which called for 80 million. i am obliged, ladies and gentlemen, for the reasons i have just mentioned, to ask you to vote on this report, in line with your budgetary votes. however, in order to tell the acp countries that some of them are not forgotten here, i ask that my name be removed from this text and i propose to my colleagues in the committee on development and cooperation, and to them alone, to cast a symbolic vote in the final vote: a negative vote.
mr president, i would simply ask for a purely formal correction to paragraph 6 of the draft compromise resolution, namely to replace the last sentence in the last part of the resolution beginning with 'in order to' at the end of the first part, that is to say after 'association council', to reinstate the text on which we have reached agreement. i would also ask that in paragraphs where it is simply mentioned 'the summit' 'the isms' be added in parentheses, in order to be consistent with the resolution as a whole, so that there is no confusion if this text is quoted in a separate paragraph. finally, i would like to thank the members of the various groups who have extended the subject of this resolution to the conclusions of the summit. i would like to say how important this resolution is after the sakharov prize and after i said yesterday in this parliament that we must link the fundamental freedom of expression and freedom of the press to all our actions, especially when we have agreements with friendly countries.
in writing. the 2006 budget is the last of the 2000/2006 financial perspective and also the last before the accession of romania and bulgaria on 1 january 2007. in short, three points: the share of agriculture and rural development in the total budget is now only 43%, which takes away from the british a strong argument that the cap is too expensive. secondly, whatever the european parliament and the commission may say, the budget is growing steadily and unchecked: the increase in payment appropriations is 5.4%, higher than that of all national budgets. finally, the agreement reached between the council and parliament is the result of a disgraceful bargaining process negotiated behind the backs of the european citizens: the council got what it wanted on the cfsp; in return, parliament has preserved its priorities: culture, youth, the environment or federalist propaganda. the only one who is not satisfied with this budget is the european taxpayer, whose taxes are being increased to pay for, among other things, his country's financial contribution to the european union. france paid in 2005: €16.7 billion. what will happen in 2006 in a union of 25 until something better comes along?
in writing. the objective set by the council and the european parliament in this area, namely the principle of an integrated service to facilitate access to air transport for disabled passengers and passengers with reduced mobility, is not only commendable but indispensable because action was urgently needed. the disparity in situations and treatment, whether in access to airports or in the assistance provided between airports and airlines, is striking. whether it is the companion who has no place next to the person with reduced mobility, the lack of medical equipment on board and on the ground such as electric wheelchairs or the lack of disability training for airport staff, it can only be seen that the principle of equality between all passengers is not respected in the same way in all european airports and airlines. i am also pleased to note that the efforts which will have to be made by the various airlines and airports should not entail any specific additional costs for disabled persons or persons with reduced mobility. it's the least i can do.
in writing. i see a double injustice in the reform of the common organization of the sugar market under way. ' - firstly for european producers themselves, since it is the large multinational sugar consumers of the nestlé type that are likely to be the main beneficiaries of the reform. the small producers could suffer from the 31% fall in guaranteed prices. 2 - but above all, this reform is unfair to the poor sugar-producing countries. once again, we're making them pay the price. the numbers speak for themselves. european producers can count on a €1.5 billion compensation package and €4.2 billion for restructuring the sector, while the acp countries have only €40 million available for the time being. that's an indecent amount. we had proposed 80 million euros in the committee on development. the lehideux report mitigates some of the adverse effects of the reform of the sugar regime in the eu by proposing: - to make aid complementary to the other financial instruments of eu development policy; - measures to diversify the economy of countries heavily dependent on sugar such as the caribbean island states or mauritius.
in writing. the lehideux report is a catalogue of good feelings that leads to nothing concrete, except for financial support of 40 million euros in 2006. the 18 acp countries, which are signatories to the sugar protocol, export 1.6 million tonnes of cane sugar to the european union at community prices each year. the reduction in sugar prices of 36% over four years adopted by the council will lead to an equivalent reduction in their export earnings. for countries as poor as swaziland and malawi, it is a blow to the wto that it forces the european union to reform its sugar sector at the request of brazil. as the acp countries rightly say, the reform is too rapid and too deep. in reality, the only winner will be brazil, the world's largest exporter of cane sugar, which will take advantage of this to increase its export market shares to the detriment of the acp countries. at a time when the wto is discussing the development cycle, the european union is setting a very bad example for africa, even though the 'everything but arms' initiative is trying to hide our divisions and our selfishness. this reform of the sugar cmo will make their poverty worse with all the immigration consequences one can imagine.
in writing. i can only welcome the extension of the fisheries agreement between the ec and seychelles, the first agreement negotiated under the partnership agreements. this agreement is an opportunity for all and a benefit for all:- it will allow community vessels to have access to seychelles' fisheries resources in a transparent and regulated manner;- in return, the financial compensation paid by the eu will be of great support to the coastal population by facilitating the development of certain key economic sectors, such as the processing industry or port services. - i would add that the agreement provides for the possibility of increasing the community financial compensation in accordance with the volume of catches. for these reasons i support this report wholeheartedly. the only shadow in the picture is the lack of consideration for the european parliament. it is not normal that we have had to wait almost a year for the text of the protocol to be transmitted, and this for technical and administrative reasons. i hope that in future the european parliament will be better associated and also more involved throughout the follow-up of this agreement. let's hope it's not just wishful thinking.
in writing. the commission's legislative programme for 2006 illustrates a certain conception of europe which is now outdated: - an anti-democratic europe, seeking to impose a constitution that the french and dutch have rejected by means of a subterfuge of a 'd' plan; - a europe without borders, open to global immigration, allowing in particular the hundreds of thousands of illegal immigrants legalised in spain and italy to settle in the other member states; - an anti-social europe, which, by implementing the ultra-liberal lisbon strategy, relocates our companies, dismantles our labour law (the bolkestein directive, which chirac had ensured in april that it was buried, will be put back under our assembly); - a europe without identity, which, by opening accession negotiations with turkey, an asian and muslim state, will soon have only a european name; - an anti-national europe, which dissolves our nations into a bureaucratic superstate. today our peoples do not need just another legislative programme, but another europe, based on what constitutes its identity: the freedom of its nations and the genius of its civilization.
in writing. the european union must publicly condemn the violations of human rights and press freedom in tunisia so that tunisian public opinion knows it. the tunisian regime is content with a diplomacy of the corridor, to ignore the increasingly worrying situation of the 401 political prisoners, the 5 political parties not allowed to speak freely to tunisian citizens, the many associations that cannot freely carry out their activities. these lawyers, journalists, workers, intellectuals are being suppressed, muzzled. let us, for once, speak directly to the tunisian people and tell them that the european parliament will not fall into the trap set by ben ali: to continue to show indulgence towards a dictatorship that is not even hiding anymore.
in writing. the european commission's initial proposal envisaged a ban on state aid to enterprises in france from 2007. this project, like that of the bolkestein directive, is part of the establishment of a highly competitive internal market, decided at the barcelona summit, where france was represented by mr chirac and mr jospin. the report by mr koterec makes some improvements: france will still be able to grant state aid, but it will be greatly reduced. european regional policy, largely paid for by french taxpayers, is therefore not content to be increasingly weak in relation to our regions (the french hainaut region has thus lost the structural funds under objective 1). by preventing france from having an independent industrial policy, it is now jeopardising the existence of hundreds of companies which, in the absence of specific public aid, will have to relocate their activities or close down. this europe, this europe which produces unemployed people, which is anti-social because it is anti-national, was rejected by our compatriots on 29 may. they want a different europe, a europe which respects national sovereignty, which will respect work.
mr president, we abstained on the joint resolution on the covert transfer of prisoners suspected of islamic terrorism by cia agents. without taking a position on the substance, we believe that if protests are to be raised against such practices, if they have actually taken place, they must come from the governments of the member states, some of which are allies of the united states of america. but we also consider, and i want to make this very clear, that the situation is abnormal. the law exists, even for those who violate it in the most brazen way, namely terrorists. it is totally contrary to our traditions that people are confined without access to the outside world and without the possibility of defending themselves. one of two things: either the prisoners of the united states of america are considered prisoners of war and must be treated as such, that is to say, receive regular visits from the red cross and be released at the end of hostilities, - i am thinking in particular of the prisoners of war who were captured in afghanistan - or they are considered common criminals in view of the facts against them and therefore must be able to be defended by lawyers, have the opportunity to defend themselves and know the charges against them. this is the foundation of our civilization. we must not allow terrorism to destroy these fundamental values of ours!

mr president, i hope that this empty chamber does not reflect our lack of interest in what happens in russia, however understandable the situation is here on a thursday afternoon. what happens in russia is in our interests; its interests are our interests. sadly, the clock in russia is now being turned back nearly to soviet times. there is, at the moment, no independent judiciary, there is no free television, and the political opposition has been totally marginalised. i will not even talk about what is happening in chechnya; human life is very cheap there. regarding ngos, what happens to them is another link in this far too long chain of sad events in russia. we cannot be the victim of the ‘nimby’ syndrome: not in my back yard. indeed, it is all in our back yard. it concerns us all. old habits die very hard in the soviet union, but we have to help russia to come back towards democracy and universal values. first of all, it is in the interests of the russian people: they deserve liberty, democracy and transparent governance. we also cannot work with a partner who does not adhere to international rules. we have to help russia become a confident nation which sees that there is no conflict between strength and a democratic, thriving civil society. we have to speak with one voice; otherwise, we reduce our position to something insignificant. we cannot have a good christmas, we cannot have a good conscience, if we do not see what is happening to our near neighbour.
